Sports.title: Anthony Joshua reveals that Tyson Fury's estranged uncle has joined his camp ahead of £150m mega-fight as Gypsy King claims: 'I've not spoken to him for years'
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua made the startling revelation that he has joined forces with Tyson Fury's uncle, Peter, ahead of their eagerly-anticipated super-fight in Cardiff in December.

Never has the calling of a sporting press conference agitated as much, if not more, attention than the event itself.

Without putting Fury and Joshua into the same room in London on Wednesday evening there would have been no chance of them sharing a ring in Cardiff two months from now.

Never has a promo prompted so many startling revelations, either. We might never have known that Fury’s estranged uncle is advising AJ on how to prevent Tyson beating him. Traveller families are usually bonded by such fierce loyalties that we can only wonder about the tensions around the camp fire.

‘Not to worry,’ said the Gypsy King about the defection. ‘I haven’t spoken to him for years.’

Nor might we have learned that Joshua took a mind-blowing pay cut in order to haul the Battle of Britain back home from the clutches of New York.

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Tyson Fury’s ticket-selling appearances

How much of a purse deduction? ‘Twelve figures’ declared his promoter Eddie Hearn. That’s £10million at least.

AJ shrugged and cited another fringe benefit picked up during the maelstrom of doubt as to whether this fight between a pair of British world heavyweight champions would ever take place. He also added Fury’s former trainer Ben Davison to his team.

Joshua said: ‘Ben’s pinpointing details which will make the difference on the night.’

Fury replied: ‘Ben can’t put muscles on that suspect chin.’

He could not resist reminding everyone that Davison has just returned from Las Vegas where he presided over Conor Benn’s two-round devastation by America’s great Latin hope, Ryan Garcia.

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Fury’s ticket-selling appearances.

Instead he advertised ‘probably the greatest fight boxing’s ever seen if you factor in the commercial aspect'.

Which includes the US$150million split equally between the two of them as they put an end to 12 years of public waiting for this fight.

Joshua said: ‘Both of us want to do British boxing proud.’

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles with Fury inviting Joshua to ‘a pint of Guinness as soon as the fight over, win lose or draw'.

Well, they are ten weeks away from them putting on their fight faces.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo WALKS OUT on Portugal: Star, 41, leaves camp after missing training again amid row with manager and vows to 'tell the truth' in cryptic statement
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo WALKS OUT on Portugal: Star, 41, leaves camp after missing training again amid row with manager and vows to 'tell the truth' in cryptic statement

Cristiano Ronaldo has sensationally left Portugal's training camp as his row with manager Jorge Jesus reached boiling point on Wednesday.

The star, 41, said in a statement on Instagram that he was heading home as a result of Jesus's comments in a tense press conference.

Jesus said there were 'no issues' with the player despite tensions between the two over his decision to leave Ronaldo on the bench for the entirety of their 2-1 win over Norway on Sunday.

The Portugal boss also admitted the player was 'angry' with him but refused to confirm whether the country's leading goalscorer would start the clash with Denmark on Thursday.

Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach’s press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp.

'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.

Após a conferência de imprensa do Selecionador Nacional, e no seguimento de uma conversa com o Presidente da Federação Portuguesa de Futebol, tomei a decisão de deixar o estágio da Seleção Nacional.



A seu tempo, direi a verdade a todos os Portugueses sobre as razões que… pic.twitter.com/j8Qrws9KTS — Cristiano Ronaldo (@Cristiano) September 30, 2026

Cristiano Ronaldo has confirmed he has left Portugal's camp amid a row with Jorge Jesus

'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.'

Portugal responded with a statement of their own, which read: 'Cristiano Ronaldo has left the national team camp. Our preparations for the next games continue with our 24 players with maximum focus on the results.'

Ronaldo had held showdown talks with Jesus in the morning, in addition to the head of the Portuguese FA following being an unused substitute in the win over Norway.

It was the first time in 18 years that Ronaldo has not featured at all for Portugal – aside from injury or suspension absences.

At full-time on Sunday, Ronaldo stormed straight down the tunnel and did not return to thank the travelling fans alongside his team-mates.

Jesus had originally planned to bring on the veteran striker for a 30-minute cameo but then decided to leave him on the bench.

Reports in Portugal claimed the talks between Ronaldo and Jesus were 'calm and cordial', but his decision to leave the squad suggests otherwise.

The shocking move means that Ronaldo will not be involved in his country's next game against Denmark.

Footage of the moment Ronaldo left the team camp has emerged on social media

It is an inauspicious start to the relationship between Jesus and Ronaldo, who opted not to retire from international duty after the World Cup.

Only a week ago, Ronaldo reiterated his commitment to the cause, saying: 'I had a conversation with our president, with our coach (about his future).

'I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want, and will finish when I feel like I'm not doing anything here.

'I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football.

'This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.'

Ronaldo will turn 42 in February and has scored three goals in five games for Al-Nassr so far in the Saudi Pro League this season.

Jesus and Ronaldo worked together successfully for a year when the 72-year-old was in charge of Al-Nassr but they could be on a collision course if the forward's playing time remains limited.

The 41-year-old was an unused substitute in Portugal's game with Norway on Sunday

Roberto Martinez stepped down after Portugal's 1-0 World Cup defeat by Spain and when Jesus was announced as his successor, he was asked the Ronaldo question.

Jesus insisted: 'As long as he's playing and is in a condition to be selected, I will pick him, within certain limits and under the conditions that I consider best for the national team.'

Goncalo Ramos, 25, scored the winner against Norway on Sunday and is considered by many to be the natural evolution up front for Portugal.

But it seems as long as Ronaldo is around the national side, the five-time Ballon d'Or winner's playing demands will continue to be an issue for the new boss.

Sports.title: Why would the likes of Erling Haaland and Marc Guehi stay at Man City when they have been lied to and betrayed? Footballers have morals and it would be hard to blame them if they now wanted out, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Why would the likes of Erling Haaland and Marc Guehi stay at Man City when they have been lied to and betrayed? Footballers have morals and it would be hard to blame them if they now wanted out, writes IAN LADYMAN

After full-time in Prague on Tuesday night, the message from the Football Association arrived pretty quickly. Neither the England manager Thomas Tuchel nor any of the players about to walk through the interview area at the Fortuna Arena would be answering any questions about Manchester City.

Eventually, however, reality will catch up with the likes of Elliot Anderson, Marc Guehi, Nico O’Reilly and the 166 other players who have represented City in the Premier League since they were first found to have been trampling all over spending rules back in 2009-2010.

This, sadly, is a matter from which nobody who wore the club’s pale blue shirt in their era of monotonous on-field success will ever be able to hide.

Not Yaya Toure, who sat and talked to the media on a sofa in the plush environs of a Hoboken hotel after being introduced as the club’s highest-paid player during City’s pre-season tour of America in the summer of 2010. Toure had just been lured from Barcelona and, understandably, the money had played a part.

Not Sergio Aguero, scorer of City’s most famous goal at the denouement of the 2011-2012 season. Not David Silva or John Stones, who both gave 10 years of service. And now, not even Erling Haaland.

City’s acolytes will argue that the club’s recent achievements – such as the 2023 Treble – should be viewed differently given that the club is accused of breaking the regulations only up until 2018. They will say that the 15 trophies won between then and now are ‘clean’.

The FA made it clear that Manchester City players such as Marc Guehi would not be answering questions on the 115 charges while on international duty

Why would Erling Haaland (right) stay when the club - and executives like Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) - have been proved wrong in their defiance on the charges?

But where did the money come from to lay the platform for all that glory? Would Pep Guardiola and his team have been able to win so relentlessly without the years of ill-gotten investment that had previously been ploughed into a playing squad that was eventually to run rivals such as Liverpool and Arsenal into the dust with such monotony?

The answers to the questions are clear and that is why so many City players from both past and present will wear the stain of their club’s dishonesty like so many modern footballers wear a sleeve of tattoos.

And that is one of the great sporting tragedies of this miserable catalogue of City sinning. Institutional skullduggery is always like this. It doesn’t just bring down the architects. The fall-out crushes the innocents too.

Senior City executives will carry the weight of their wrong-doing for a lifetime but so too will the club’s supporters and players.

They are the ones who have been able to pretend for so long that none of this was true, that none of it would ever be proven, that it was all part of a campaign by the established Premier League clubs to keep City in their traditional place some way down the hierarchy of relevance. This, after all, is what their club was telling them.

But now that the truth is known, it leaves City’s players in a quite dreadful spot, one in which no sportsman or woman should ever be placed.

For if sport is not honest and fair then it loses its legitimacy. If sport is not honest, achievements pale to nothingness. So as City players past and present look now at their medals and awards in their cabinets at home, they may just see them start to rust.

The likes of Toure and Aguero and Silva and Stones have no choice but to somehow make peace with it all. None of this was their doing.

The likes of Sergio Aguero may start to look at the medals in their trophy cabinet at home a little differently in light of the verdict

Why would Elliot Anderson – a young Geordie raised on the sporting values of the North East’s great Wallsend Boys Club – not question the wisdom of turning down other interested clubs?

Footballers are not stupid but they know their place. They are paid to play. They will perhaps take solace from the fact that out there on the grass, battle was always fought gamely and fairly. Those memories will remain and sustain them to a degree.

As for the modern group, preparing for a clash with Liverpool of all people on the resumption of the Premier League a week on Sunday, what motive is there now to remain at the club that has effectively been lying to them just as much as it has been to the rest of us?

Haaland had suitors from all across Europe when he signed for City in May 2022. We know this because City told us at the time. It was a coup, they said. It was proof of the club’s modern standing and power.

The great Norwegian has repaid that £50million transfer fee spectacularly in the four years that have followed. The goal tally sits at 169 and counting across all competitions. He has done his bit.

But everywhere he goes now, the whiff of this week’s judgement will follow. This is a crime that is not of his making but his achievements now stand as tainted – they will say – and who is to say they are not correct? With that in mind, why would Haaland not feel betrayed? Why would he stay?

Why would Anderson – a young Geordie raised on the sporting values of the North East’s great Wallsend Boys Club – not question the wisdom of turning down other interested clubs when he left Nottingham Forest last summer?

Why would Guehi – a player of deep Christian faith – not look back and ask himself why he didn’t move to Liverpool as had originally been the plan?

Footballers have a remarkable ability to leave the serious stuff in the dressing room when they run out to play. It’s part of the mental strength that enables them to operate under such extremes of stress and public attention. But we should not confuse that with a lack of emotional intelligence.

City supporters will carry the weight of the club's wrongdoing for a lifetime

Of immediate concern to City’s current squad will be the prospect of expulsion from the Premier League and what that would do in terms of their income and their standing in the game.

However, as they wait for news of punishment and indeed the outcome of a City appeal that will undoubtedly drag this sorry affair out even longer, we should not presume that simple matters of right and wrong don’t matter to them also. They do.

City’s players have heard the noise for years and now they know it has its roots deeply embedded in a sordid and embarrassing truth. They have to come to terms with that now and if some of them decide it would be more easily done some place far away from the Etihad Stadium then it would be hard to blame them.

Sports.title: MAN CITY, WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: When will they be punished? Can Premier League look at post-2018 accounts? Is anyone criminally liable? How much can rivals sue for? And what now for ex-City chief Omar Berrada? MIKE KEEGAN reveals all
Sports.content:
MAN CITY, WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: When will they be punished? Can Premier League look at post-2018 accounts? Is anyone criminally liable? How much can rivals sue for? And what now for ex-City chief Omar Berrada? MIKE KEEGAN reveals all

Eight years on from the start of the biggest scandal in recent British sporting memory, we finally have a verdict. But we don't yet have all the answers.

While the football world is reeling from the bombshell news that Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges against them, the Premier League dropped the other shoe on Tuesday night – revealing in full, excoriating detail the scale of the cheating.

The club remain insistent they are innocent, and that they intend to appeal, despite the League presenting such overwhelming evidence that City cooked the books to the tune of £900million in a nine-year period from 2009 to 2018.

So what happens now? And when will it all finally end?

Here, Chief Sports Reporter MIKE KEEGAN answers the big questions that remain after the most explosive week in the history of the Premier League.

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of charges against them by the Premier League

Pep Guardiola won six league titles across 10 seasons at City

What is the timeline now - what information is still to come out and when?

The first landmark date is this Friday, which is the deadline for City to submit an appeal. An appeal was always viewed as an inevitability given the club continue to protest their innocence and chief executive Ferran Soriano has now confirmed one will be forthcoming.

The Premier League handbook goes into great detail about the time constraints surrounding appeals as part of an attempt to expedite the process. For example, any hearing can only last for five days, should be concluded within 12 weeks of the initial verdict and witness and expert statements should run to no more than 30 pages.

However, the first hurdle will be the make-up of a new panel. The chair of the existing panel should ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’ inform the parties involved of the identities of the proposed individuals.

Objections should then be made within two working days. Given how this has played out so far, this could be the first stage that suffers a delay. With so much riding on the choice of the panel, and so much at stake, an objection may well be forthcoming should either side have misgivings over a proposed individual.

Legal experts believe it is unlikely there will be a conclusion this season and that the case may well fall under exceptional circumstances, with those timelines not applying. With regards to a sanction, the Premier League are refusing to comment on whether that will come before the appeal is finished. However, it would appear there is a desire within the League to speed things along.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters now faces the prospect of kicking out the most successful team in his league for the last 15 years

What will happen to the witnesses judged to have given dishonest evidence?

Good question. Section 29(b) of the released judgment said that 'certain... factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest'. The identity of these people, who gave evidence on behalf of City, has not been revealed.

It would appear the Premier League are pushing for redactions to be removed, with a clue given at the bottom of their bombshell statement on Tuesday.

It stated that while the League were ‘only permitted to publish a redacted version of the summary of the Commission’s "core findings"’ that ‘the process remains ongoing and any further information related to the proceedings that has not been published by the Premier League remains confidential’. They also vowed that, ‘unless legally prevented from doing so’ they would ‘publish the full decision’.

One to watch.

Why were the panel members not named?

If you were asked to rule on such a hugely-emotive case as this, would you want the public to know your identity?

As the Premier League have noted, the process is ongoing and there is a hope that more material will be released. The exact reason for the panel not being named is unclear at the moment, but that may change further down the line, depending on legal arguments.

Are there any grounds for criminal prosecution?

That remains to be seen. The priority for both parties right now will be the appeal.

The difficulty here is that there is not really a precedent in this country. In Italy, suspended sentences were handed out to former Juventus executives, including ex-chairman Andrea Agnelli, with regards to a false accounting case.

Agnelli got 20 months, while ex-sporting director Fabio Paratici – by then managing director of football at Tottenham – was handed 14 months.

There are few parallels for criminal punishment - in Italy, Juventus chairman Andrea Agnelli (second left) and sporting director Fabio Paratici (right) were handed suspended sentences

How will the compensation claims work?

Four of City's Premier League rivals – Arsenal, Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur and Liverpool – lodged legal claims ensuring that they would not be ‘out of time’ in the event that City were found guilty.

Each will already have an idea how much they are going to claim for. The most obvious avenue is the argument that City cost them European qualification and it would appear that, in that area, Spurs have the strongest case. Between 2009 and 2018, they finished one place outside the Champions League spots, with City ahead of them, on four occasions.

The irony here is that a process instigated by former Arsenal chief executive Tim Lewis could net their north London rivals a huge windfall, with £200million mentioned.

It is not just, however, failure to qualify for Europe. Knock-on effects, such as an inability to sign a certain level of player, could also be considered.

The likelihood is that an independent arbitration panel would sit and decide on level of payout, as was the case when Burnley won a £35m payout from Everton in June over the Toffees' PSR breach.

For time purposes, it could be that all four cases would he heard at the same time, although each club may want their own situations to be dealt with individually.

Arsenal are one of four clubs who have reserved the right to seek compensation against City

Tottenham can feel most aggrieved - City denied them Champions League qualification four times in the nine-year period being investigated

Would compensation payments count towards future financial calculations?

It is highly unlikely, given that it would run the risk of creating a vicious circle in which City breach year after year, and be viewed as a double punishment.

Are there any grounds for UEFA to revisit their own City case?

UEFA will wait to see the result of the hearing in full before making a decision. But Daily Mail Sport understands it is highly unlikely they will revisit the case, despite the Premier League stating City were 'significantly in breach' of both their and UEFA's rules.

The verdict obtained by City at the Court of Arbitration for Sport when they overturned their two-season Champions League ban in 2020 would be incredibly difficult to reverse given it upheld some of UEFA’s findings but not others, which it found were ‘time-barred’. City instead received a fine of €10m and had their ban rescinded.

Could the Premier League look at transactions post-2018 now?

They could. Whether they would want to, given the expense and effort that went into this case, is another issue.

At the moment, the feeling within Premier League Towers is one of vindication, and that will linger should City’s appeal fail. Would they want a second leg having won the first so convincingly?

How could City being put into the EFL work in practice? Would EFL clubs have a vote or just be told this is happening?

The EFL have declined to comment. However, there is a rule (11.6.2) that seems to exist for such situations.

Should City be given a points deduction that only sees them relegated to the Championship, then it is simple. They will be relegated. If, however, the sanction relegates them to League Two, it gets a little complicated.

First, they would need to apply to the FA to re-enter the pyramid. If that were successful, their absence would mean one more team would need to be promoted from each of the EFL divisions next season, to make up for the gap in the Premier League.

City could be kicked all the way back down to League Two - but would first have to apply to re-enter the pyramid

Could City’s auditors face any action?

BDO have audited City's accounts for years, and still do. But the Premier League found City 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of their finances from their auditors and football regulators'.

When contacted by Daily Mail Sport, BDO said they ‘remain bound by confidentiality so cannot comment on this occasion’.

Some would view the prospect of action against the firm as incredibly harsh, although we understand BDO could still face an investigation by the Financial Reporting Council (FRC). Sources say the regulator is 'aware' of the situation and 'looking into it to see if there is anything that falls under its remit'.

The FRC refused to comment.

BDO could argue they only acted on information they were given and point out that had it not been for the hacker Rui Pinto (rather than the Premier League’s compliance team) none of these details would have come to light.

What does this all mean for Omar Berrada?

The Manchester United chief executive joined them in 2024 from City, where he held a number of executive roles from 2011 including chief operating officer.

United have declined to comment. That said, it would be hard to imagine a world in which club officials did not carry out the relevant due diligence when Berrada was appointed in 2024 – almost a year after the City charges were made public.

Sports.title: Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp refuses to join calls to strip Man City of titles after seismic guilty verdict - despite previously claiming he would throw a PARTY if charges were proven
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp insists he is at peace with the amount of trophies he won at Liverpool and will not lobby for more amid calls for Manchester City to be stripped of titles. Klopp’s friendly rivalry with City boss Pep Guardiola defined an era of the Premier League but it has been confirmed this week that the Manchester club cheated their way to success by financial doping, in a judgment that is pending an appeal. Some of the sanctions on the table include relegation or stripping City of titles, in which they won six in the Guardiola era – several of which Liverpool were close to, with Manchester United and Arsenal the closest challengers in other seasons. And Klopp said: ‘Of course I’ve heard about that, but I haven’t given it much thought. I can only wait and see. ‘I have big respect for Pep Guardiola and City’s style of football. They played fantastic football and were a top-class opponent for us. ‘If any sanctions are handed out, I have nothing to do with it. I’ll wait and see. I’m far from preparing for a title or anything like that. Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool side went head-to-head with Pep Guardiola's Man City team in one of the Premier League's defining rivalries Man City beat Klopp's Liverpool team to two Premier League titles, edging their rivals by a point on both occasions ‘I’m absolutely fine with what we achieved at Liverpool. We fought hard on the pitch. ‘I can’t say more about that because I don’t know the details and I’m not interested in them.’ Klopp was speaking ahead of Germany’s game against Serbia. He previously said that he would throw a party and foot a bill in Mallorca should City be found guilty but the new German boss was more measured this time. An independent commission ruled that Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period peppered with ‘sham’ deals. In a damning 40-page verdict, published on Tuesday, found City, artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules. Klopp's Liverpool team had gone head-to-head with Guardiola's City side in one of the defining rivalries of the Premier League era, finishing as runners-up on two occasions. Liverpool finished second behind City in the 2018-19 season by just a point, with the title race going down to the final day of the campaign. The Reds ended the season on 97 points, the highest tally achieved by a second-placed side, as City were crowned champions on 98. The following campaign saw Klopp's Liverpool side emerge as runaway champions in the Covid-19 affected season, ending 18 points clear of City. Another nail-biting title race between the teams came in the 2021-22 season, with Man City again pipping Liverpool by a point. Klopp's Liverpool side finished a point behind champions Man City in the 2018-19 season Liverpool responded by ending their long-wait for the league title the following season Klopp's side again finished as runners-up by a single point in the 2021-22 campaign Guardiola's side won the league on 93 points, with Liverpool ending on 92. After slipping 13 points behind Man City in early stages of the following season, Klopp was asked about what Liverpool needed to do to keep competing with their rivals ahead of the sides meeting in October 2022. 'You will not like the answer about that and you have the answer already, nobody can compete with City,' Klopp replied. 'You have the best team in the world and you put in the best striker on the market, no matter what it costs, you just do it. 'City will not like it, nobody will like it, but you know the answer. We cannot act like them, it is not possible, not possible. 'It is just clear and again you know the answer. There are three clubs in world football who can do what they want financially. 'It is legal and everything fine but they can do what they want. It is exactly the fact, we have to look here and we need that, we have to look here and make it younger, here a prospect and there a talent. 'You compete with them, it is not a problem at all for me, it is like it is. Don't ask me that question because you open this discussion and it is me telling you. You all know it, you should know, it is not possible to deal with that. Klopp claimed in October 2022 that 'nobody can compete with Man City', suggesting that they were one of three clubs in world football who can 'do what they want financially'

Your browser does not support iframes.

'I heard the Newcastle [sporting director Dan Ashworth] say there's no ceiling for this club - he's absolutely right. 'There's no ceiling for Newcastle, congratulations, some other clubs have ceilings.' Reports quoting senior City sources suggested they felt Klopp's comments were 'borderline xenophobic'. Liverpool explored legal action following the report, while Klopp rejected the claims at his next press conference. 'In this specific case, I don't feel it at all,' Klopp said. 'I know myself. And you cannot hit with something which is miles away from my personality. 'If I was - I cannot remember the word - like this I would hate it. I would hate myself for being like this.' The dispute came months before Man City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023. When asked about the charges, Klopp responded: 'I have absolutely nothing to say about that.' After leaving Liverpool at the end of the 2023-24 season, Klopp offered a light-hearted response to the potential for the Reds to be awarded two Premier League titles if City were found guilty. 'You leave this club having won the Premier League once, but there could be a court decision that means you have won the Premier League three times,' comedian John Bishop mentioned at 'An Evening with Jurgen Klopp' in May 2024. 'If you organise a bus parade I am in,' Klopp joked in response. 'How long it takes, I don't care how long.'

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher joins calls for Man City to be STRIPPED of titles after bombshell guilty verdict - and compares 'delusional' chief executive to Donald Trump
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher has called for Manchester City to be stripped of their titles after the club was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules.

The Premier League confirmed on Tuesday that the Etihad club had been found guilty of breaching its rules over a nine-year period by creating 'sham' contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel £900million into its football operations.

City, who continue to deny any wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles, during that period. City's CEO Ferran Soriano claimed on Tuesday that the guilty verdicts against the club were based on 'a single false accusation' and a 'Premier League conspiracy theory'.

In his column for The Telegraph, Carragher argued those honours should be stripped from the club, claiming the 'honours boards of Liverpool, Manchester United and Arsenal would look different in a world in which City followed the rules'.

The former Liverpool defender, 48, said: 'City are in denial, refusing to acknowledge their reputation is shattered after being found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges against them.

'Ferran Soriano, City’s chief executive, sounded more like Donald Trump referring to “conspiracies” and issuing a series of “alternative facts”. His statements were delusional and factually incorrect when he insisted they did no wrong and attempted to present the verdict as an “opinion”, when it is rooted in years of investigations and legal arguments.'

Jamie Carragher has called for Manchester City to be stripped of their titles after the club was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules

Carragher argued that fans' anger should be directed towards the ownership, but that the players will instead be 'cast as the scapegoats for the sins of their executives'

Carragher argued that fans' anger should be directed towards the ownership, but that the players will instead be 'cast as the scapegoats for the sins of their executives'.

'That is bound to have a psychological impact,' he said. 'One or two City players may already have an exit strategy in mind if they wish to add honours without a shadow cast over them.'

He added: 'The titles have to be taken off City. The punishment has to be severe to give the rules meaning, establish a precedent and guarantee a deterrent for future owners who may be tempted to follow City’s lead.'

Wayne Rooney, meanwhile, argued that the club's rivals should not be awarded Premier League titles retrospectively - despite the suggestion from his former team-mates Rio Ferdinand and David de Gea.

Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, Rooney said: 'I wouldn't feel comfortable about accepting another Premier League medal if I'm being honest, because I don't think we deserve it. We didn't do enough that season to win the league.

'I'm thinking as their players, they're there doing everything they can to win the Premier League title and in their minds they've done it.

'And, if those players have got no understanding of what's going on above them, then if that happened to me - if all of a sudden Manchester United have been doing the same and I'm getting my Premier League medals taken away from me - I'd be absolutely devastated.

'They might take them away but I wouldn't want it because I don't feel as a team we deserved it that year because we obviously didn't finish first.'

'One or two City players may already have an exit strategy in mind if they wish to add honours without a shadow cast over them,' Carragher added

Rooney did, however, argue that he believes City should be relegated.

He added: 'I'd put them in the lowest league they can go in and then put restrictions on them in terms of how much money they can spend for the next three or four seasons.

'If you're just putting them in the Championship, and I get that's a massive punishment, they're going to come back up. Whereas, I feel if they have got restrictions... League Two, whatever... that could be very difficult for them.

'For instance, if they got a 20-point deduction for the next three years, then players won't want to stay there. If it's the Championship for a season, you could talk players round.

'I'd go as big as I can really.'

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Jurgen Klopp speaks, Pep Guardiola statement, punishment latest
Sports.content:
The latest news on Manchester City's charges after the club were found guilty of alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football's Manchester City charges live blog for Wednesday, September 30.

The Premier League officially announced the club's guilty verdict on 114 breaches of financial rules on Tuesday afternoon, four days after media reports broke the news.

A statement from the league read: "An independent Commission has found Manchester City FC guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation."

As a result, City have until Friday to appeal the decision, which the club are likely to do as they continue to protest their innocence.

Manchester City also released a statement of their own in the wake of the Premier League's confirmation. It read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Stay tuned for the latest news and updates in our live blog below as the saga continues to unfold...

Ex-Manchester City star Craig Bellamy is sure that Erling Haaland will not be distracted by the club’s ongoing legal battle. City have been found guilty by the Premier League, although they maintain their innocence.

‌



A punishment has not been forthcoming, although relegation, a points deduction and a huge fine have all been mentioned. Wales boss, Bellamy, who was at the Etihad between 2009 and 2011 remained tight-lipped when asked about the situation on Wednesday.

‌



He said: "I've played for so many clubs we'll be here all day [if we spoke about them]. This doesn't involve Norway tomorrow."

‌



"We can talk about it another time," he added. "But at this present moment, off the back of three losses, playing Norway tomorrow, it's the furthest thing on my mind."

Bellamy is set to come face-to-face with current City star Erling Haaland, with his Wales side set to take on Norway in the Nations League. But he does not believe that the forward will allow the ongoing scandal to affect his performances.

Man Utd's crisis meeting that led to Erik ten Hag sacking as Michael Carrick under pressure

Manchester United have consistently found themselves in managerial chaos

View 3 Images Michael Carrick is under pressure at Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

The managerial merry-go-round at Manchester United has served as a constant source of chaos. The Red Devils are now led by Michael Carrick after the former United midfielder signed a deal until 2028 with the option of a further year after impressively leading the club to Champions League qualification last season.

‌



Carrick's initial appointment as interim boss saw him lead United to 12 wins in their last 17 Premier League games. However, the honeymoon period is well and truly over at Old Trafford after just one win in their opening five fixtures, alongside their shock EFL Cup exit against Brighton earlier this month.

‌



Carrick, 45, will no doubt be feeling the pressure of the hot seat, but club bosses will surely be keen to bypass the mayhem that has existed in the previous situations of Ruben Amorim and Erik ten Hag.

‌



The Portuguese boss is now at the helm of AC Milan after being sacked from United in January 2026, ending his tumultuous 14-month reign. Amorim began his second season in charge under instant pressure, having guided United to a record-low 15th-place finish in the Premier League in the 2024/25 campaign.

The club went without an away win until their 2-1 victory over Manchester City in December, while their embarrassing exit from the Carabao Cup at the hands of League Two side Grimsby Town earlier that season led to intense speculation over Amorim's position.

‌



Reports at the time suggested club executives had held discussions with key United players to get a sense of the mood in the dressing room. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox were believed to have consulted captain Bruno Fernandes, among others, in their aim to gain better insight into the squad's views.

View 3 Images Ruben Amorim was sacked after a miserable 14-month spell with Man United (Image: Getty Images)

The situation within United was similar to the circumstances behind the seven-hour meeting between Ten Hag and his former bosses in October 2024, with the Dutchman's firing coming later that month.

‌



The discussions were held at Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Knightsbridge offices in London, with co-owner Joel Glazer, chief executive Berrada, then-sporting director Dan Ashworth, and director of football Wilcox all meeting to confer over the state of United.

Board member Jean-Claude Blanc, chief operating officer Collette Roche and chief financial officer Roger Bell were all understood to have been present for the conference. While a meeting of such magnitude doesn't seem to be on the horizon when it comes to Carrick's position, the United boss must turn his side's fortunes around and fast to prevent such a situation.

Sports.title: Man City set to be punished THIS SEASON as 'Premier League rivals get wish'
Sports.content:
Man City set to be punished THIS SEASON as 'Premier League rivals get wish'

Manchester City have been found guilty by the Independent Commission and now await their punishment while they make their appeal over the ruling

View 2 Images Manchester City could receive a points deduction quickly (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

Manchester City are set to receive a punishment this season after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules and failing to cooperate with the division's investigation. Premier League rivals are pushing for the sanctions to be rapidly imposed.

‌



City intend to appeal the verdict and a sanction for their indiscretions has not yet been decided. A separate hearing will be held to decide the club's punishment.

‌



The appeal must be filed by Friday, October 2, and Premier League sides are pointing to new regulations that were agreed in June that should now fast-track the process, reports the Sun. According to those rules, any hearing should be concluded 'no later than 12 weeks after filing of the appeal.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

That timetable would bean the appeal would need to be resolved by Christmas Day, but given the timing, the appeal could be heard from December 14. From there, the board would have 30 days to produce a verdict.

The Premier League have said that they 'are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans'.

‌



There is a 'very high chance' that Manchester City's situation is resolved by the end of this season to avoid additional problems unfurling in the future, according to Football Finance expert Kieran Maguire.

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Depending on the deduction, waiting until next season would give teams who have missed out on Europe or been relegated the opportunity to argue that their fortunes would have been greater if the punishment had been administered sooner.

‌



Maguire added that applying a punishment is often a swifter process than the initial hearing, as seen with points deductions for Nottingham Forest and Everton.

Maguire told BBC Radio 5 Live: “I think there’s a very high chance it will be resolved because if it isn’t we end up with a situation like that of Burnley and Everton where a club could be relegated, Manchester City are not given a deduction this season and it’s given next season instead and the club which finishes 18th could say had the deduction been applied sooner we would not have been relegated so that adds to the complication.

‌



“Looking at the Premier League’s press release it does seem it is keen for this to be resolved as quickly as possible. If you take at the length of time it took in respect of Forest and Everton, once they had heard the evidence, actually applying the tariff was the quick part of the equation. It is listening to the evidence which is the torturous period which we have had up to now.”

Even after the announcement of any sanction, Manchester City are likely to exhaust every avenue they can to overturn the verdict. Maguire believes that City will have a greater chance of success trying to take the case outside of Premier League jurisdiction to the High Court.

Any argument is more likely to be successful if it attacks the people involved rather than the evidence in his mind. City have previously been successful in fighting a verdict when they were initially kicked out of the Champions League before seeing a two-year ban overturned.

‌



View 2 Images Manchester City have been found guilty by the independent commission following their legal battle with the Premier League. (Image: PA Wire)

“If they were going to appeal against the initial verdict they have to prove that the composition of the panel was flawed, either in the selection process or they have been able to identify bias in the individuals concerned," Maguire added. "When I’ve spoken to sports lawyers, the universal response to that is that it’s almost impossible but that’s not the same as impossible.

“The other issue would be could they try to take this outside of the football bubble and say it is ultimately a commercial dispute between two bodies and, therefore, the Premier League doesn’t have the right to impose such penalties and try to get it resolved in the High Court.

‌



"When I’ve spoken to legal professionals, they think it highly unlikely but it’s always a possibility.

“Manchester City have previously overturned a UEFA verdict based on the strength of their lawyers and some of their lawyers do have a fantastic reputation for being able to do things which in normal circumstances would be considered highly unlikely.

“The evidence seems to be overwhelming. Reading the summary report, one of Manchester City’s defences seems to be that the Premier League wasn’t in a position to hold this hearing because of the way the evidence had been obtained. That was very firmly rejected by the commission and I can’t see that overturned.

Article continues below

“As for what appears to be an overwhelming amount of evidence and the lack of faith in the Manchester City witnesses, I can’t really see anything based on hundreds of thousands of pieces of evidence and 7,000 pages of testimony for how it could be overturned from a legal point of view. It has to be an attack on the people involved.”

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
