00:00:52

So those Israeli citizens getting on their phones and starting to tell the story so the world could hear. That plane regained altitude, eventually landed safely in Saudi Arabia. The airline says they are still investigating. They encourage all parties to avoid speculation on the motives. But already the stories from inside that fuselage are pretty jaw dropping and scary. Let's talk about it. Live to CBS News national security contributor Joseph Zacks. Joseph, good to have you with us. So I guess one of my first questions, as we start to see the people getting off the plane now returned to Israel, is how could a commercial pilot go undetected as a potential terrorist? Well, that's a very good question, Reed, and thank you for having me on the show. I do think that it's important at this very early stage of the investigation to reserve judgment on exactly what happened and what the motives were, and see how this plays out. Nevertheless, this was a very serious incident and one that may have been inspired either through some jihadi motivation. It could have been sponsored by-- and here I'm doing exactly what I offered not to do. But it could have been sponsored by a country in the region. Or it could have been a mental health crisis that the co-pilot had. So time will tell exactly what happened, as well as, to answer your question, whether there needs to be a different process in place with respect to assessing and vetting pilots and/or monitoring and/or checking them prior to their entering a plane to for a flight. I think you to give pilots and crews, and justifiably so, some leeway. They do have to go through security procedures like the rest of us do, but perhaps not the full scrutiny that other passengers do. This could change in light of this event. I think it's important for our audience to get an idea of just how frequently this flight path takes off from where it took off from and goes into Tel Aviv. In fact, I have a friend who's booked to go in that very same plane, that very same route, in 10 days from now, knows that a lot of Americans, in fact, travel into Tel Aviv via, of course, Dubai. Talk to us about security measures that are in place, especially given the fact that, yes, you also have a very tense situation there in the Middle East, not the least of which added to the tension that seems to be transmitted by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who does seem to want to land on a conclusion here very quickly. Well, I think it's a very good thing that there is some air transit between Dubai and Israel. I think the strength of the UAE-Israeli relationship is a very good thing and that it serves both countries well. But also it makes it somewhat vulnerable as a target because nefarious actors may view that as an area to be exploited. I've been through the Dubai airport numerous times. Their security is quite satisfactory, from my optic. But I am certain that this will-- and I would also hasten to add that normally, flights from any country going to Israel undergo-- passengers undergo a great deal more scrutiny than going to other places. But again, here the situation seems to have been where a co-pilot was involved. And so I think that there will be a look at the vetting of pilots, co-pilots, and crew members on flights to Israel, perhaps even more intensely than previously done. One would shudder to think what would have happened had this situation not been commandeered and under control there in the skies. What were the possibilities if they hadn't gotten this plane under control? Yeah, I think that it would have been a very serious event for a number of reasons. First of all, potentially a horrific loss of life. Secondly, this is coming on the heels of a very contentious Israeli election, which could have caused political backlashes, but also caused reactions because of the heightened political situation in Israel that would not be helpful at this point in time. As far as scenarios, one could envision it could have been a hijacking. It could have been an attempt to crash the plane, either with intent to simply kill the passengers on board or to undertake a 9/11-style attack, where the plane entered into Israeli airspace and would look to crash the plane into either an Israeli skyscraper or military complex or the Knesset. There are a whole number of scenarios. I think that one would have been least likely, because apparently somehow someone in the cockpit was able to squawk that the plane was under duress. So that, I think, from accounts, led the Israeli Air Force to scramble its jets and be prepared to undertake emergency procedures, should the event have deteriorated. And you've just been seeing on your screen a lot of those passengers getting off to live to tell the story. We're glad we're able to use those words, lived to tell the story of what happened there, the scare in the sky. So Joseph Zacks, to your point, much more to come as we learn more about the pilots who were involved in this and the crew who stepped forward and said, not today. Continuing breaking news coverage, once again, as passengers arrive back in Israel after a cockpit attack on a FlyDubai flight.

World.title: Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
World.content:
Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps

Emily Feng/NPR

Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.

That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.

Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.

Sponsor Message

Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

World.title: Police questioning can shape a sexual assault case. Their approach is often wrong
World.content:
Police questioning can shape a sexual assault case. Their approach is often wrong

toggle caption John Munson/AP

The allegations from a former Cornell University student who says she was drugged and gang-raped at the school in 2024 has led to widespread condemnation for the school and investigators.

The case is also raising questions about how police handled the initial investigation.

Earlier this month, the woman, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit detailing allegations against seven men she said assaulted her. Prosecutors have subsequently reopened the investigation.

Details in the lawsuit differed from a statement Doe provided to Cornell University Police following the alleged attack in 2024, according to excerpts shared by Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten. The 2024 statement is central to why his office did not pursue criminal charges two years ago, he said.

Sponsor Message

Van Houten said that Doe's 2024 statement "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped" and "described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

There are, however, several instances in Doe's statement shared by Van Houten where she says she could not remember certain details, did not consent to certain activities and was increasingly intoxicated as the night continued.

Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG in an interview that Doe's statement was taken by "an experienced investigator" trained in sexual abuse investigations "over an extended period of time." Cornell University Police did not respond to questions about details of the length, time and place of the interview or other details of the manner of questioning before publication.

Many police lack training on sexual assault victim response

Trauma researchers and advocates for sexual assault victims say an initial statement like Doe's often cannot be taken at face value and more investigating needs to be done.

Gaps and inconsistencies in an assault survivor's police statement are often a product of a victim's trauma and of how officers question them – not evidence that she's unreliable, according to Dave Thompson, a certified forensic interviewer and a consultant who trains investigators in interrogation techniques.

Sponsor Message

"Anybody that interacts with survivors or victims or witnesses to crimes should be trained in a trauma-informed approach," he said.

That's an approach that trains investigators to act in a way that anticipates how trauma survivors might respond differently after an assault, which can include impacts to their behavior and memory. This approach centers a survivor and works to prevent approaches to questioning that could re-harm them.

Rebecca Campbell, a psychology professor at Michigan State University, said this is all done while understanding that their accounts may not initially be clear, complete or chronological.

But most U.S. police are not trained in this approach, Campbell said. For nearly 30 years, she's studied trauma and sexual assault.

A study by the Bureau of Justice Statistics for the Census of Law Enforcement Training Academies analyzed subject areas offered to police recruits during basic training. The average length of the core basic training program was 833 hours.

In nearly 94% of surveyed police academies that offered training on sexual assault, trainees received on average seven hours of training on the issue, according to the report. They received six hours of training on victim response in the nearly 88% of academies that offered instruction on this issue.

In lieu of meaningful training, Campbell explained, "What we see consistently in research is that responding officers and detectives will very often treat the victim as the subject to be interviewed and to be interrogated."

That impacts how comfortable victims are with sharing necessary information to investigators and ultimately affects an investigation.

Sources for this story were speaking generally about sexual assault investigations and are not involved in the Cornell investigation or questioning by police.

What is the impact of trauma to the body?

Scientists and researchers have examined how survivors of serious trauma and especially sexual assault can frequently struggle to remember the events leading up to, during and after the event.

Sponsor Message

"Our memories don't work like a video recorder that we can just rewind, hit play and remember from start to finish. We might remember the sound. The feeling of an impact. Maybe a scream. We remember bits and pieces," Thompson, the certified forensic interviewer, said.

It's important that investigators know that too, rather than dismiss memory lapses as falsified details or concluding that the story has too many inconsistencies, he said.

It's important "that we're not expecting memory to go from start to finish," he said. "And we're allowing that person a safe space to remember and recall and retrieve details that may be most relevant or present in their state of mind."

Tracy Matheson established a foundation, Project Beloved, to create special police interrogation rooms across the country to make the environment for victims reporting a traumatic event more calming and conducive to this approach.

Matheson's 22-year-old daughter, Molly Jane, was raped and murdered in 2017. Her killer, Reginald Kimbro, was sentenced to multiple life sentences for her daughter and another woman's killing and additional sexual assaults in 2022.

After this tragedy, Matheson educated herself on the impact of trauma to the brain. She learned that during those events the brain switches to survival mode.

"It's picking out things that may seem insignificant, but in the long run actually corroborate whatever it is that the victim is reporting happened," Matheson said.

Entrenched problem hurts investigations

Michigan State University's Campbell said she can't speak to how the Cornell case was handled. But she said that in her research, prosecutors and police often treat inconsistencies from traumatized victims as a reason to stop investigating, citing credibility concerns, rather than as something to follow up on.

"We actually don't see that same behavior in other types of crime," she said.

When there's a discrepancy, "That is something that merits more evidence, more follow up, more interviews to figure out why there is a discrepancy or is there really even a discrepancy? They don't do that in sexual assault cases."

Sponsor Message

This is part of the problematic dynamic for victims, who struggle with reporting sexual assaults already because they fear they won't be believed or helped, she said.

"And they're met with blame and skepticism," Campbell said. "And it becomes a vicious dynamic of more blame, more withdrawal." Eventually, police shrug their shoulders and say, "She didn't give me the information," she said.

Data shows that from January 2021 to December 2025, law enforcement documented an average of 127,798 reports of rape, according to RAINN, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organization. FBI crime data shows that law enforcement clears 26% of the reported rape cases. (That can mean someone was arrested or a suspect died and not necessarily that they were charged or convicted.)

An even bleaker statistic shared by RAINN shows that from a 20-year review of reported sexual assault cases, 89% of cases were "founded," meaning that investigators determined the crime likely happened. But only 8% of those cases ended in a conviction.

Campbell said research she and other scholars have done shows that in a vast majority of cases, police make no effort to find or interview suspects.

"And in cases where it is an assault and that occurred between people who know each other for whom there could be text information and texts and social media. Again, research suggests about 80% of the time the police never go get that information," she said.

Part of that is due to the complexity of some of these cases, Campbell added. But during her decades of research, she said law enforcement personnel have told her repeatedly that resources and staffing are not prioritized to help solve these cases.

The Cornell case, unfortunately, highlights these longstanding and entrenched patterns, she said.

"We have tried through different policy initiatives and avenues to create change and to make things fair and equitable and trauma informed," she said. "It's like one step forward, two steps back."

World.title: Trump officials changed forms for overseas voters amid a GOP push to restrict voting
World.content:
Trump officials changed forms for overseas voters amid a GOP push to restrict voting

toggle caption Mladen Antonov/AFP via Getty Images

The Trump administration has made last-minute changes to key absentee-voting forms for U.S. citizens living abroad, raising concerns about confusing some overseas voters during this year's midterm elections.

The revisions to two forms came in late August from the Pentagon. The department runs the voting assistance program that provides forms allowing eligible overseas citizens, plus U.S. military members and their families, to register for and participate in federal elections.

Weeks before a Sept. 19 deadline for states to send those voters midterm ballots, the Pentagon submitted "emergency" requests to bypass the usual months-long process for changing federal forms.

Sponsor Message

Among the changes was removing a checkbox for an overseas U.S. citizen to identify as having "never lived in the United States."

The removal leaves only two response options for those without an active-duty military connection. Both options require overseas citizens to make a sworn declaration: Either they intend to return to the U.S. or are uncertain about returning.

But some U.S. citizens who were born abroad have never lived in the United States at all.

Many states and Washington, D.C., allow what are often referred to as "never-resided" citizens to vote if they have a relative who last lived in that state or territory before leaving the U.S., including a parent or legal guardian serving in the military.

Since 2024, however, Republican officials have been pushing to block these U.S. citizens from voting.

In lawsuits, GOP officials have argued state laws and other rules permitting voting by never-resided citizens violate state constitutions. They also have claimed in court filings that these U.S. citizens are disproportionately registered as non-Republican voters and allowing them to cast ballots hurts GOP chances of winning elections.

While Republican court challenges have been successful in North Carolina, they have been rebuffed twice in Michigan as similar lawsuits continue in Arizona and at least five other states.

For now, eligible never-resided voters can continue to register and request ballots through any alternative ways provided by the state or territory where they are eligible to vote.

And the Pentagon's Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) says state election officials can keep processing previous versions of its forms. Asked by NPR how long that can continue, the Pentagon said in a statement: "States administer elections and can process any form or application that provides the information required to verify a voter's eligibility to vote in their jurisdiction."

Sponsor Message

Still, many overseas and military voting advocates are worried the new federal form changes, which were reported earlier by the outlet Democracy Docket, are setting up the latest hurdle to the ballot box for U.S. citizens living abroad.

Trump officials removed an overseas voter category that's been on forms for more than a decade

Some version of the checkbox for never-resided voters has been on what's known as the "Federal Post Card Application" and the "Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot" since 2013.

"I actually worked that regulation to change the form. But I didn't want to do it right in the middle of the 2012 election, so I had it effective come 2013," says Bob Carey, a retired U.S. Navy captain who led FVAP until departing in 2012.

Carey recalls the idea of adding a category for never-resided voters came from some state election officials and overseas voting advocates.

"At the time, I was sort of saying to myself, 'OK, this won't make that big of a difference. I'll add the block,' " Carey adds.

But more than a decade later, the Pentagon says it has changed its interpretation of a federal law known as the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act.

"It has recently come to our attention that the current format of these forms may confuse voters about the information they are required to provide under Federal law and their eligibility to use these forms to register and vote," Sean O'Keefe, the Pentagon's deputy under secretary for personnel and readiness, wrote in a letter about the August emergency requests for changing the forms.

It's not clear what exactly prompted the Pentagon to reassess these forms, which now also include revised language about voter identification.

But days after a White House agency approved the requests, FVAP said the forms "have been updated" in social media posts. The Pentagon started a public comment period about each form more than a week later. And guidance for state election officials was not posted on FVAP's website until about a month after the forms changed.

Sponsor Message

In a statement, the Pentagon said FVAP has also directly notified election officials and voters by email, though it provided no additional details.

Some military and overseas voting advocates say the Pentagon should do more outreach in the middle of voting season for the midterm elections.

"If I was the under secretary of defense for personnel readiness, to which FVAP reports, or the secretary of defense, I'd be calling up the [FVAP] director and saying, 'Spam the crap out of everyone,' " says Carey, who now serves as executive director of the National Defense Committee, a veterans advocacy organization focused on voting and other civil rights.

Overseas voting advocates worry the changes will cause — not eliminate — confusion

Sarah Streyder, executive director of Secure Families Initiative — a group that advocates for military families and challenged President Trump's failed push for mail-in voting restrictions for the midterms — says she's concerned about the lack of transparency surrounding the Pentagon's process for changing the forms.

"What were the voices prompting this change? Where did this come from? Military families are stakeholders who should have been included, because we can speak most authoritatively on what truly causes confusion with these forms and what doesn't," Streyder adds. "That's our form you're messing with. And you didn't even ask us for the input. It's just very insulting."

The Pentagon emphasized in a statement that the forms were changed to "eliminate voter confusion."

But Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the U.S. Vote Foundation, an advocacy organization for overseas voters, says she expects the opposite to happen.

"I definitely believe that the new version of the form will create far more confusion than we ever encountered with any previous version," Dzieduszycka-Suinat says. "The law hasn't changed. States still run this program the way Congress wrote it. However, the fact that it's being presented differently at the federal level within this 90-day window [before Election Day] — it doesn't give the states time to implement it, to train their people, to inform voters, to change instructions or any of it."

Sponsor Message

Dzieduszycka-Suinat notes these last-minute changes to the forms come shortly after the Republican National Committee ramped up its legal fight this year against state laws that allow never-resided citizens to vote, including in Colorado, Nebraska, Nevada, New Jersey and Virginia.

"It's hard to ignore the fact that a spotlight has been shown onto this particular slice of voters," Dzieduszycka-Suinat says. "And it's very concerning that they've simply been wiped off the form without discussion."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: How Ukrainians are coping with new, more deadly Russian attacks
World.content:
How Ukrainians are coping with new, more deadly Russian attacks

Zanny Minton Beddoes, The Economist's editor in chief, just visited Ukraine. She says, despite all its drone weaponry, Kyiv is under extraordinary bombardment, as Russia tries to make it unlivable.

Transcript

DAVE DAVIES, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. Since Russia invaded Ukraine 4 1/2 years ago, Ukrainian forces have held their own on the battlefield with support from Western allies, and morale among the country's civilian population has held up, despite punishing air attacks. But our guest, Zanny Minton Beddoes, editor in chief of The Economist, says the war is changing in ways that bring a new level of terror to Ukrainian citizens and pose serious threats to the country's economy.

Minton Beddoes recently returned from a reporting trip with a team of journalists to Ukraine, where, she says, both sides in the war are developing new weapons and refining tactics with lethal consequences. One example, so-called safari hunting drones that identify a person or vehicle as a target, then follow as the target flees in terror. The drone eventually dives and crashes into the target, detonating a deadly explosive charge. We've invited Zanny Minton Beddoes back on the show to talk about Ukraine and catch up on some other important topics, including the war with Iran, trade, tariffs and the state of U.S., European and Canadian alliances.

Zanny Minton Beddoes is a former economist for the International Monetary Fund who joined The Economist magazine in 1994. She holds degrees from Oxford University and Harvard University and is a regular commentator on television and radio. We recorded our conversation yesterday.

Zanny Minton Beddoes, welcome back to FRESH AIR.

ZANNY MINTON BEDDOES: Thank you so much for having me.

DAVIES: You and this team of journalists from the economist recently made an extensive trip to Ukraine. You've been there before. Why did you feel you wanted to make this kind of investment in this subject now?

MINTON BEDDOES: So you're right. I've been there four times since the invasion by Russia, the full-scale invasion - the first, I think, three weeks after the invasion, when I went to Kyiv and was the first journalist to interview President Zelenskyy. The reason I go is because I think this is the most important geopolitical conflict in Europe in, you know, the last 70 years. And I actually have a kind of personal soft spot for Ukraine. I lived there for a few months 30 years ago. I find it a fascinating country. And I - you know, I feel that you can only really understand something, particularly a conflict like that, if you actually see it close up.

And I have to say, Dave, this is a very sobering trip. And it was probably the most sobering since the very first time I went, which was, the first time, in 2022. The Russians were still just outside Kyiv. The city was virtually empty. You know, we went to see President Zelenskyy kind of in bunkers. And, I mean, it was in his palace, but there were sandbags everywhere. It really felt like a place at war. But the subsequent two times, when I went to Kyiv, it felt like a normal city. The war felt far away because the city then had very good air defenses. And, yes, there were occasional air alerts, but you felt as though you were in a very safe city.

This time around, I went to Kyiv, and then I went to visit the brigade headquarters of one of the drone brigades, much closer to the front, in a location that I'm obviously not going to disclose, but much closer to the front. And Kyiv itself - and this is, I think, really important for people to understand - in the last couple of months, but really the last few weeks, has been under extraordinary bombardment from the Russians. And they are basically trying to make life unlivable in a city of several million people.

And there are two big things that have changed that have given the Russians an advantage. The first is that the Ukrainians have run out of interceptors for ballistic missiles, what are called PAC-3 interceptors produced by the U.S., which for the past couple of years have really helped them to defend themselves against ballistic missiles. And because these interceptors are in extremely short supply - they were used heavily in the Middle East recently in the Iran War - the Ukrainians have essentially hardly got any left. So the Russians are able to bombard the city at night with ballistic missiles.

And the second is that the Russians have made an innovation to their drones. Their kind of workhorse drone is something called the Shahed drone, which was originally made by Iran, that the Russians started producing at scale. And they have essentially attached jet propulsion to those drones, which makes them go much higher and much faster and thus makes them much harder for the Ukrainians to intercept. And Ukrainians had built sort of defensive drones that could intercept the Shaheds with a sort of 95% success rate. But now that they have these jet propulsion attached to them, that interception rate has gone down closer to 40%, and the Russians have enormous quantities of these drones that they are just sending into Ukraine, essentially, all day and all night now.

DAVIES: What does that mean day to day for civilians who are used to air raid sirens, right? I mean, this is not like they're not used to living in a wartime.

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think the difference is that, you know - if you're living in Kyiv, you have an app on your phone. And I had it on my phone when I was there. And it goes off every time there is a you know, ballistic missile or a jet Shahed close - within, you know, a few, I think 50 or 100 kilometers. And basically, it's going off the whole time. And you are trying to live a normal life. And so you're looking, and you become normalized to this quite quickly, and you look at it and you say, well, is it likely to be in my part of town? Looks not too far away, so I'll - you know, if it's too close, you might go to a shelter. You might just keep an eye on it. But increasingly, it's happening all day, and you're suddenly discovering that the Metro isn't working. You're unable to get your kids from school. There's been an attack. A supermarkets blown up, you know. And every day, people are killed.

DAVIES: You paid a visit to the operation center of an elite drone unit in the Ukrainian army. Share with us what you saw there.

MINTON BEDDOES: So Ukraine has several of these unarmed systems brigades, as they're called, which are units that specialize in drones. And they were set up often by civilians, technologists, sort of separate from the army structure, but they work with the army structure. And they are in the vanguard of what this war is about, particularly at the front lines. And it is very different from what you imagine, you know, warfare to be from the movies. A drone-based war is one where the actual front lines - there are no people visible. There is what Ukrainians call the kill zone, which is now something like 20 to 30 kilometers each way from the contact line, where, essentially, anything that moves will be shot down, shot at by a drone within seconds or minutes.

DAVIES: From both sides?

MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, from both sides. There are hundreds of drones in the air - surveillance drones, drones, attack drones. That means that nothing can really move. So the few people who are there on both sides are, you know, in underground dugouts. They are often supplied by drone, or they're supplied by unmanned ground vehicles, essentially kind of robots on wheels. It's a dystopian hellscape. To be clear, I wasn't anywhere near there. I was sort of close to it, but well out of that area.

Then these drones are manned and sort of piloted by people in the brigade headquarters of the sort that I went to. They have huge screens, and it's like a cross between a sort of dystopian video game and a startup. There are huge numbers of computer screens. There are people who are plotting where the Russians - assets are. They are sending surveillance drones to go and find them. Then they're sending in drones to attack them. And the other side is doing that, too. And the area around the front line is now basically a sort of no-man's-land where nothing can move. And, you know, the Ukrainians are clearly trying to disrupt Russian supply lines by attacking well beyond the front lines. And then, of course, they're also increasingly hitting refineries much further into Russia. So this is a - on both sides, a drone-based war, whose characteristics are very, very fast innovation.

DAVIES: And I mentioned in the introduction, these so-called safari drones, where a pilot located somewhere is looking at what the drone sees. They identify a target - might be a person, might be a vehicle - and essentially kind of track them from the air as if they're a safari hunter and then smash the drone into the target, blow up a charge, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: That's exactly - and that's what happens on the front line in this kill zone the whole time. What is sort of newer is that the Russians are doing the same thing to attack civilians in front-line towns, and increasingly and alarmingly, they have the capability to reach bigger cities, potentially Kyiv, with this kind of drone, too. So the notion of safari-hunting individuals to kill them is now no longer some sort of dystopian fantasy. It's something that can happen.

DAVIES: The dreadful video that I've seen of a man, who - and there's this drone buzzing around above him, you know, six or eight feet in the air, and he's dodging around, trying to get behind a truck to kind of avoid it. And eventually, the drone dives into him, and he wasn't killed, but he was seriously injured. But just seeing it just seems - is utterly terrifying.

MINTON BEDDOES: It is. And what was really sobering to me is it was tough enough seeing all of this at this sort of center of this war. But what I realized is that these are tactics and capabilities that can be used by the Russians elsewhere. And if you remember just a few weeks ago, there was a narrow escape at Leipzig Airport when there was an attack, which - a drone was attacking a cargo plane at the airport. It was foiled, but it was in Germany, and the German government has said that the Russians were behind it. And I think there was realization for me, and in one of the conversations I had with the senior people at this drone brigade - became clear to me that their view is, these are the capabilities that the Russians have. Don't think that they're going to be confined just to Ukraine.

And I think there is a growing concern amongst European politicians and intelligence services that there will be more of this. We've had alarms raised from the Polish government. We've had alarms raised from Balkan governments. We've had alarms raised across the board that the Russians may well be planning to do more of this. And what became clear to me is that it is technologically totally doable now.

DAVIES: We need to take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll continue our conversation in just a moment. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF LOS SUPER SEVEN SONG, "CALLE DIECISEIS")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR, and our guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. We're looking at the war in Ukraine, and we'll be discussing some other topics, including the conflict in the Middle East and the state of Western alliances. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, the Ukrainians have been effective in sending drones, behind the lines in Russia and attacking, you know, military infrastructure, energy infrastructure. And one of the ways that they have been able to operate it is by using these Starlink satellite hookups, which are, you know, operated by SpaceX, Elon Musk's company. I understand that Musk does not let Ukraine use those for attacks inside Russia. Is that right?

MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, that's right. Starlink is available to the Ukrainians over Ukrainian territory, including the territory that is Ukrainian, but the Russians are occupying. But it is not available to them over Russia. And what that means is that the Ukrainians lack the ability to go after the launch sites, for example, for ballistic missiles. So there is a huge plea from the Ukrainians to the Americans to basically push SpaceX to allow them to have access to Starlink over Russian territory so that they can go after the launch sites from which these ballistic missiles are raining down on them.

Interestingly and alarmingly, something that I hadn't really focused on until I went to Ukraine and sort of really delved into this, the Russians have been and are building their own version of Starlink called Rassvet, which is still in its early stages. I think they put a couple of dozen or so satellites into space, nowhere near as many as Elon Musk has with SpaceX. But nonetheless, this capability is growing, and most people think that sometime in the next year or so, the Russians will have some Starlink equivalent, which will mean that they will be very easily able to direct and monitor drones going anywhere over Ukrainian territory, which will be another big blow to the Ukrainians.

DAVIES: And if the Ukrainians haven't had access to the Starlink system in Russian territory, how have they been able to manage these attacks on Russian facilities?

MINTON BEDDOES: I mean, there are other ways of guiding, but they're not as good as Starlink. The Ukrainians are incredibly innovative. And I think the important thing for people to understand is that thus far, Ukraine has sort of been ahead of the Russians in drone innovation, and they've been amazing at building up this drone industry. They've been always in a sort of cat-and-mouse game, somewhat ahead of the Russians. The Russians have been able to scale up. They're, you know, a bigger economy. They're good at scaling up their innovations. And what's slightly alarming now is it seems as though the Russians are actually ahead on innovation as well as an ability to scale.

I have no doubt that the Ukrainians will come up with new innovations, both in defensive drones and other areas. The question that is more uncertain right now is, do they have the financial capability and financial support to scale those innovations? And that's what really matters right now, because the truth is that Ukraine is very, very dependent on financial support. Unfortunately, there's no support coming from the U.S. anymore. When the Trump administration came in, the - until then, there had been a lot of support from the United States. Now there is really essentially none. Ukraine is financed by the Europeans, and the question is whether the Europeans will step up the pace of their financial support such that the Ukrainians have the money to scale up their drone program, which is essential to defend themselves.

DAVIES: Yeah. I want to talk more about that in a moment. But I also wanted to just note the level of Russian casualties in this war. It seems that the Ukrainians have been able to inflict terrible punishment on the Russian forces, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: The level of casualties are just extraordinary, something on the order of 40,000 people a month - Russians - killed and wounded. This is an unfathomable number of people. But one thing that's important to remember is we've been talking about all of the ways in which Russia is bombarding Ukraine. But Ukraine is, you know, essentially holding the front line and actually making a few gains in certain places.

So the sort of overall picture of this war is that the Ukrainians have held off the Russians. The front lines have been basically stable. The Russians, at incredible cost - 40,000 people a month - I mean, it just - you know, and you can't - it's hard to imagine those numbers. And they're still not able to really make a lot of progress. In some areas, they're gaining a tiny bit of ground. In some areas, they're losing. But basically the front lines are stable. So what the Russians have decided to do, particularly in recent weeks, knowing that they are not making serious progress at the front line, is to try and break the morale of Ukrainian civilians by completely bombarding the cities.

DAVIES: You know, there's a graph that you have in the article that came from your trip. It's a bar graph that shows, by year, how much money the Western allies have contributed to Ukraine's defense, and they're color-coded. You know, so much for the EU, so much for the United States, so much for other countries. And it was stunning to look - and I think it's in 2025 that the U.S. portion disappears. I'm not sure that much of the United States realizes that U.S. support for Ukraine has vanished completely.

MINTON BEDDOES: Yep. There is essentially no financial support for Ukraine from the United States. To the extent that there is any weaponry going, it is weaponry that is being bought by the Europeans on behalf of the Ukrainians from the U.S. When - you know, when President Trump came in, it became very clear that he did not intend to continue supporting Ukraine, and that has happened completely. And I don't think that's that well-known. And what is even less well-known is the degree to which the Europeans have stepped up and basically are single-handedly supporting Ukraine.

Now, this is because it's also, of course - it's our continent. It's in our own interest as Europeans to do that. But I am very clear, having just been there, that the situation is very, very stark right now and that I don't think the rest of the world has realized the degree that Russia is attacking civilians - there's no simpler way, no other way of putting it - attacking civilians and civilian life - and that, in order to be able to survive that and mount a defense, the Ukrainians need faster and more financial support so that they can scale up their defensive capability and so that they can survive. And this country has been extraordinarily resilient in the last 4 1/2 years. And yet it looks to me more difficult than it has for a long time in this war...

DAVIES: Yeah.

MINTON BEDDOES: ...Without financial support.

DAVIES: One of the issues is - is Zelenskyy still trusted as a leader? I mean, there have been some corruption cases. There are pieces of legislation in the legislature which have not been adopted. What's your sense of Zelenskyy's leadership and to what extent his credibility is undermining the kind of support either in the country or among allies?

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think there is growing frustration politically within Ukraine with President Zelenskyy and his leadership. I think that's - in some ways, that's kind of normal after 4 1/2 years of war. There is corruption in Ukraine, undoubtedly. The anti-corruption unit, which has been set up and is funded by the European Union as an important part of the prerequisites that Ukraine has to have to eventually become a member of the European Union - this organization is effective, is powerful, is unearthing corruption. There is corruption in the highest echelons of government around - or at least there are accusations of it in the highest echelons of government.

You know, this makes it more difficult. And as you say, Parliament - the Ukrainian Parliament has not passed some elements of some laws that the Europeans would like them to have passed as part of the sort of cleaning up of Ukraine. So that's very frustrating for the Europeans. It's not a perfect political situation.

On the other hand, this is a country fighting for its existence. And I'm not sure that this is as much a story of terrible corruption in Ukraine as it is a good-news story of the effectiveness of an anti-corruption unit shining a spotlight. And I see it as a sort of - a good sign that they're unearthing this and that they are, you know, shining the light on corruption where it is. And that's all part and parcel of Ukraine becoming more and more like the, you know, part of Europe that it should be.

But it's very difficult right now. You know, there should have been elections. Were it not for the war, there would have been elections. President Zelenskyy has been president a long time. In any country, he definitely is not someone who is so focused on institutional reform as he should be. There are huge shortcomings to elements of what President Zelenskyy does. But I wouldn't conclude from that that, you know, it's a terribly corrupt place, and therefore, we shouldn't support it. I think it's remarkable what the Ukrainians are doing, given what they're facing.

DAVIES: All right. We're going to take another break here. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. She'll be back to talk more after this short break. I'm Dave Davies, and this is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF BELA FLECK, EDGAR MEYER & MIKE MARSHALL'S "TRAVIS")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. We're speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes, editor in chief of The Economist. We're discussing trade tariffs, the economic impact of the war in Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Minton Beddoes just returned from a reporting trip to Ukraine, where she conducted interviews and visited the operations center of an elite drone unit in Ukraine. We're also looking at the state of U.S. relations with our longtime allies, including Europe, Canada and the United Kingdom. We recorded our conversation yesterday.

All right. Well, let's talk about some other things going on in the world, starting with the conflict in the Middle East. President Trump says the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, and plenty of oil is flowing. The reality is somewhat different, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: Well, I actually think some oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz under the new arrangements that the U.S. military has put in place. Exactly how much is the matter of some debate, but there is certainly some oil flowing at greater cost. But that doesn't mean that we're back to where we were before the war. I mean, clearly, Iran is trying very hard to control the strait. Clearly, you now have the additional concern of what is happening with the Houthis, who are also trying to control another route out of the region. So there is lots of debate about just how much oil is getting out. But what's very clear, Dave, is that there isn't as much as there was before, and there certainly isn't refining product coming out as there was before. And that which is is much more expensive.

DAVIES: Right, and prices remain very high. Do you see any prospect for a resolution of this conflict within the foreseeable future?

MINTON BEDDOES: Both sides say that, you know, there is a deal to be done, but that deal is the one on their terms. I think it seems to me unlikely that there is going to be a serious resolution anytime soon because Iran is determined to have a resolution much more on its terms, which President Trump is not willing to have. And Iran - you know, the Iranian regime is showing that it has an incredible capacity to endure economic pain. And I think where we are now is we have a U.S. government that is convinced that the more it can tighten the economic screws on Iran, at some point, the Iranian regime is going to have to cave and come to a deal on U.S. terms. And we have an Iranian regime, which, of course, has several factions within it, of which at least the hard-liners are absolutely not - determined not to cave and have shown themselves willing to inflict incredible pain on their population.

So my sense is that the likely outcome is some version of the status quo for a while. And then either President Trump decides that he's going to go and try and bombard them into submission, or we go back to the agreement that was, you know, temporarily reached a few months ago, which is much more advantageous to Iran.

DAVIES: There was a story a while back that the Saudis had asked Trump to bomb the Houthis, who are making gains against the Saudi-backed regime in Yemen, and that Trump thought about doing it but in the end didn't. I mean, the problem, of course, is that when you increase hostilities in one place, there's a reaction elsewhere. You know, the Iranians can attack American allies. And Trump's kind of in a box here, isn't he?

MINTON BEDDOES: I actually think that that was a very meaningful moment. That decision, you're right. It appears that the Saudis asked for help, and, you know, President Trump decided no. If you stand back from this, we may well find that however this war turns out, it ends up being a turning point in the U.S. relationship with the region. And this was the story we put on our cover last week and looked into in some detail. And let me explain why I think that. You know, what have we learned from this war now? First of all, we've learned that the Gulf countries which relied on U.S. bases for their security have found that, actually, having U.S. bases doesn't necessarily provide you with security.

DAVIES: It can make you a target, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: It can make you a target. We found that there's been a huge use of U.S. munitions, which is going to have knock-on effects for U.S. security all around the world. And we've learned that probably going forward, you know, what U.S. bases remain in the region will have to be moved and probably put underground to be safe because we are now in this new drone-based warfare, which changes the calculus. If you add all of that together, it seems to me that it may well be that the sort of medium-term impact of this is fewer U.S. forces in different places and, thus, less of a U.S. footprint in the region. And instead, players from Iran, depending on what happens there, to Turkey, to, of course, Israel on the other side are going to be shaping the region sort of with less of an active U.S. involvement than there was. I think we may look back in a couple of decades and see this Iran war as being a turning point. I mean, I'm not suggesting the U.S. is going to leave completely, but I think the U.S. is going to be less involved than it was.

DAVIES: Let's talk about the state of U.S.-Western Europe alliances. You know, Trump condemned European countries that declined to support his war against Iran and help him with the blockade of Iran. He made all those bellicose statements about acquiring Greenland. There have been lots of tensions over tariffs and trade. What's the state of the Western alliances at this point?

MINTON BEDDOES: Well, there's just been a great agreement on Greenland - right? - where we've now got a formal agreement to the status quo effectively.

DAVIES: Right, kind of it gives the U.S. access to places that it pretty much had access to already access to before.

MINTON BEDDOES: Which it had access to before, exactly. Look, I think the big picture is that, first of all, the Europeans have woken up, not before time, to the need to build up their own defensive capability, to spend more on defense. And frankly, President Trump deserves a lot of credit for pushing the Europeans to do that, because for too long, the Europeans have been freeloading off the United States.

At the same time, however, there is a growing sense within Europe of, we're just not sure whether we can rely on the U.S. And, you know, Greenland was one example. But more broadly now, you know, if, for example, we were talking earlier about the risk of Russian hybrid attacks or Russian attacks on European countries - now, these won't be, you know, full-on invasions with tanks rolling across the border, but they will be - they are already attacks. Now, what does NATO do in that environment? You know, is this going to get anywhere near an Article 5 collective-security moment? And even if it was, what would the United States do?

And I think in Europe now, there is a growing recognition that we just can't rely on the U.S. And now, being Europeans, we're spending a huge amount of time talking about this and not doing very much. But there is a sense that there is a new world now. And that new world is one where the Western alliance that sort of, you know, was set up by the Americans after the second world war and underwritten by the United States is now in a different phase. And I'm not quite sure which of the stages of grief we're at, but there's...

DAVIES: (Laughter).

MINTON BEDDOES: ...A kind of, you know, recognition. And I don't think - people haven't really worked out what to do. And so you have, you know, Prime Minister Carney of Canada basically - you know, he's declared it a rupture and is calling for the middle powers to work together. Within Europe, there are some Europeans who are still saying, eschew it (ph), absolutely. We can't do anything without the Americans. We must keep this alliance going. Then there are others - you know, the French in particular - who are pushing and always have in a sort of Gaullist way for a more European-only approach. We're not yet at the stage of having a coherent, let alone an effective response in Europe. But I think it's - there is no doubt that the world what was, to use a very grammatically accurate phrase, has gone.

And I'm not in the kind of business of pearl-clutching for what was. I think the challenge now for Europeans and for many others around the world is to, in a kind of eyes-wide-open way, say, OK. This is the United States we have now. It is the United States that has a different view of alliances than it used to. It's extraordinarily powerful. It's the country leading in the AI revolution that is going to shape warfare and our economies and everything else. What's our relationship with this country, and what are we going to do for ourselves? And that's the question we're beginning to ask ourselves in Europe. Unfortunately, we don't yet have a good answer.

DAVIES: All right. Let's take another break here. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll talk more after this break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF CHARLIE HADEN'S "EL CIEGO (THE BLIND)")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. And my guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. We're looking at the war in Ukraine and other topics, including the conflict in the Middle East and the state of Western alliances. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, we were talking about how European governments are not quite sure what to make of the United States. And, well, there's just been a lot of ruptures over a lot of issues. And it seems to me that if you wanted to characterize President Trump's foreign and trade policies in a word, the word would be erratic, right? I mean, you just never know what's going to happen. Tariffs go up, go down. He gets angry about this. He gets angry about that. And I wonder if European leaders see in him someone who leads with such a personally impulsive style that once he passes from the scene, which will happen in a couple of years, it can return to something like the kinds of - set of relationships that existed before.

MINTON BEDDOES: So I'm going to slightly take issue with your characterization. I think erratic doesn't quite do justice...

DAVIES: OK.

MINTON BEDDOES: ...To what's going on. I think there is a kind of mindset behind what this administration does that is a very clear one. It's not as though they're going sort of willy-nilly from one position to another completely orthogonal one. I think broadly, this is an administration that believes in wielding American power for America's own benefit, doing so in a transactional way rather than an - believing in alliances and doing so without any embarrassment, and, you know, focusing on that power and the wielding thereof.

And to sort of put it somewhat extremely, it is a sort of slight mafia don approach. But it's - it is very much rooted in America First. We are going all out to maximize American power - you know, hence the administration's focus on being on the accelerationist side of artificial intelligence. It's, we are going to dominate. And we are going to use our ability to dominate, whether it is in economic sanctions, whether it is in acts of war, to achieve our own purposes. And everybody else is either with the program on our terms, but it's all about us.

And if you look at the world through that prism, and you think alliances aren't very important, and you think international rules aren't very important, and you - the United States - can kind of bully your way around because you are the most powerful country, then the relationships with the rest of the world kind of make sense.

DAVIES: I think you're right. There is a coherent set of goals here. I - there - but there's also a way in which, you know, the strategy and tactics themselves can vary widely. I mean, the tariffs can be really high and then go back really low, and...

MINTON BEDDOES: Yeah.

DAVIES: You know, it's - you know.

MINTON BEDDOES: I think that's 'cause President Trump uses tariffs as his own personal sort of, you know, stick with which to beat people and countries to show kind of displeasure. So tariffs, if you are a country that pursues a policy he doesn't like. Tariffs, if he thinks it's an unfair trading arrangement. Tariffs, if he's just generally displeased with what the country is doing. I'm not going to pretend there's a kind of economic logic to it. There isn't. And you're right. He sort of changes his mind every five minutes as to which countries he wants to wield them against and for what. It's not a coherent economic policy toolkit. It's not even terribly effective, actually. And of course, ultimately, the people who suffer are American consumers.

It's also a very, very difficult position for others to work out a coherent policy response to. If you're a European country or if you're any of America's trading partners and you're not quite sure when there's a tariff threat - is it real? Is it going to last? Is it going to change? What does it mean? - it's like a massive tax on global commerce the entire time.

DAVIES: Are Europeans looking towards the midterm elections to alter the course of American foreign policy at all, do you think?

MINTON BEDDOES: I think everyone around the world is transfixed by American politics, particularly right now.

DAVIES: Really? Gosh.

MINTON BEDDOES: I think there is...

(LAUGHTER)

MINTON BEDDOES: There is a - an expectation, a hope, that something will change after the midterms. I mean, the - they - you know, Europeans can look at the polling as well as anybody else. And you know that - I think according to our own forecast - we, as you know, have a midterm forecast model, which gives - I think it's, like, a 93% chance now that the House goes to the Democrats. And it's something like a 60% chance that the Senate does.

DAVIES: I read that.

MINTON BEDDOES: There's a sort of...

DAVIES: And I was surprised by that. Yeah.

MINTON BEDDOES: Yeah. There's a hope that that will happen. I have to say, my own expectation is that even if that happens, I don't expect an enormous change in American foreign policy. In fact, if anything, I worry that President Trump will focus more on foreign policy if the Democrats are in charge in Congress as a way of distracting attention. And there's an awful lot that the president can do, as you know, without Congress in the foreign policy arena.

DAVIES: Well, you know, Canada is an interesting case. I mean, you mentioned this. Mark Carney made that speech in Davos about middle powers having to seek an independent path and not rely on the alliances they have in the past. I mean, he's also said recently that he speaks frequently with President Trump and that they get along personally. I mean, what do you make of him, his course? And he's also talked about joining the EU as - what? - an associate member or something. And if - I don't even know if that's a thing.

MINTON BEDDOES: I actually think Mark Carney has done a really extraordinary job at managing a situation that is very, very difficult as Canadian prime minister. And I've known Prime Minister Carney for a while. He used to be a - you know, when he was governor of the Bank of England, and before that, he was a central banker in Canada. And I used to write about economics, so I've known him for a long time. And I am struck by how well this technocratic former central banker has become a very effective politician.

And his - as far as I can see, his strategy is one to really try and reshape the Canadian economy to make it more resilient - to, you know, cut regulation, to build up its defense, to make it a much more effective domestic economy. He also wants to try and build up trading relationships with others - you know, particularly Europe, but also, you remember he was in China not so long ago - so that he - over time, the Canadian economy becomes less reliant on the U.S. But I think he's also very well aware that at the moment, the Canadian economy is incredibly integrated with the U.S.

So there is this difficult balancing act between trying to work with President Trump, negotiate with President Trump, but also, politically, he can't cave to whatever, you know, crazy demands the American administration may make. And so I think it's very sensible to be talking a lot to President Trump and to try and have a working relationship. It's also important to stand up when something completely impossible is put on by the American side and to try and do the reforms that make your own economy as strong as possible and to try and build up relationships with others. It's a tough thing to do all of those things, but actually, I think he's been doing pretty well.

DAVIES: We need to take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll continue our conversation in just a moment. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF TODD SICKAFOOSE'S "BARNACLE")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. And our guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, there have been right-wing populist parties that have made significant gains in a number of European countries - France, you know, Germany, Italy, of course - Giorgia Meloni. I'm just wondering how you think that affects relations with the United States. Does Trump find friendly voices and support there that reinforce his own goals, do you think?

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think next year, 2027, is going to be a really pivotal year for Europe. There are elections in a number of European countries, but most importantly in France. And right now, as you know, Marine Le Pen leads the polls. I think there is a very real chance that Marine Le Pen, head of the RN - the populist-right party - could be the next president of France. And at the same time, the more extreme, right-wing AfD in Germany is not anywhere near power at the federal level, but is certainly the most successful party at the polls and winning at state-government level.

Europe could see populist right-wing governments in power in one or more countries next year. The question is, what does that mean for the whole European Union project? What does it mean for Europe's own decision-making? What does it mean for Europe's willingness to continue to support Ukraine? And what does it mean for Europe's relationship with the United States?

And I think it's an - there's sort of an interesting thing to watch here, 'cause on the one hand, you're right that some of these parties have had very close ties with MAGA, you know, have very strong ties with the Trump administration. But on the other hand, the more sort of bullying the Trump administration is towards Europe, the more difficult it is for a populist nationalist party to be too closely associated. So if you look - for example, Giorgia Meloni, the prime minister of Italy - she was very close to President Trump. But over time, she has had to distance herself because it's just very unpopular domestically.

So I think there are two separate questions. Will there be populist, nationalist governments in Europe next year, and what does it mean for Europe? And then separately, how will those governments behave towards the United States? And I don't think necessarily those two things point in the same direction.

DAVIES: And how do those populist parties regard Russia and its, you know, territorial ambitions in Ukraine?

MINTON BEDDOES: It's interesting. There's an interesting division between them. Giorgia Meloni has been very pro-Ukraine, very clearly, you know, with the European mainstream in supporting Ukraine. Interestingly, just in the last couple of weeks, Marine Le Pen and her party put out a statement loudly criticizing the Russian hybrid attacks in Europe and saying how unacceptable it was. The one party that is seen as being very pro-Russian, very determined to end support for Ukraine, is the German Alternative fur Deutschland - the German AfD. And that's the party that people are most worried about as being really, very close to the Russians.

DAVIES: Interesting. Over the summer, the United Kingdom got a new prime minister - Andy Burnham. What are some of the challenges he faces? Seventh prime minister in the last decade, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: I know. We change our prime ministers...

DAVIES: (Laughter).

MINTON BEDDOES: ...You know, like we change our clothes nowadays. I - Prime Minister Burnham is a more natural politician than his predecessor. He's a man comfortable on social media. He's authentic, as they like to say. He's got some serious challenges. We don't have the world's reserve currency - the dollar. We're a much smaller market. And our debt - gilt yields. I mean, that's what British debt is called. Gilt yields are rising very sharply. And he has a big challenge.

You know, he needs to raise some money to make the books balance. That almost certainly has to come from cutting welfare spending, reforming - breaking some promises to pensioners. It's politically tough, but it has to be done. So one question is, will he be bold enough to do that, even though it was something that in their manifesto, his party said they wouldn't? Where would he find...

DAVIES: He's a Labour - (inaudible) - Labour Party, yup.

MINTON BEDDOES: He's a Labour prime minister, yes. The second is, will he do what is necessary to enable the British economy to grow faster? There's, again, a very well-known list of things that needs to be done - planning reform to make it easier to build houses, infrastructure reform, improvements in the tax system. You know, there are very kind of - the interesting thing about the U.K. is that there's a sort of - if you put a whole bunch of economists and technocrats in a room, they would come up with almost the same list of what needs to be done. It's just politically difficult.

DAVIES: What are his relationships like with President Trump and the EU, the European Union?

MINTON BEDDOES: Prime Minister Burnham met President Trump for the first time last week at the U.N. By all accounts, it was a cordial conversation. He's a very personable guy. He is very comfortable in his own skin. I think, even though he said some fairly, you know, critical things about President Trump in the past, he's a very affable man. I'm sure it would have been a good conversation. You know, Prime Minister Burnham, like every British prime minister right now, is having to navigate a path where you keep the U.S. on sight. I mean, we're very proud of the special relationship. We're very proud of, you know, having a kind of better relationship with the U.S. than many other Europeans, but at the same time, trying to work with other European countries.

DAVIES: OK, last question. At his speech in the United Nations, President Trump talked about U.S. power and I think said to the victor belongs the spoils. How was that received by Europeans?

MINTON BEDDOES: That goes back to what we were discussing earlier. I do think there's just a very different world view from this administration. It's one about, you know, exerting U.S. power. It's about power and power projection. And it's about victors and spoils. And that is very different from the alliance-based view that not just Europe, but America's other alliances, its Asian allies, have long thought the Western world was based on.

And I think everyone is coming to terms with that, is trying to understand whether this is President Trump specific or whether this is a new American posture, and what it means for others. It's trying to make sense of that. Every country I go to, every government official I talk to, wherever, that's the single most important question. Where is the U.S. going? What do they want? What kind of a world do they want? What role do they want to play? How do they see this working?

Because whether we all like it or not, the U.S. is the most important player in the room. And so we all have to understand what it wants. And for those of us who, you know, thought that a world based on rules and alliances was a world that was not just good for the world, but good for the U.S., this is a big change.

DAVIES: Right. And the question is whether there's a real change in the American mentality about it, or is it really just this particular president who is pretty unique?

MINTON BEDDOES: And I think we won't know the answer to that until after '28.

DAVIES: Right. Zanny Minton Beddoes, great to talk to you. Thank you so much for speaking with us.

MINTON BEDDOES: Thank you. Lovely to talk to you.

DAVIES: Zanny Minton Beddoes is editor in chief for The Economist. We recorded our conversation yesterday.

On tomorrow's show, Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow. She just released her 12th studio album and is still touring. She says the job feels different now that she's in her 60s. I hope you can join us.

To keep up with what's on the show and get highlights of our interviews,
