World.title: ‘Transparent and competitive, but also cause for concern’: PACE report on Armenia’s elections
World.content:
PACE report on Armenia’s elections

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe’s election observation mission has published a report on the parliamentary elections, which took place in Armenia on 7 June.

“The elections were competitive, and citizens had a genuine choice between different political forces and alternatives,” the report says.

Observers also found the process well organised and transparent, with no serious incidents.

At the same time, they identified several serious problems. In particular, they expressed concern over a post-election dispute involving the invalidation of voting results at polling stations 10/51, 35/65 and 12/13. PACE experts believe that if officials had counted those votes, the opposition Prosperous Armenia party could have crossed the four per cent threshold and won seats.

Meanwhile, the Central Election Commission said the annulment of the results at these polling stations did not affect the election outcome. It therefore decided not to hold repeat voting there. However, PACE described the decision as “unsatisfactory, given the significance of its consequences”.

“A perfectly acceptable option would have been to hold repeat voting at the relevant polling stations. The CEC rejected this without providing serious justification. Authorities should base such an important decision on strong, transparent and verifiable grounds. Unfortunately, that did not happen,” said Swiss politician Damien Cottier, one of the report’s authors.

Armenian journalists also noted that MPs from the ruling party and the opposition selectively presented PACE’s assessment to the public. They quoted and highlighted the parts of the document that supported their respective positions.

“Politicians often resort to such tactics. In English, there is an expression for this: cherry-picking. Politicians select and present only the findings that portray them in a positive light, while ignoring or downplaying the negative ones,” Factor TV said in a report.

Main concerns

“Interference by the Russian Federation and foreign information operations in a Council of Europe member state have reached unprecedented levels,” the report says.

According to the PACE mission, Russia used economic restrictions and tough diplomatic rhetoric to influence the election results in favour of the pro-Russian opposition.

The report also identifies the following problems:

abuse of administrative resources,

biased coverage on public television and by key opposition media outlets,

some Karabakh Armenians being unable to vote because bureaucratic delays prevented them from obtaining Armenian citizenship,

unprecedented external interference and geopolitical pressure.

PACE recommendations

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called on Armenia to amend its electoral code:

“The law should clearly require repeat voting whenever the fundamental right of a political force to have representation [in parliament] comes into question. It should also establish a clear threshold and procedures for such cases.”

The observation mission also recommends that the Armenian authorities take the following steps:

strengthen the resilience of the electoral process and democratic institutions, particularly by increasing national capacity to identify and counter Russian information operations and economic pressure tools;

broaden the range of people who can challenge electoral disputes in court, extend appeal deadlines and introduce more flexible remedies for violations;

ensure the independence of the process for appointing members of electoral commissions;

fully regulate the use of administrative resources and effectively punish any abuse of them;

end the selective prosecution of opposition figures and guarantee compliance with all procedural rules in election-related court proceedings;

guarantee the right of all political forces to hold peaceful assemblies;

simplify documentation requirements for displaced people and vulnerable groups of voters, and speed up the citizenship and registration processes.

PACE said it stood ready to work with the Armenian authorities to address all these issues.

Ruling party and opposition representatives on the report

Hayk Konjoryan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction and deputy speaker of parliament, emphasised that the report described the elections as “well organised”. He also highlighted the following points from the document:

voters had a genuine choice between political alternatives,

observers gave the electoral process a positive assessment at the vast majority of polling stations they monitored.

Konjoryan also highlighted the PACE observers’ assessment that the elections took place amid major geopolitical transformations. They described the scale of external interference in Armenia’s affairs as “unprecedented and alarming”.

The deputy speaker also pointed to the report’s description of the economic restrictions and political pressure that outside actors imposed on Armenia during the pre-election campaign. The report explicitly says that the goal was to influence voters and encourage them to vote for opposition forces.

“According to the report, the election results show that society demonstrated its democratic resilience despite unprecedented external pressure and the shortcomings identified. The PACE report says that the elected authorities received a clear mandate from the people, which they must now carry out with honour,” Konjoryan concluded.

Narek Karapetyan, head of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, focused on other points in the report. He highlighted the following problems identified by European parliamentarians:

“On unlawful detentions

The number of searches and arrests of opposition politicians, activists and candidates has increased significantly.

The observation mission stressed that these measures undermined electoral fairness and had a significant chilling effect on the opposition’s election campaign.

On administrative resources

The ruling party used official government platforms, public infrastructure and administrative levers to support its campaign. This significantly distorted the campaign environment and prevented opposition forces from competing on an equal footing.

On pre-election bribery

While law enforcement agencies promptly launched high-profile investigations into alleged vote-buying and illegal campaign financing by opposition factions, they dealt with similar allegations and complaints against ruling-party representatives far less thoroughly or more slowly.

On election fraud

“Prosperous Armenia” could have crossed the four per cent threshold for entering parliament, won seats and deprived the ruling party of its three-fifths majority.”

“A one-sided approach”: Factor TV’s assessment

Journalists from Factor TV examined the report itself as well as MPs’ comments.

In their view, Konjoryan and Karapetyan presented diametrically opposed interpretations of the same document:

ruling-party MP Hayk Konjoryan completely ignored the parts of the report that criticise the authorities and highlight abuses of administrative resources and shortcomings in the electoral process.

opposition MP Narek Karapetyan focused only on accusations against the authorities, while ignoring sections that confirm the legitimacy of the elections and document external pressure.

“Both sides present only the half of the truth that suits them. But even combining these two perspectives does not provide the full picture. For example, the report contains statements that criticise both the authorities and the opposition.”

The document says:

“Extreme polarisation in society and mass protests created a tense domestic political environment. Years of confrontation and ongoing [unfinished] legal and institutional reforms have weakened confidence in the possibility of achieving political change through institutions and elections.”

The journalists concluded that each side highlighted passages criticising its opponents while leaving out criticism of its own political force.

PACE report on Armenia’s elections

World.title: Iranian ambassador calls history of Georgian Queen Ketevan “controversial”, sparking criticism in Georgia
World.content:
Scandal over Iranian ambassador’s remarks in Georgia

Iranian ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Mojani has announced the publication of his own research on Georgian Queen Ketevan. His remarks about the need to “re-examine” history have drawn criticism from a Georgian historian and MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party. The dispute centres on the ambassador’s references to different historical accounts without specifying which generally accepted facts he is questioning.

What did the ambassador write?

Mojani, a historian by profession, posted a photograph on Facebook showing the facade of the Iranian embassy with an image of Queen Ketevan projected onto it. He wrote that, for him, the image symbolises a historical memory surrounded by “numerous conflicting accounts that persist to this day”.

The ambassador promised to publish the findings of his preliminary research soon. The study will focus on Queen Ketevan and draw on Georgian and Iranian sources. Mojani stressed that it would not represent Iran’s official position but rather his personal perspective as a historian, which could be refined or revised in the future.

Mojani has not yet published either the study itself or the sources he intends to use.

Why did the post spark criticism?

Queen Ketevan was tortured to death in the Iranian city of Shiraz in 1624 on the orders of Shah Abbas I. Historical sources and academic studies document her martyrdom. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates Ketevan as a saint and commemorates her on 26 September.

Against this backdrop, some interpreted Mojani’s reference to “conflicting accounts” as a suggestion that the ambassador was questioning the history of Ketevan’s martyrdom.

Historian and lecturer Giorgi Javakhishvili believes the ambassador’s statement goes beyond his diplomatic mandate. According to him, “Queen Ketevan’s martyrdom is a fact.” Javakhishvili also accuses Mojani of disregarding the methodology and ethics of historical research.

Georgian Dream MPs react

Nikoloz Samkharadze, chairman of parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, urged the ambassador to “stick to diplomatic protocol and refrain from delving into history”. Samkharadze said he would discuss the incident with Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili when she returns to Georgia.

MP Irakli Kadagishvili said Mojani’s statement had nothing to do with the embassy’s work, stressing that the ambassador should perform his duties within the scope of his authority.

MP Aluda Gudushauri expects the foreign ministry to respond, noting that “no one can change or distort the true course of our history — reality is what it is and what we know it to be”.

The ambassador’s previous statements

Mojani’s posts have sparked controversy in Georgia before. On 31 March, he wrote that “countries that willingly or unwillingly surrender their space and territory to foreign adventurers sooner or later pay the price within their own borders”. The ambassador did not name any specific country, but some analysts and politicians interpreted the post as a threat against Georgia.

Scandal over Iranian ambassador’s remarks in Georgia

World.title: Abkhazia and Russia agree to mutually recognise customs inspection results
World.content:
Abkhazia and Russia have agreed to mutually recognise the results of customs inspections. The agreement is expected to speed up the clearance of goods at the Russian border on the Psou River.

Negotiations on the agreement took more than four years. Russia’s Federal Customs Service and Abkhazia’s Customs Committee signed the relevant protocol on 25 September.

The protocol provides for the electronic exchange of information on customs inspection results. This means that if one side has already inspected goods or a vehicle, the other side can use the results of that inspection in certain cases instead of conducting it again.

Abkhazia’s Customs Committee said the new mechanism should reduce border crossing times and ease pressure on checkpoints.

“This is particularly important during the holiday and citrus seasons, when passenger and vehicle traffic increases. We expect the new electronic cooperation mechanisms to shorten the time needed to complete the necessary procedures and improve the capacity of border checkpoints,” said Customs Committee head Otar Khetsia.

Previously, customs officials from both Abkhazia and Russia inspected each shipment separately. Disputes often arose when one side questioned the documents provided by the cargo owner and required the entire shipment to be unloaded. This caused queues at the border, much to the frustration of cargo owners.

Abkhaz officials say that the mutual recognition of customs inspection results is standard international practice and does not infringe on the sovereignty of either side.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia-Russia customs deal

World.title: Removing Catholicos Garegin II from office to resolve crisis: Armenia debates special report
World.content:
Report on crisis in Armenian Church

“Violation of vows of celibacy and proper conduct, politicisation of the Holy Altar, spread of foreign [Russian] influence and persecution of clergy.” These are among the arguments cited by the Public Relations and Information Centre as evidence of a crisis in the Armenian Apostolic Church. The centre prepared and published the report at the request of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.

The 74-page document sets out not only information identified from open sources that its authors say demonstrates a crisis, but also proposals for resolving it.

Among the steps proposed to resolve the crisis is the removal of Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. The report refers to him not as the Catholicos, but as the “de facto head of the Church”.

The authors stress that reform should be carried out by the Church itself, with the participation of clergy and believers, while the state should act within its legal powers “without interfering in the Church’s internal canonical autonomy”.

Meanwhile, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin has described the report as “unconstitutional, anti-canonical and unlawful in both content and form”.

In a statement issued in response, the senior clergy called on the authorities to “end the persecution of the Church and respect its centuries-old sovereignty and self-governance”.

Human rights advocates have also raised concerns about the document. Anna Melikyan, a lawyer and expert on international humanitarian law and human rights, argues that the government has no right to interfere in the internal affairs of a religious organisation unless “a crime or administrative offence” has been committed.

Religious freedom expert Izabella Sargsyan focuses on information contained in the document that she says “violates human rights and the right to privacy”. She said the report reminded her of “a tabloid publication”.

Pashinyan: ‘Situation in Church far more critical than I thought’

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan commented on the report shortly after its publication. In a video address posted on his Facebook page, Pashinyan said he had reviewed the document and concluded that the actual situation in the Church was far more complex and critical than he had initially believed:

“If I were to sum up the report in one sentence, it proves that the Church has been captured by Ktrich Nersisyan [Garegin II’s secular name] and a group of clergy and laypeople who support him.”

In a recent interview, Pashinyan did not rule out establishing an investigative commission in the National Assembly that would propose legislative changes based on the problems identified in the report.

Report cites allegations of ‘paedophilia and homosexual tendencies’

The report lists 16 points that its authors say demonstrate a crisis within the Church. One concerns alleged violations of vows of celibacy and proper conduct by senior clergy. The document also says such cases have not received appropriate attention or investigation from the Church’s senior leadership.

The authors include cases of child sexual abuse among violations of “proper conduct”. According to the report, allegations have also been made against the Catholicos’s brother:

“The most serious allegations concerning the sexual abuse of children relate to the brother of the de facto head of the Armenian Apostolic Church [Garegin II] – Archbishop Yezras Nersisyan, Primate of the Russian and New Nakhichevan Diocese.”

The document also says there are claims concerning his “homosexual tendencies”. It cites various articles, open letters – mostly by defrocked clergy – and media reports as supporting material.

The report includes personal information about both those whose accounts it cites and those accused of “paedophilia” or described as having “homosexual tendencies”.

“Moral decline has become entrenched within the Church’s internal structures. Some clergy suspected or accused of sexual offences, particularly paedophilia, not only go unpunished but also enjoy the protection of the senior leadership,”the document says.

Among the alleged problems within the Church highlighted by the report are:

the Catholicos’s alleged violation of his vow of celibacy;

alleged persecution and defrocking of clergy by the Catholicos;

overt political activity by the Catholicos and several senior clergy;

the use of Church premises and the Holy Altar for political campaigning;

the alleged use of the Church by the Catholicos and members of his family to promote foreign influence;

a lack of financial transparency and alleged misuse of Church property;

the ordination of relatives and alleged clan-based governance;

the failure to convene a National Ecclesiastical Assembly for 27 consecutive years and the absence of a unified charter;

divisions within dioceses in the diaspora.

What action plan is proposed?

The report proposes a five-step roadmap for overcoming the crisis:

reviewing and promoting the reform programme;

removing the de facto head of the Church (the Catholicos);

electing a locum tenens;

adopting a unified Church charter;

convening a National Ecclesiastical Assembly in accordance with procedures set out in the new charter and electing the Catholicos of All Armenians.

Mother See calls report ‘an act of political retribution’

“The ‘report’, compiled using public funds and based on accusations and defamatory claims circulated on social media and in the media, is an act of political retribution, vindictiveness and unacceptable interference in the internal life of the Church,” the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said.

The clergy called on the Armenian authorities to build Church-state relations on the basis of mutual respect, a clear separation of powers and the primacy of national interests. They also called for:

“an end to the persecution of clergy and the popularly elected Catholicos of All Armenians through fabricated accusations and defamation;

action strictly within the framework of the Constitution, national legislation and international law, in line with proclaimed democratic principles, guaranteeing freedom of conscience, religion and belief in the country and strengthening social solidarity rather than division;

existing problems and disagreements to be resolved through dialogue, without preconditions and without resorting to futile ultimatum-style rhetoric.”

According to the Mother See’s statement, the authorities are attempting to artificially create a crisis within the Church:

“Any initiatives to reform the Church that are driven by political arbitrariness, manipulation or coercion are unacceptable. Efforts to address the challenges facing the Armenian Church and improve its functioning are carried out exclusively on the basis of decisions by the Church’s highest canonical governing bodies.”

Expert commentary

According to religious freedom expert Izabella Sargsyan, the government has no right to interfere in the Church’s internal affairs or prepare reports of this kind.

She argues that the report is unacceptable from the standpoint of legality, ethics and human dignity:

“This is not simply about freedom of religion or belief, or about an abuse of power by the government. It concerns personal data and the publication of names, including that of a minor who was allegedly subjected to sexual abuse.”

International humanitarian law and human rights expert Anna Melikyan stressed that Armenia’s Constitution clearly defines the relationship between the government and religious organisations, including their freedom of activity, separation from the state and autonomy:

“Freedom and autonomy mean that the government has no right to interfere in the internal affairs of a religious organisation, including its choice of governance system or efforts to bring it into line with canonical and ethical norms.”

She insists that neither the executive nor the legislature can decide who should lead a religious organisation or what internal rules it should adopt unless a criminal or administrative offence has been identified:

“If there are facts that provide reasonable grounds to suspect clear criminal or administrative offences, there are other mechanisms for responding to them – through criminal or administrative proceedings.”

The human rights expert says the confrontation between the government and the Church should be viewed in terms of the legality of the government’s actions in order to prevent possible unlawful interference.

She says an effective system of checks and balances should operate in a democratic state to prevent governments from being tempted to overstep their powers:

“All states and governments face this temptation, and if they encounter no resistance, they will seize as much power as they can.”

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Meydan TV case: ‘Investigator, prosecutor and judge in this case is Ilham Aliyev’
World.content:
Journalist testifies in Meydan TV case

On 28 September, journalist Shamshad Agha, founder and editor-in-chief of the Arqument.az website, testified at Baku Court on Grave Crimes in the Meydan TV case. He rejected the charges against him, said there were inconsistencies in the criminal case materials and linked his arrest to his journalistic work.

In his testimony to the court, the journalist also said he had been subjected to violence during his detention and threatened that members of his family would be brought to a police station unless he disclosed the password to his phone.

“The 30-volume criminal case is based entirely on groundless accusations. This whole collection of papers they call a ‘criminal case’ has been fabricated,” Shamshad Agha said.

On 6 December 2024, Meydan TV journalists Ramin Deko (Jabrayilzade), Aynur Ganbarova (Elgunesh), Aysel Umudova, Aytaj Ahmadova (Tapdig), Khayala Aghayeva and Natig Javadli were detained. They were charged under Article 206.3.2 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code with smuggling committed by a group of people acting in prior conspiracy. The criminal proceedings against them became known as the “Meydan TV case”. Journalists Shamshad Agha, Nurlan Libre, Fatima Movlamli, Ulviya Ali and Ahmad Mukhtar were later also arrested in connection with the case. In August this year, the charges against the journalists were expanded, with additional charges brought under other articles of the Criminal Code.

Meydan TV says the arrests are linked to its journalists’ critical reporting.

The full version of the article is available in the Azerbaijani-language section.

Who am I?

I am Shamshad Agha – Shamshad Islam oglu Aghayev, a citizen of Azerbaijan, a journalist and poet who has faced repression at the hands of the political and ideological heirs of Stalinism.

I was born on 1 September 1982 in the village of Shivla in Lerik District. My childhood unfolded against the backdrop of the pain the Karabakh conflict brought to those close to me. I grew up during the so-called “transition period”, tending lambs on mountain slopes with a book in my hands.

My father worked as a teacher for 40 years. His library and the books he gave me largely shaped my worldview and my understanding of injustice and the need to resist it.

At school, we studied literature from the period of Stalinist repression. The fate of intellectuals who fell victim to the “Red Terror” instilled in me a deep rejection of Stalinism and shaped my attitude towards its political and ideological heirs.

I particularly remember the words of repressed Azerbaijani writer Yusif Vazir Chamanzaminli: “I learnt to resist oppression and injustice from my mother.” My mother taught me the same. If I lose her while I am in prison and cannot attend her funeral, I am certain she will know that I did not side with injustice and oppression.

Azerbaijan’s state television recently broadcast a film about literary critic Seyid Huseyn, who was repressed under Stalin. Because of his family ties to one of the leaders of Azerbaijan’s independence movement and his closeness to an opposition party, he was executed after a 20-minute trial, while his wife was sentenced to eight years in exile.

And this is being shown by the state television of a country whose authorities today, in my view, persecute women and imprison them for writing and speaking the truth. I am certain that if the Siberian camps still existed today, they would be sent there too.

That is the irony of history and fate.

When did I become involved in public and political life?

I became actively involved in public and political life during my university years. In 2003, I was an activist in the student movement. Following the presidential election, whose results I considered unfair, pressure on politically active students at the university intensified. In solidarity with the opposition Musavat party, which was facing pressure at the time, several other students and I joined the party.

At the same time, I wrote articles, short stories and poetry, which were published in regional and national publications. While still a student, I joined the Union of Writers of Azerbaijan, but later left it and, together with like-minded writers, established an independent literary association.

In 2007, I graduated with honours from Lankaran State University and spent three years teaching Azerbaijani language and literature at the school I had once attended. At the same time, I continued working with media outlets and reporting on problems in the region.

In 2010, I committed myself fully to journalism, and in 2014 I established the independent website Arqument.az, of which I remain founder and editor-in-chief.

In 2016, together with Akif Gurbanov and Alasgar Mammadli, we founded the School of Democracy to train young journalists. Today, many of its founders, teachers and graduates are in prison on charges that I consider politically motivated.

Today, journalists, civil society representatives, activists and politicians facing repression by the Azerbaijani authorities are the voice of the country’s disenfranchised citizens

In my view, Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Meydan TV remain among the last platforms for freedom of expression in Azerbaijan. I am proud of my work with these independent media outlets and of my colleagues who are now on trial or in prison.

Journalism begins with doubt and courage. My colleagues have reported on the consequences of war, spoken out against restrictions on media freedom and continued their work even from prison. Some have received international recognition, while others have trained a new generation of journalists.

It is partly thanks to colleagues like these that I remain who I am. I’m glad you’re here, guys.

Why was I arrested?

In 2022, when Azerbaijan adopted a new law “On Media”, I actively opposed it and described it as a “death sentence for independent media”. I believed the authorities were seeking to push independent journalism out of the public sphere because, despite the considerable resources available to state and pro-government media, the public continued to trust independent sources of information.

While working as a presenter at Toplum TV, I heard even officials and MPs acknowledge that audiences placed greater trust in information from independent media. Meydan TV, which was established outside the country, also continued to overcome restrictions on access to information. In my view, the authorities chose to confront independent media through pressure rather than competition. The new law and the creation of a media register were part of this process. The Venice Commission also criticised the law. Many journalists, experts and civil society representatives who opposed it subsequently ended up in prison.

After the arrests of Abzas Media staff, I was approached, according to my account, by representatives of the security services who offered me co-operation, praising my professionalism and saying they needed my views as an expert. I refused. Further attempts were then made to contact me through intermediaries, and I later received a warning that I could be arrested. Despite this, I continued to refuse to co-operate.

Later, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin said after a visit to Baku that he had discussed joint action with the Azerbaijani side against Western-oriented media outlets and organisations. Soon afterwards, Sputnik Azerbaijan published an article mentioning me and Arqument.az, which I head, including our critical stance towards Russia over its war against Ukraine.

I saw this as a warning that I was about to be arrested. At the time, I continued meeting friends and defending my detained colleagues, and received several verbal warnings telling me to back down. But I could not do so. Otherwise, I would not have been able to look my colleagues – or former participants in our journalism training programmes who were already in detention – in the eye.

I did not back down out of heroism, but out of shame

One police officer told me that many people were afraid to protest because even mentioning certain names could have serious consequences. I replied that it was not about courage. We speak out because we are ashamed to remain silent in the face of injustice. It is this feeling that compels us to overcome our fear.

In my view, an authoritarian system seeks to suppress such civic courage by portraying independent journalists as people who supposedly “work for foreign powers”. But we are here because we spoke about what was happening in our own country.

How was I arrested?

At around 1am on 5 February 2025, I was detained near Neftchilar metro station. I say that I was beaten during my detention as officers demanded the password to my phone, and that I was denied medication for high blood pressure.

I was then taken to my home, where my brother and underage daughter were present. According to my account, one of the officers hit me when I told my family that I had been detained. I was not shown a court order authorising the search. Officers searched the flat and seized computers, phones, press cards and documents.

After finding no money in the flat, they again demanded my password and threatened to take my brother and daughter to the police station. To make them stop, I gave them the password. Despite my requests, my lawyer was not allowed to be present during the search.

At the Baku Main Police Department, I was asked to provide the password to my computer. I say that I was again subjected to violence, but I did not disclose the password. I refused to give evidence without a lawyer present.

After being questioned in the presence of my lawyer, during which I said my prosecution was politically motivated, I was placed in a temporary detention centre. On 6 February, Judge Rafael Sadigov ordered that I be remanded in custody. I consider the decision political and hold President Ilham Aliyev responsible for it.

After the court hearing, I was transferred to the Baku pre-trial detention centre. The stories of prisoners I met there reinforced my belief that the judicial and law-enforcement systems are unjust.

All this is happening in the 21st century in a country that is a member of the Council of Europe.

In my view, the existing system has an interest in the constant production of criminal cases, while investigative bodies seek to preserve their influence and privileges. Yet the state should not only prosecute alleged offenders but also address the causes of crime.

When a country has so many criminal cases and prisoners, society should consider the quality of governance. Where violence becomes an acceptable tool, it is difficult to speak of justice.

Every day in the pre-trial detention centre, I hear people praying and cursing those they believe are responsible for injustice. I wonder whether all this will ever end, and I am certain that it will. The authorities may try to drown out discontent through controlled media and entertainment, but in my view, one day it will turn into open protest.

Azerbaijan’s problems are not limited to media freedom and political rights. The country also faces serious social problems. According to official statistics, around 2.9 million people have registered medical conditions – almost a third of the population. I believe that talk of stability and victories conceals deep problems within society.

In my view, journalists are turned into political hostages precisely because they write about these problems. Meanwhile, those who investigate corruption and the transfer of state funds abroad are accused of receiving money from overseas. It is particularly disheartening that society often tolerates corruption and injustice. But I am certain this will not always be the case.

Alleged irregularities in the criminal case

I believe the 30-volume criminal case is based entirely on groundless accusations and was compiled in violation of the law. The prosecution alleges that I falsified documents but, in my view, has failed to provide convincing evidence.

In court, I pointed out that under Article 52.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, criminal case materials must be drawn up on specially numbered forms. I asked for these to be presented to the court, but it emerged that no such forms existed. On this basis, I believe the legal requirements governing the preparation of the case were not followed.

In my view, the prosecutor’s office should have discontinued the case, but instead effectively endorsed the alleged violations. I therefore hold both the prosecution representatives and the leadership of the prosecutor’s office responsible for them.

As a result, I believe that neither the 30 volumes of case materials nor the 600-page indictment based on them has proper legal validity. I maintain that numerous provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure were violated during the investigation and preparation of the charges. That is why, in seeking to prove my innocence, I am constantly forced to refer to domestic and international law, while the investigation and the court, in my view, disregard its requirements.

Under rulings by the Plenum of Azerbaijan’s Supreme Court and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, detaining a person requires evidence linking them to an offence and specific grounds for their detention. I believe the prosecution has provided no such evidence and that my detention is therefore unlawful.

At almost every hearing, I point to alleged violations and file motions, but the court rejects them. In my view, the charges are politically motivated and the case is not being examined objectively.

The investigator, prosecutor and judge in this case is Ilham Aliyev.

If President Ilham Aliyev has evidence that I was involved in smuggling or falsified documents, let him present it to the court. I am confident that an objective examination of the case materials will establish my innocence.

There are numerous contradictions in the case materials. I had never met Ulvi Tahirov and saw him for the first time in court. We had never communicated, and his testimony does not mention my name. Investigators have also presented no evidence linking me to Ramin Jabrayilzade, who, according to the case materials, was found with €38,000 when he was detained.

A record dated 16 January 2025 already identifies me as a defendant, even though I was not detained as a suspect until the night of 5 February. I was also linked to €40,000 from the Abzas Media case, although I am being tried as part of the Meydan TV case.

Investigators also cite my telephone conversations with Aynur Ganbarova, although their content has not been established. Another piece of purported “evidence” was a document stating that I had allegedly received €1,370, but a forensic examination commissioned by investigators found that the signature on it was not mine. An examination of my phones, laptop and storage devices also found no material of significance to the investigation.

I also consider the charge of illegal business activity to be unfounded: Arqument.az was officially registered in 2015, while I registered with the tax authorities as an individual in 2017. Investigators have also failed to specify which documents I allegedly falsified and used.

The claim that I repeatedly travelled abroad in 2024 and engaged in smuggling is also untrue: I did not leave the country at all that year.

I therefore believe that investigators have failed to present convincing evidence to support the charges of smuggling, illegal business activity, money laundering, document forgery and tax evasion.

As you can see, the prosecution has presented no evidence that I received grants from any organisations, engaged in money laundering or was involved in smuggling. Nevertheless, I remain in custody on the grounds that I might abscond from the investigation.

I consider this argument unfounded. In July 2024, as part of the Toplum TV case, an investigator conveyed through another witness that he wanted to question me. I called him myself and voluntarily went to the Baku Main Police Department the following day, where I gave evidence as a witness. If I had intended to abscond, why would I have contacted the investigator myself and gone in for questioning?

I was subsequently banned from leaving the country. The investigator justified the restriction by saying that I would allegedly be arrested in the near future. However, eight months passed, and I was eventually detained not in connection with the Toplum TV case but the Meydan TV case. According to my account, the investigator later said that if I had not been arrested in this case, another reason would have been found because the decision to arrest me had already been made.

I therefore consider the entire process unlawful and an act of politically motivated repression. In a country where political will takes precedence over the law, it is difficult to speak of a fair trial.

As Tolstoy wrote, when those who are supposed to uphold justice themselves commit injustices and show no respect for the law, human life or universal values, sooner or later this leads to grave consequences.

World.title: Local man in Abkhazia confesses to killing Russian tourist
World.content:
Killing of Russian tourist in Abkhazia

A local man in Abkhazia who allegedly killed a Russian tourist has confessed to the crime following his arrest. Edgar Abukhba had previously served a prison sentence for a serious offence – rape involving extreme violence.

Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry said it had detained a suspect in the killing of Russian national Amina Bikbova.

Amina Bikbova

A 26-year-old woman from Orenburg, Russia, was on holiday in the Abkhaz city of Gagra, where she met 25-year-old local fruit seller Edgar Abukhba.

The two exchanged messages for a couple of days. Then, on 24 September, Abukhba invited her for coffee, according to Amina’s friend. She has not been seen since and did not contact her family.

Concerned about their daughter’s disappearance, her parents contacted Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry.

A day later, the ministry announced that it had detained a suspect in the killing of the Russian tourist. He was identified as Edgar Abukhba.

Edgar Abukhba

Abukhba initially denied any involvement in Amina Bikbova’s disappearance. He said they “had coffee, and later a guy came to pick her up and drove her away”.

He later confessed to the killing and told investigators where he had hidden the body.

According to Abukhba’s account, after coffee he took the woman to the rented apartment where he was staying. They had sex, after which he strangled her.

He then planned to dump her body in the Bzyb River. But he was unable to carry the body all the way to the river, so he left it, wrapped in a blanket, on the riverbank.

Edgar Abukhba had previously committed a similar crime.

In July 2019, he lured a Russian tourist into the former Abkhaz Council of Ministers building in Sukhum and raped her with extreme violence. He then tried to kill her, striking her repeatedly on the head with a brick. The woman survived, but was left permanently disabled.

A lower court sentenced him to 19 years in prison. However, Abkhazia’s Supreme Court, hearing his appeal, took into account that Abukhba was 17 at the time of the crime and was therefore considered a minor.

His sentence was reduced from 19 to nine years in prison.

Abukhba was released on 2 February 2024.

If Abukhba is found guilty of killing Russian tourist Amina Bikbova, he could now face a life sentence.

Commentary

Sukhumi blogger Ruslan Shakov published a commentary asking whether the killing could have been prevented and whether anything could have been done to stop Abukhba from committing another serious sexual offence.

“The more I look into Amina’s story, the fewer questions I have about ‘who specifically released Edgar Abukhba’ and the more I have about what happened after his release.

“It is important to understand that there was no single judge who simply decided to cut his sentence.

“Abukhba was sentenced to nine years for raping a Russian tourist, robbery and causing grievous bodily harm. The case then went through several levels of court. Because of the way sentences are enforced in Abkhazia, he was actually released on 2 February 2024, after serving about 4½ years.

The nine-year sentence itself was not formally reduced. But that is not really the main question.

What happened to him after he was released?

Abkhazia has a law providing for administrative supervision of people released from prison. And this is where I have questions.

Were any monitoring or preventive measures put in place after Abukhba’s release? Who is responsible for assessing the risk that someone who has committed such a violent crime could do it again, and how is that risk assessed?

I am not saying that administrative supervision would necessarily have saved Amina. No one can know that. But when someone who has committed such a crime returns to society, the work should not end on the day of his release.

A systemic reform of the security system is needed: reviewing certain provisions of criminal law, tighter controls on firearms, and strengthening the Interior Ministry in terms of personnel and technical capacity. […]

And then there are the comments directed at Amina.

Yes, it can be said that you should not go to the home of someone you barely know. But a risky decision does not make someone responsible for their own murder.

Amina may not have known who she was dealing with or what was in his past. The authorities did.

At the same time, I disagree with attempts to attribute the crime of one individual to all of Abkhazia. After the family reported her disappearance, law enforcement identified and detained a suspect and found the woman’s body. The investigation is continuing.

But good police work after a killing does not remove the main question: could something have been done before it happened?

And here I would like to see not a search for one guilty agency or one particular person, but an honest examination of what needs to change in the law and across the security system to prevent similar cases from happening again.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘Which neighbouring country would you visit?’ Tbilisi street poll – VIDEO
World.content:
Travel poll in Georgia

We asked people on the streets of Tbilisi which of Georgia’s neighbouring countries they would like to visit and why.

We also asked whether they had previously travelled to any countries in the region, why they chose those destinations and what impressions they came away with.

The answers vary widely. Turkey is mentioned most often, with respondents drawn by its picturesque coastline and the Bosphorus. Many also say they would be happy to visit Armenia or Azerbaijan, while some look further afield and name more distant countries in the region.

Russia is rarely mentioned in a positive context. Instead, it is named by almost every respondent when asked which neighbouring country they would not like to visit.

Through this survey, we sought to find out how well people in Georgia know the countries of the South Caucasus and their other neighbours, what interests them about these countries and what stereotypes they hold about them.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Russia discuss military and military-technical cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. Meetings are being held as part of the 6th Azerbaijan International Defence Exhibition “ADEX-2026”, organized at the Baku Expo Center, to discuss issues related to the development of Azerbaijan’s military-technical cooperation with other countries.

This was stated in a report by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense.

According to the report, on September 30, Minister of Defense of the Republic of Azerbaijan Colonel General Zakir Hasanov met with a delegation from the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation headed by Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov.

The sides discussed the role of military and military-technical cooperation in ensuring peace and security in the region, as well as other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijani Defense Minister holds meetings with UK and Slovak counterparts (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. On September 30, a number of meetings were held as part of the 6th Azerbaijan International Defense Exhibition ADEX-2026, focusing on issues of Azerbaijan’s military-technical cooperation with other countries, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense reports.

According to the ministry, Azerbaijani Defense Minister Colonel General Zakir Hasanov held meetings with the defense ministers of the United Kingdom and Slovakia, who were participating in the international exhibition.

The Defense Minister emphasized that Azerbaijan is interested in cooperation with the United Kingdom and the Slovak Republic in all areas, particularly in defense and security, and expressed satisfaction with the current state of these relations.

The UK Minister of State for Defense, Lord Vernon Coaker, and Slovak Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defense Robert Kaliňák expressed their satisfaction with their visit to Azerbaijan and participation in the exhibition, noting that cooperation between the defense structures of the two countries in the areas of military education, military-technical innovations, as well as other fields, continues on a positive trajectory.

During the meetings, the ministers discussed future plans for cooperation in the areas of defence and security, military and military-technical fields, and held a broad exchange of views on matters of mutual interest.

World.title: Kazakhstan ready to become long-term supplier of critical raw materials to Germany
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. Kazakhstan is ready to become a reliable and long-term supplier of critical raw materials to German industry, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the Kazakhstan-Bavaria Technology Forum in Munich.

"As German industry seeks to strengthen supply security and diversify sources of essential resources, Kazakhstan is ready to become a reliable and long-term supplier of copper, titanium, aluminum, beryllium, tantalum and niobium,” Tokayev said.

According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan’s cooperation with Bavaria should increasingly focus on advanced technologies, high-tech manufacturing and joint access to new markets.

The President highlighted the broad presence of major Bavarian companies in Kazakhstan, including Siemens, Siemens Energy, Knauf and Horsch.

He also informed representatives of Bavarian businesses about the measures being taken to improve investment conditions, including the work of the Investment Headquarters under the Government and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).

Tokayev identified advanced manufacturing as one of the key areas for mutually beneficial cooperation. Kazakhstan is expanding production capacity in mechanical engineering, metallurgy, electrical engineering and industrial components, while further productivity growth will increasingly depend on automation, robotics and digital production management.

The President noted that companies such as Siemens and KUKA are global leaders in industrial automation, robotics and advanced manufacturing technologies, while major Kazakh enterprises, including Qarmet, can provide stable demand and reliable industrial partnerships.

“Our ambitions can be expressed in a simple formula: ‘Made in Kazakhstan using Bavarian technologies and with German quality,“ Tokayev said.

World.title: Kazakhstan keen to develop logistics hubs along TITR with Bavarian businesses
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed that Bavarian businesses jointly develop industrial and logistics hubs along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR).

According to the presidential press service, Tokayev made the proposal while speaking at the Kazakhstan-Bavaria Technology Forum, which brought together business, industrial and technology leaders as part of his official visit to Germany.

Tokayev outlined prospects for cooperation in microelectronics and semiconductor production.

According to the President, Bavaria has created one of Europe’s leading ecosystems in semiconductors and microelectronics, bringing together globally recognized companies such as Infineon Technologies, Siltronic and Rohde & Schwarz.

“For Kazakhstan, a realistic starting point is not large-scale chip manufacturing, but those segments of the value chain that directly contribute to the development of our industry,” Tokayev said.

He noted that the energy, mining and metallurgy, transport and manufacturing sectors are increasingly dependent on power electronics, sensors, measurement systems and sophisticated automated control systems.

In this regard, Tokayev proposed launching a special partnership program involving the Bavarian Chips Alliance and bringing together relevant Kazakh companies, research organizations and development institutions with Bavaria’s semiconductor industry ecosystem.

According to Tokayev, reliable transport and logistics connectivity is crucial for bringing new production facilities to international markets.

In this regard, the President proposed that Bavarian businesses jointly develop industrial and logistics hubs along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route.

The Kazakhstan-Bavaria Technology Forum concluded the President’s official visit to Germany.

World.title: 'The living conditions are so bad': Ex-detainee's warning for Hiep Tran
World.content:
A man who faced a similar fate to Australian human rights activist Hiep Tran, who has been charged with terrorism offences in Vietnam, says he believes his friend is facing years behind bars.

Chau Van Kham was released in 2023 after being detained in Vietnam for four and a half years on terrorism charges.

He said Mr Tran, who was detained by Vietnamese authorities earlier this month, is likely facing squalid conditions inside prison, with his every movement watched by an officer from the secret police.

"The living conditions are so bad," Mr Kham said.

"The heat, no fan, the lights are very small, no sunshine … it was a 12-metre square room for two people, including toilet, bathroom."

Family says activist abducted in Cambodia

Mr Tran, 50, from Melbourne, was charged this week after being abducted in Cambodia, according to his family.

Vietnamese authorities allege he was caught trying to cross the border illegally with forged documents.

Hiep Tran travelled to Cambodia with a colleague to visit human rights activists. (Supplied)

Mr Tran is a member of Viet Tan, a pro-democracy organisation the Vietnamese government considers a terrorist group, and was in Cambodia to meet with fellow human rights activists.

He has not been heard from since September 18 and missed his return flight to Bangkok the next day.

A Norwegian colleague, Nguyen Duc Thuan, and another man have also been detained.

Mr Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, said the Vietnamese government's claims made no sense.

She said he was due to fly out on September 19 and that she was going to meet him at the airport.

"On the news from Vietnamese authorities, they said they tried to break in and pass the border late at night on Friday the 18th. How can it be possible?" she said.

Chloe Dang says she does not know where her husband is being detained. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Ms Dang said neither she nor the Australian embassy in Hanoi was told he was in custody until Vietnamese state media reported it.

"I still don't know if he's OK, because until now we still don't know where he's being held and how his wellbeing is," she said.

"I really hope the Australian government can do something so we can get him to return home safely."

'Transnational repression'

Viet Tan executive director Duy Hoang believes Mr Tran was abducted by Vietnamese intelligence and brought back under fabricated charges.

"This is a real example of transnational repression. It's shocking," Mr Hoang said.

Duy Hoang says there was no evidence to suggest the men were planning to enter Vietnam. (Supplied)

He said the border crossing Vietnam cited was far from where Mr Tran was on the morning of September 18, and that the itinerary showed no plan to enter Vietnam.

He said authorities were now trying to "cover their tracks".

Mr Hoang said Vietnam had a track history of targeting its own citizens abroad but that the detention of both Australian and Norwegian nationals was unprecedented.

He called on the Australian government to demand consular access to the three men.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government was providing consular support to Mr Tran's family.

'Be confident'

Mr Kham said that when he was detained in 2019 on similar national security charges, it was weeks before Australian officials were granted consular access.

He does not believe Mr Tran will receive a fair trial.

"It's hopeless. They will keep them until they find out who in Vietnam cooperated with them. If not they will punish them into saying what they want," Mr Kham said.

Mr Kram says he worries Mr Tran will not receive a fair trial. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Mr Kham was sentenced to 12 years in prison before high-level negotiations through his lawyer and Australian government figures secured his release.

He said his advice to Mr Tran was to stay calm and relax.

World.title: Teenagers charged over bag snatches after allegedly targeting lone women
World.content:
Three males have been charged after youths allegedly carried out robberies in Melbourne's south-east targeting mostly lone women.

Two 16-year-olds and an 18-year-old man were arrested as part of an investigation that also involved a number of home invasions, petrol drive-offs and other offences allegedly committed by offenders last week.

Police are investigating the group over 21 incidents.

Police say two cars were stolen from outside a Glen Waverley gym about 5pm on Monday, September 21.

They say those vehicles were driven around Melbourne's bayside and south-eastern suburbs, where mostly women were targeted in a number of robberies last Thursday night.

A 64-year-old woman was dragged by several offenders and had her groceries stolen while waiting at traffic lights outside Chadstone Shopping Centre around 7:45pm.

A short time later, another woman was punched in the face and had her designer purse stolen at the same shopping centre.

Just after 8pm, a woman was shoved to the ground and had her bag stolen on the Princes Highway in Clayton before a woman had her handbag stolen as she left a hairdresser on Bluff Road in Highett.

About 8.40pm, offenders armed with a machete chased a male worker at a convenience store on Bluff Road in Black Rock before stealing cash.

Police are also investigating whether the same group of youths snatched a bag from a 54-year-old woman near the intersection of Bluff and Highett roads in Highett earlier in the day and stole a 74-year-old woman's bag as she walked along Beach Road in Beaumaris a day earlier.

Police collect evidence during the arrest of an 18-year-old man. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

An 18-year-old from Springvale has been remanded in custody on a series of charges including aggravated burglary, car theft and theft.

One of the 16-year-olds has been released on bail after being charged with car theft and handling stolen goods, while the other remained in custody on a string of charges including aggravated burglary and committing an offence while on bail.

Police say no-one has been charged in some of the robberies, and they continue to appeal to anyone who witnessed the incidents or has footage to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

World.title: For love, not money — Tasmania's elite eight ready to represent the map
World.content:
He's the 202-centimetre 17-year-old West Australian, who was the raging favourite to be taken at pick No.1 in next year's AFL draft.

His name is Axel Walsh, and if Tasmanians are unfamiliar with the baby-faced beanpole, they won't be for much longer.

Axel Walsh says he's excited about playing with the Devils. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Rise of Tasmanian Devils, JackJumpers leads to sports academy Tasmania's sports sector is creating jobs at a scale not previously seen, galvanising academic pathways for those seeking careers in sports management.

Walsh is one of eight elite 17-year-old footballers who have been pre-listed by the Tasmania Devils, a year ahead of when they were due to be drafted, as part of the club's bespoke list concessions.

And if he turns out to be half as good as his football heroes, the Devils have a superstar on their hands.

"I think a lot of people would go Luke Jackson," he said, when asked what his closest AFL player comparison would be.

"I have a lot of respect for his game.

"But someone I've always looked up to is Max Gawn. You see the success he's had, and I've looked up to him as a leader off the field as well."

Axel Walsh has family connections in Tasmania, which he says made it an easy choice to accept the Devils' offer. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

It was an easy decision for Walsh to accept the Devils' invitation to join the team, a year ahead of his official draft year.

Family ties encourage decision

With an aunty, uncle and three cousins residing in the Hobart suburb of Glenorchy, Walsh already considered himself "somewhat Tasmanian" before signing on.

"I knew if the opportunity presented itself, it was going to be an easy option to say yes," he said.

Walsh said he got "goosebumps" at Tuesday night's draft style event in Hobart, where he and seven other young guns were unveiled as the Devils' first ever AFL listed players.

He said he was struck by a club-produced hype video that chronicled Tasmania's football history, previous failed bids for an AFL team, and the importance of the state's famous "map" insignia.

"It's very important. The people of the island have wanted that for a long time so to have the opportunity to wear that on the jumper, it's very special and something I'm looking forward to," he said.

" It was a bit of goosebumps watching it; 1866 was where it all started, here we are in 2026, so it's feeling real now with the first eight being signed. "

Walsh was the first player unveiled at Tuesday night's event in Hobart. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Walsh was the first player unveiled on Tuesday, and is the highest profile player of the initial crop.

But he's not feeling the pressure to perform early.

"I'm really competitive. I want to win, and I hate losing," he said.

"I feel like pressure is a privilege, and we have that pressure because of the opportunity we've been given.

"I don't think there's pressure, just excitement."

It's a mindset reinforced by Devils' list boss, Todd Patterson.

Todd Patterson says each player's experience within the team will be customised to them. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

"We need to understand that each of them is on a different journey," Patterson said.

"Some of them might only have one kick in the VFL. That's OK. We just need to be patient with their development timelines.

"For some of them, it'll be really customised."

Walsh and his seven new teammates will split their time between the Devils' VFL, the Tasmanian under 18s, the gym, studying and visiting their home states next year.

Sales pitch began this year

Patterson was part of the team that lured the club's first players south — a process that started earlier this year with the delivery of "letters of interest" to about two dozen of the country's best under 18 players.

Part of the sales pitch was financial.

Each player will make about $150,000 next year, having penned four-year contracts with the club.

Hugh McCallum is the only Tasmanian from the pool of eight selected for the Devils. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

But Patterson insists the intentions of each of the players is pure.

"What they earn, what they'll end up earning and all that stuff, we are thinking about that and the strategy — but I think we could have offered them one dollar, and they would have been here," he said.

" They're just excited about the opportunity to leave a legacy. "

Each player signed has unique on- and off-field attributes.

Victorian Jake Miller is already a quasi-Tasmanian, boasting an impressive golf swing and having a mother who works for Cadbury.

Fellow Victorian midfielder Griffin Barker's highlight reel showcases a player who has perfected the "don't argue" — his favourite players are Harley Reid and Dustin Martin.

While on-baller Baxter Sruk accepted his Devils guernsey as AC/DC's Thunderstruck blasted throughout the venue.

Angus Brown at the Tasmanian Devils' team announcement. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

For another Victorian — gun small forward Angus Brown — moving to Tasmania was never a given.

"I wasn't in the initial interest letter back in the start of the year, I had to work my way up and find a patch of form," he said.

"I found out in May there was a letter of interest and then I pursued an interview with [recruiter] Derek Hine."

Even then, there was an element of trepidation for the Victorian who has placed an emphasis on finishing year 12, and pursuing higher education in tandem with a flourishing career in the AFL.

Tasmania Devils daring to dream The Devils weren't supposed to make the VFL finals. They were barely even supposed to be in the league.

"I'm someone whose pretty studious and I want to finish my studies," he said.

"The club has been open and flexible about my studying and pursuits academically, so that's probably my biggest thing.

"But when I got here and was able to experience the amounts of development, it was an easy sell."

It was the signing of Ken Hinkley as senior coach, and then the appointment of development guru Nigel Lappin that sealed the deal.

Momentum for the Devils is growing, boosted by their VFL and VFLW debuts this year. (Tasmania Football Club)

"The development opportunity here is something you're not going to get at any other club.

"I think the calibre of coaches and staff we've got is immense," he said.

"The sell is the experience, the dedication to the program and development was the biggest thing."

As for his on-field prospects, the 174-centimetre pocket rocket has this message for Devils fans:

"Something I pride myself on, is that while I'm not the biggest on the field, I think I have the biggest heart when I'm out there playing," he said.

"It'll be a dream come true," he says, of making his AFL debut.

World.title: 'They can't stop': Wadeye elders desperately try to end violent feud
World.content:
Leaders and organisations in the Northern Territory's second-largest Indigenous community, Wadeye, say they fear it is only a matter of time before someone is killed in ongoing clan feuds and are appealing to the NT and federal governments to help find solutions.

Groups of up to 150 people armed with crossbows, machetes and spears have been fighting in the Daly region community over the past two weeks, attacking homes and police, burning cars and seriously injuring one man.

The violence is part of a decades-old feud between some of Wadeye's 24 clans, who are crammed together in overcrowded housing on Kardu Diminin clan land.

A house in Wadeye that was burned in the recent unrest. (ABC News: James Elton)

Over many years the feuding has regularly sparked serious violence in the community of 2,500, including the death of a man and damage to 125 houses in 2022.

Mathawurr clan community leader Desmond Longmair said two weeks ago an armed mob attacked his house in Wadeye and burnt his car, and NT Police had been unable to answer his phone call for help.

"People just came running this way with axes and metal bars and they smashed this car, and they had petrol in a coke bottle and sprinkled it and set fire to it," he said.

"We had kids here, and I told them to put a petrol drum and fill it with water and jam it to the door so they couldn't break down the door."

Mr Longmair said he was so dismayed by fighting between members of his and other families that after the attack on his house, he and other elders forced younger family members to meet at one of the town's football ovals to apologise and agree to a truce.

Desmond Longmair helped to negotiate a truce between the people fighting in Wadeye. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"I keep telling my boys not to do that. I think they're doing it for some sort of fun — they're bored, don't want to work, they just want to make themself big and like a hero," he said.

Up to 100 people in armed Wadeye 'disturbance' Northern Territory Police say up to 100 people were involved in an armed "disturbance" in Wadeye overnight.

"I went over with the other boys from the Creek Camp and all my boys and I shook hands, we grabbed each other and I said: 'Promise me no more, that's it.'"

But the truce hasn't held — two police vehicles were smashed when 150 people began fighting on Monday.

Mr Longmair said as people arrested for fighting were gradually released from prison after serving sentences, they resumed tit-for-tat attacks, and he feared someone would be killed.

"When somebody dies that trouble keeps going, or somebody gets out of jail, they open up that old trouble," he said.

Payback spreads violence

Fighting among people from Wadeye hasn't only been contained to the community, with incidents also occurring 400 kilometres away in Darwin.

Two weeks ago, ranger Joshua Bunduck's nephew was injured in fighting between 30 armed people from Wadeye in the city.

His nephew had only just been released from prison and was critically injured in the brawl.

"Young boys and young girls came with rocks and machetes, they damaged his skull, but the hospital machine showed it hasn't damaged his brain," Mr Bunduck said.

Joshua Bunduck's nephew was critically injured in violence between Wadeye residents in Darwin. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Mr Bunduck said he was concerned the incident would spark more attacks because under his cultural law it would be up to his nephew to decide whether his family should seek what they call "payback".

"Family are very worried for him; it's up to him to decide what they're going to do, whether to get revenge or not," he said.

He said Wadeye's fighting continued because "that's what they do; some can't stop".

Arthur James Junior Karui, 50, who was in and out of youth detention and prison when he was younger, often after fighting, said he was now trying to get his sons and nephews to stop.

Arthur James Junior Karui has been pleading with his sons and nephews to stop the violence. (ABC News: James Elton)

"I was doing that when I was young, because of jealousing over women problems, and I was in prison, but I've calmed down now and got a good job in construction," he said.

" We want to stop all those young boys fighting and killing each other; I keep telling them to get a job. "

Robert Ninnal Melpi, an assistant teacher and a board member of Wadeye's Aboriginal-led Thamarrurr Development Corporation, which represents all the clans, said the violence was affecting children.

"It's a very sad community. The kids are really negative at the moment, no one's going to school, nearly 500 kids are staying at home out of it," the Wulthirri clan member said.

Weapons have 'potential to kill'

NT Police Central Division Superintendent Virginia Read said her officers had made dozens of arrests in relation to the Wadeye violence, seized dozens of weapons, stopped some of the large quantities of black market alcohol from coming into the community, and tried to support elders in their attempts to pressure their families to stop.

Virginia Read says police are looking to bolster officer numbers in Wadeye. (ABC News: James Elton)

"The weapons that are being used have the potential to kill people — something as simple as a house louvre, makeshift axes, right down to the rock on the side of the road," she said.

"You have these people living together that don't like each other, and we get continuing rolling issues, so, how we can fix that?

"I think we can only keep doing what we're doing working with the families and letting them have the say on how this problem can be fixed."

One of many locals desperate to stop the violence, Wadeye Kardu Diminin traditional owner Margaret Perdjert, said she wanted more support from the NT and federal governments to repair burnt houses and build more public housing.

Margaret Perdjert says the community's housing issues need to be addressed. (ABC News: James Elton)

"There's a lot of empty houses around the community, so rebuild those houses and people can move there," she said.

" We want the government to come out here and see what's happening out here. "

Ms Perdjert also said more homes in surrounding homeland communities would allow warring families to escape the community's pressure-cooker atmosphere more regularly.

Mark Tunmuck-Smith, another Thamarrurr Development Corporation board member, called on governments to relax rules that prevent people with public housing from also getting money for a house on their clan homeland, because the violence in Wadeye was so serious.

Seven arrested over violent brawl Seven people have been arrested in Darwin after a brawl allegedly left a man in a critical condition.

"We need to change some rules and come up with a better plan immediately because we are crying out loud that we want to move back to our homelands where we feel safe," he said.

The Yekyederr clan member said he would also like to see more rehabilitation program funding for released prisoners at risk of restarting fighting.

"They come out and they're still doing the same thing. They need to be out on the bush, country, that's where their spirit is," he said.

He said one of his biggest fears was that the violence would lead to the community losing its rich culture and identity, and he appealed to residents to work together.

Mark Tunmuck Smith wants more investment in homeland communities. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"It is really hard to stop. The solution is within ourself, in the community itself; it really comes down to us, to take ownership and move on," Mr Tunmuck-Smith said.

Benildus Narndu, a Yeknanga clan member, was another of the community leaders who brought young people together to apologise two weeks ago.

"We want to help our young boys stop everything because this payback is getting worse," he said.

" We are worried about our young boys killing each other with a crossbow, we don't want that. "

He said one solution should be making sure more young men go through their traditional ceremonies and spend more time learning their culture.

One of the homes damaged in the recent community violence. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"If we stop our culture, what will take its place? Everything is going to be spoiled, everybody is going to be hurting, bringing more drugs like cocaine, alcohol," he said.

Looking for solutions

Deputy chief executive of the Thamarrurr Development Corporation, Tracey Leo, said the organisation was continuing to run aged care, housing maintenance and youth diversion services during the violence — which had included a machete attack in the corporation's takeaway store that police couldn't respond to for 24 hours.

"The very obvious response is increased police resources," she said.

"Despite the numbers on paper, our understanding is we only have two active police officers on-shift at a time."

Superintendent Read said she was not aware of slow police response times and that she was in the process of recruiting more officers to Wadeye's 17 police positions, which would soon be increased to 19.

The NT Police Force is recruiting more officers to Wadeye. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

To help provide long-term solutions, Ms Leo said the NT and federal governments should commit more funding for services that could better tackle the underlying stressors in the community.

"There's no alcohol rehab facilities, there's no psychologist, no counselling services; the women's safe house in the last 12 months, on a number of occasions, has been so overwhelmed with people it's had to shut down," she said.

"People are drinking to get some relief from these pressures, and the fighting is an expression of trauma and frustration, so let's come together and look at the stressors that we can get under control quite quickly and easily.

Tracey Leo says the underlying pressures people in the community are feeling need to be addressed. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"The generation coming up now are wholly welfare dependent, have not known work; a lot of young people aren't going to school, can't speak English, have never seen anything but dysfunction.

"So I have grave concerns about Wadeye unless we can grab these things and turn it around, and even then it would take another 20 years to turn this around."

NT Aboriginal Affairs Minister Steve Edgington said the Territory government had recently built five new houses in Wadeye and had promised 36 more within a year.

He said the government had listened to the community's appeals for more investment in homelands housing, and he called on the federal government to provide funds as part of its $4 billion commitment to NT remote housing.

"To build on homelands, this is a whole new bucket of money that's needed, and consideration given to how we tackle housing on Aboriginal land in the homelands," he said.

Some new houses have been provided by the NT and federal governments in the Manthathpe homeland community near Wadeye. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

On a visit to Wadeye in May, Mr Edgington said he also started discussions with community members on how alcohol could better be managed there.

In a statement, a federal government spokesperson acknowledged the importance of homelands and said it was "investing in housing and essential infrastructure".

"The National Indigenous Australians Agency is working closely with the NT government, local organisations and the community in response to the recent issues in Wadeye," the statement said.

World.title: Australia strikes back to avoid ODI whitewash ahead of Test series
World.content:
Australia avoided a whitewash in their ODI series in South Africa, with Pat Cummins's encouraging comeback and the return to form of Adam Zampa and Alex Carey inspiring them to a rain-interrupted win in Potchefstroom.

The final day-nighter was eventually called off under the lights on Wednesday as rain ruined the finale, but Australia could still celebrate a satisfying 45-run (DLS method) victory on a day when they were vastly improved after their capitulation in chases in the first two matches.

Half-centuries from the rejuvenated Carey (74 off 88 balls) and captain Mitch Marsh (56 off 42 balls), plus 48 from Ollie Peake, helped propel Australia to 9-322 after they had been put in, with South Africa at no point then threatening to pull off the highest successful ODI chase ever at the ground.

By the time the rain, which had also delayed the start by half an hour, returned to quite spoil the fun, Australia were already in full control.

Zampa (2-34 off six overs) rediscovered his best after recent struggles and Xavier Bartlett earned a couple of key early wickets (2-25 off five) as only Ryan Rickelton (71no off 81 balls) looked likely to trouble the visitors with South Africa limping to 4-145 off 28 overs.

Cummins may have returned as bowler only, not as the captain, with Marsh keeping the job for the third and final match, but his return seemed to enthuse everyone, with his 0-17 off five probing overs suggesting he'll be in fine shape to lead his troops in the first Test in Durban on October 9.

Stand-in Marsh again did his bit, leading from the front, as he powered to his third half-century of the series following his 60 and 84 in Durban and Johannesburg.

He and Travis Head (24 off 20) again provided an electric start with a 78 stand at nine runs an over, and this time the middle-order built much more assiduously against a Proteas side who weren't helped by resting key spinner, player-of-the-series Keshav Maharaj, and captain Temba Bavuma among four changes.

Cameron Green had an eventful time, taking a fearful beamer from Bosch straight into his box, but recovering to hit the next delivery, also a fast full-toss, courageously for six, only to then be bumped out next ball by a short one, seemingly suffering a muscle injury in the process.

Zampa was back to his squeezing, probing best, luring the dangerous first-match centurion Matthew Breetzke to be stumped on 25 and trapping Tristan Stubbs lbw for 14.
