World.title: Housing waitlist cancellations a 'systems level problem', advocates say
World.content:
Colin Betts dons his Santa suit, collects his vibrant signs painted with positive messages, and walks barefoot out to the roadside.

Accompanied by his faithful dog, Meri Rose, the 66-year-old brandishes the signs to the honks and waves of the passing traffic.

Nicknamed the Barefoot Santa of Gympie, Mr Betts has been a public fixture in the regional Queensland town for the past decade.

Colin Betts is known as Gympie's "Barefoot Santa". (ABC News: James C Taylor)

"It's all in fun and laughter, laughter's good medicine," he said.

"A bit of positive energy, that to me means a lot."

Mr Betts lives with post-traumatic stress disorder and has been on the verge of homelessness for five years, squatting in an abandoned home with no power or hot water.

Colin Betts says he was unfairly removed from the social housing waitlist. (ABC News: James C Taylor)

But that house is being relocated and Mr Betts has weeks to find a new place to sleep.

Last month, he went to the local housing service centre to enquire about his status on the social housing waitlist.

Mr Betts was shocked to learn he had been removed from the list in 2025 for being uncontactable by housing officers.

He said the officer confirmed Mr Betts's current phone number was on the housing department's system, and he denied missing any calls from them.

Mr Betts lives entirely on Centrelink payments, spending his money to buy crystals that he hands out around town. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

"I said 'you've got my phone number'" … why couldn't they catch up with me?" he said.

" I'm just one of hundreds being taken off the list. The system's not broken, it's non-existent. "

Gaps in record keeping

Mr Betts was one of thousands of social housing applicants removed from the waitlist for being uncontactable in the last financial year.

Queensland Housing Minister Sam O'Connor told a July budget estimates hearing 2,419 applicants were removed for being uncontactable in 2025-26, making up nearly one-third of all cancelled applications.

Department of Housing policies require staff to make "reasonable attempts" to contact applicants before cancelling their application.

There is no minimum time frame nor number of contact attempts required before an applicant is deemed uncontactable.

However, a government audit for the last financial year found the department could not adequately monitor whether staff were making reasonable attempts to contact applicants.

The June report from the Queensland Audit Office (QAO) said the department did not compile data on how applicants were contacted, nor how many times they were contacted before their applications were cancelled.

Fiona Caniglia says reform is needed to introduce clear parameters for the cancellation of applications. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Fiona Caniglia, CEO of housing and homelessness group Q Shelter, said there were many reasons why homeless people could be difficult to contact, including illness, unpaid bills and fears about answering the phone.

"I think we've got a systems level problem here," she said.

"It would be wrong to give up too soon when we're talking about some of the most disadvantaged people in our community," she said.

Policy reform needed

Ms Caniglia said the report identified systemic issues that needed policy reform, including the introduction of clear parameters for the cancellation of people's social housing applications.

She said agencies should need to wait at least six months — and have made at least six attempts to contact someone — before being able to remove them from the waitlist.

Ms Caniglia also said the department needed to address gaps in record keeping which could have led to people at risk of homelessness having housing applications cancelled.

There were 2,419 people removed from the social housing register for being uncontactable in 2025–26. ( ABC News: Chris Gillette )

"A failure to implement transparent, consistently managed policies could lead to the public perception that applications are being cancelled due to political pressure to reduce the size of the waitlist," Ms Caniglia said.

The number of people on the waitlist was reduced by 4,245 between the LNP state government coming to office in September 2024 and July 2026.

In a statement to the ABC, Mr O'Connor said that was due to an increased supply of social housing and more frequent and thorough reviews of social housing applications.

He said officers made "reasonable, multiple attempts" to contact all applicants.

"No direction has been issued to prematurely cancel applications," Mr O'Connor said.

"Applications are only cancelled in very limited circumstances.

"We're properly managing the system to ensure every effort can be made to get housing help to vulnerable Queenslanders as quickly and early as possible to help prevent homelessness."

'I don't want to live on the street'

In Gympie, Mr Betts said any assurances from the government over improved housing supports were "just words".

"'We're helping people, the housing's coming down', yeah nah," he said.

Last week Mr Betts bought a van using more than $5,000 donated to him from a public fundraiser.

Colin Betts plans to live in a van with his dog, Meri Rose, once he can no longer squat in an abandoned house. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

He planned to live in the van with his dog, Meri Rose, once he could no longer squat in the abandoned house.

"The people in Gympie are beautiful people; they are so good to me," he said.

"I don't want to live on the street because I know what it's like."

World.title: Mother demands answers after traumatic birth at Queanbeyan Hospital
World.content:
Warning: this story discusses birth trauma.

A mother who experienced a traumatic birth at a regional New South Wales hospital said her daughter could have died due to clinical failures during her labour.

The Southern NSW Local Health District has apologised to the woman for her "distressing" experience at Queanbeyan Hospital.

The hospital's maternity unit has been grappling with major turmoil in recent months.

NSW Health said four general practice obstetricians had "withdrawn their service" amid clinical and cultural concerns, including tensions with midwives.

Mother demands answers

A woman, who would like to be known as Kate, said she felt "completely abandoned" for hours after arriving in labour at Queanbeyan Hospital in May.

Despite reporting contractions five minutes apart and requesting an epidural as early as possible, the mother said she was not assessed by her midwife or offered any pain relief.

"She never checked how dilated I was, she didn't ask about my contractions, she wasn't asking about the pain, she wasn't monitoring the baby's heart rate at all," Kate said.

She said she became increasingly distressed as she progressed rapidly through labour "completely alone".

"The only time I was eventually given gas was when I became so overwhelmed by the pain that I rang the bell and begged for it," Kate said.

NSW Health says four general practice obstetricians recently walked off the job at Queanbeyan Hospital. (ABC News: Luke Stevenson)

By the time the epidural was arranged, the mother said it was too late to be administered.

"The midwives were on the phone trying to call other doctors for backup and everyone's rushing around," she said.

" They couldn't organise a C-section because the [baby's] heart rate was too low, so by the time they got theatre ready, she would have been brain dead. "

Her daughter was delivered "blue and floppy" with her umbilical cord wrapped around her neck.

She said her baby was in critical distress and required immediate resuscitation.

Kate says her daughter had to be resuscitated immediately after being born. (ABC News: Gregor Salmon)

Kate is demanding answers from Queanbeyan Hospital about how her labour was allowed to progress as it did.

"How did a woman arrive at hospital in labour, spend hours in a birth suite, repeatedly ask for pain relief, and yet nobody knew how her labour was progressing and nobody recognised that her baby was in serious distress until it became a critical emergency?" she said.

" Because from where my husband and I were sitting, it felt as though the emergency occurred because nobody was paying attention. "

NSW Health apologises

In a statement, the Southern NSW Local Health District said representatives had spoken to the mother about her ordeal and concerns.

"Her family's experience is not in keeping with the district's and the community's expectations of the care provided at the Queanbeyan Maternity Service," the statement said.

"Since her time in the hospital, the district has established a task force to implement improvements that will support clinical safety and improve workforce culture to meet the needs of the community."

Commission called in

Kate's case is part of a string of recent clinical, cultural and workplace issues at the Queanbeyan maternity service.

NSW Health said locum doctors had been brought in to replace four general practice obstetricians who recently advised they were "temporarily unable to provide services at Queanbeyan Hospital".

NSW Health says the Queanbeyan Maternity Service continues to be staffed by highly skilled clinicians. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

It has coincided with the rollout of the district's Midwifery Group Practice program, designed to provide continuity of care for expectant mothers.

"During this time, we can reassure women and their families that Queanbeyan Hospital is staffed by experienced and caring maternity clinicians," the statement from the Southern NSW Local Health District said.

The Clinical Excellence Commission — the lead agency for NSW patient safety — and the Ministry of Health have also been called in to make recommendations to improve the maternity service.

The district has also appointed a temporary Obstetric Health Head of Department, who started work this week.

"The district acknowledges there are always areas to improve the delivery of care and has identified opportunities where our maternity services can be strengthened," the statement said.

But Kate said despite its previously excellent reputation, she would "absolutely not" recommend the maternity service to other expectant mothers.

"It was really scary," she said.

" [My daughter is] doing really well, thank God … but I just think I would hate for this to happen to someone else. "

In August, the federal government established a Senate committee on women's health, which includes examining pregnancy and postpartum health care. Submissions close on October 9.

World.title: ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save Flight FZ1073
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastAviation ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save Flight FZ1073 David Crowe Updated October 1, 2026 — 7:28am ,first published 7:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A gruesome brawl was underway at the front of Flight FZ1073 when one passenger chose to force his way into the cockpit to prevent a disaster. That passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, is now recognised as a hero who stopped one of the pilots from sending the flydubai Boeing 737 MAX crashing to the ground. Yaniv Hayoun says he learned how to pull the plane out of a nosedive by watching a Canadian documentary series. AP Photo/Tomer Appelbaum Yaniv Hayoun says he confronted the co-pilot in the cockpit. AP Photo/Tomer Appelbaum He did not act alone: several others joined him in a fight that lasted at least 20 minutes to defeat the co-pilot, who is now under arrest over a suspected act of terrorism.



Related Article Updated

Aviation Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster But Hayoun’s account reveals how close things came to a catastrophic mass murder of 174 passengers and crew, almost all of them Jewish. “When I went in, I saw the terrorist on the controls, between the two seats. There were no pilots in the seats,” Hayoun said. “I grabbed the terrorist, put him in a hold, and first of all pulled him outside.” Loading



The aircraft cabin was a scene of chaos at this time. The flight had left Dubai about two hours earlier and was above Saudi Arabia on its way to Tel Aviv. Israeli authorities say the key suspect, an Omani man working as the co-pilot, had turned on the lead pilot with a knife and begun stabbing him. Witnesses said the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of the wounds took effect. The plane’s captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of his wounds took effect. Hayoun described what happened in several accounts including a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when the passengers and crew finally made it to Tel Aviv on a second flight.



He saw what the pilot with the knife was attempting to do: “He was trying to destroy the controls in order to disable the plane.” The aircraft was racing toward the ground at this point. Flight tracking sites, including Flightradar24, show that the plane dropped 14,000 feet (4300 metres) in less than 30 seconds. “I jumped back in there, grabbed the controls, started pulling the controls,” Hayoun said in his meeting with Netanyahu. He mimed his action with the controls as he gave his account. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayoun. AFP How did he know what to do? “I watch Mayday,” he said. This is a Canadian television documentary series that examines air crashes, hijackings and bombings.



Another passenger, Assaf Rajwan, joined Hayoun in confronting the co-pilot. In an interview with Israeli news outlet Channel 12, he said he heard shouting from the cockpit when the plane was in its dive. “We kept the terrorist neutralised for 55 minutes,” Rajwan said, in an account reported by The Times of Israel. “I can’t believe I was in Thailand a few hours ago on a family vacation. “Life is stronger than everything, and we decided to fight for it.” Passengers who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, during a flight on FlyDubai plane, arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



Assaf Regavim, one of the passengers who helped to overpower the co-pilot. Getty Images A third passenger, Tzvika Manes, said his wife and young daughter were at the bathroom when the struggle began in the cockpit. Manes said the captain fell out into the cabin as the co-pilot was stabbing him, while the aircraft was falling rapidly and passengers were thrown about in the turmoil. Manes described his daughter screaming: “We don’t want to die.” He moved out of his seat to get to the cockpit. He said it took about 20 to 25 minutes for the three men to subdue the co-pilot. They used headphone cords to tie him up.



In a video shared by one person on the flight, the captain is covered in blood as some passengers support him and praise him for saving the aircraft from disaster. The co-pilot is seen tied up nearby and apparently unconscious. The wall of the cabin is splashed in blood. The flight tracking sites show it took another 90 minutes for the aircraft to land at Tabuk Airport in the far west of Saudi Arabia. Another stroke of luck saved the passengers and crew. On board were two pilots. They joined the passengers at the front of the aircraft and took control. While these two pilots have not been named, some reports have described them as a South African and a New Zealander.



One passenger, Daniel, told Channel 12 that he thought the aircraft would be destroyed in a repeat of the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington DC in 2001. When the off-duty pilots took over, Daniel said, they kept to the cockpit and focused on securing the aircraft. Israeli passenger Haim Lazarovich celebrates a safe return home. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit People celebrate the arrival of the replacement aircraft in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit “The pilots locked themselves in the cockpit, and we had no contact with the pilots,” he said. He added that two of the flight attendants were of no help.



“All kinds of thoughts were running through our heads, but [then] we heard the pilot start speaking to the passengers and telling them that they were going to land.” At that point, he said, things calmed down. Once on the ground, the passengers and crew were helped by Saudi healthcare workers. “We immediately felt safe because they were really amazing and generous. So many soldiers and nurses and doctors,” said Lital Shahar, a passenger travelling with her four daughters. A plane carrying passengers from an earlier Flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport. Getty Images Passengers embark on a Flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



Shahar told The Times of Israel the passengers and crew survived due to two miracles. “I felt sick. There are no words to describe what we experienced,” she said. “There were two miracles – that Israelis were on the plane who heroically went into the cockpit. And that there were off-duty pilots onboard who could land the plane in Saudi Arabia.” The captain of the flight is being hailed as a hero for resisting the co-pilot and opening the cockpit door. A photo showing Yaniv Hayoun on flydubai FZ1073 with blood on his shirt. Amichai Stein/Twitter



Captain Machchhar was helped by an Israeli dentist, Doctor Shota Musayev, who went to the cockpit. “When I heard screaming, after 10 seconds I ran – I didn’t wait,” Musayev told The Times of Israel. “When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape, with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head. “I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure.” Netanyahu praised Captain Machchhar for his bravery.



The flight making its safe landing back in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” the Israeli prime minister said. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals. I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery. He is a true hero.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie says there is a “deep level of denial and contempt” in Labor’s approach to economic management after the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates to a 15-year-high this week and inflation increased through August.

McKenzie accused the Albanese government of failing to accept responsibility for its role in driving up inflation through high levels of government spending.

“Everyone watching this has seen real wages go backwards, the largest drop in living standards in the developed world, and highest interest rates of industrial countries other than Iceland. They are the real economic indicators of the level of incompetence of this Labor government,” she told Nine’s Today show this morning.

Senator Bridget McKenzie. Alex Ellinghausen

Appearing alongside the Victorian senator on a regular panel was Environment Minister Murray Watt, who noted Labor reported a lower deficit in its final budget outcome than it had inherited when it came to office.

“It’s also far lower than was predicted when we first came to office, so that’s the result of the changes that we’ve been making and the savings that we’ve made,” he said.

“The great bulk of spending that is happening in the economy at the moment is not from government; it’s actually coming from the private sector, and that is because we are continuing to reduce government spending.”

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street falls late as bond market ramps up pressure
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street falls late as bond market ramps up pressure Stan Choe Updated October 1, 2026 — 6:51am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of the US stock market fell as Wall Street contended with the downside of a US economy that keeps powering through its many challenges. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent to close out its third losing month in the last four. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 443 points, or 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.2 per cent. Wall Street slid lower to wrap up a losing September. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 6.36am AEST pointing to a loss of 51 points or 0.6 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US69.58¢. US stocks turned lower after data reports suggested the US economy was even stronger during the spring than earlier thought. That helped yields remain high in the bond market, which in turn kept up the pressure weighing on stocks and all financial markets.



The day began with gains for stocks following an encouraging report that said inflation wasn’t as bad across the United States last month as economists expected. It said the cost of living for US consumers was 3.4 per cent higher overall in August than a year earlier. That was not as high as the 3.7 per cent inflation rate that economists expected, even if it remained worse than the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The report followed others from earlier in the month about inflation during August, but it’s the one that the Federal Reserve prefers to use. Shorter-term Treasury yields fell as traders pared bets that the Fed will raise its main interest rate next month to get inflation further under control. They now see just a 37 per cent chance of that, down from the coin flip’s chance seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. That helped the yield on the two-year Treasury briefly fall toward 4.83 per cent before it pulled back to 4.89 per cent, where it was late Tuesday. But longer-term yields rose in the bond market. That’s in part because worries about high inflation are just one of the reasons longer-term yields have jumped in the United States and around the world.



Related Article Mergers & acquisitions Giant gold miner eager to keep $38b Australian mega-deal alive The seemingly solid US economy is another. Besides Wednesday’s better-than-expected report on the overall US economy, another update said growth in business activity in the Midwest was also stronger than economists expected. Much of the strength in the US economy is due to consumers, who are increasing their spending by more than their incomes are rising. “The consumer remains resilient, in a much better position than previously thought,” according to Gary Schlossberg, global strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Other factors sending Treasury yields higher are also continuing to churn, including worries about the big debt loads that Washington and other governments worldwide are supporting.



Oil prices, meanwhile, rose in their latest swings amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the flow of crude to be fully restored. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 1.9 per cent to settle at $98.03 per barrel. It all helped the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the bond market, drop as low as 5.20 per cent in the morning before rising to 5.29 per cent. That’s up from 5.26 per cent late Tuesday, and it’s back to where it was more than two decades ago in 2002. The 30-year Treasury yield, which takes into account expectations for inflation and economic growth many years down the line, climbed to 5.64 per cent from 5.59 per cent late on Tuesday. Higher yields slow the overall economy by making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while undercutting prices for all kinds of investments. On Wall Street, Cal-Maine Foods dropped 0.7 per cent after the country’s largest egg company reported a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected. With plenty of eggs available in the market, Cal-Maine Foods saw a sharp drop in prices it could charge, compared with a year earlier.



Helping to limit the market’s losses was Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which rose 3.9 per cent. It increased its forecast for revenue from its networking business, which is benefiting from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist MongoDB climbed 3.4 per cent after the database company’s board boosted its program to send cash to shareholders by $US1 billion ($1.44 billion) through buybacks of its own stock. That helped MongoDB recover some of its sharp loss from earlier in the week, after it said Chirantan “CJ” Desai was stepping down as CEO for a senior role at Meta Platforms. All told, the S&P 500 fell 19.30 points to 7,651.54. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 443.87 to 50,906.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 63.52 to 26,861.06. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 1.9 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 fell 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.

World.title: He beat cystic fibrosis and became a Wallaby. Now Nathan Charles is fighting another cruel disease
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby He beat cystic fibrosis and became a Wallaby. Now Nathan Charles is fighting another cruel disease Iain Payten October 1, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nathan Charles’ voice breaks momentarily before he steadies himself and gets back to a lifelong routine, sizing up the next wave of adversity and figuring out how to manoeuvre. “I find it strange – I won’t use the word funny – but it’s ironic I was born with a life-threatening illness, and gave that a red-hot crack, and now this other thing comes along,” Charles said. “Something else is striking me down, rather than what I’ve been dealing with my whole life.” Former Wallaby Nathan Charles, pictured at home after revealing his motor neurone disease diagnosis. Audrey Richardson After being diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at three months of age, Charles made history by overcoming the condition and playing rugby for the Wallabies in 2014. He is believed to be the only cystic fibrosis sufferer in the world to ever play a contact sport professionally. Last month, however, Charles and his family received a second devastating blow.



After a steady decline in his health, the 37-year-old was diagnosed with motor neurone disease, the same crippling condition NRL star Jai Arrow and former England rugby player Lewis Moody are fighting. MND has no cure. Nathan Charles playing for Wallabies during a 2014 Bledisloe Cup Test in Sydney. Cameron Spencer “It has been extremely challenging and overwhelming, and at times quite cruel,” Charles said. “But I’ve got a lot of great people around me. It is what it is, and you’ve got to get on with it, so that’s what I’m trying to do.” Charles has already had more than his fair share of difficulties in life.



After being diagnosed with cystic fibrosis – a genetic disorder that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system – Charles’ parents were told he may not survive past his 10th birthday. But after a regimen of blowing up balloons as a toddler, medication and playing lots of sport, Charles thrived and became a talented footballer. He was chased by the Bulldogs but chose rugby, and after working his way through the ranks with Sydney Uni and the Western Force, Charles played for the Wallabies in four Tests in 2014. He started at hooker for Australia against the All Blacks in 2014 in front of 68,000 people at Accor Stadium. After a 10-year career, Charles retired in 2018 and later worked as chief executive of Rugby WA and helped run Sydney Uni rugby. He is also a tireless ambassador for cystic fibrosis charities. Loading In December last year, however, Charles started feeling “a bit off” at the gym. Medical checks showed nothing.



“It was probably when I went to the neurologist for the first time in March and, naturally, you type in your symptoms and the first thing that comes up is MND,” Charles said. “At that point, I didn’t believe it was that, but in July, when things were getting worse, I definitely had a bad feeling in my gut.” Charles was diagnosed with MND on September 13. His first thoughts were concern for his fiancée, Steph Bailey, parents, David and Heike, and his brother, Matthew, sister-in-law Andy and niece Oakley. “Because I felt as though this would impact them greater than it would me,” he said. “I had a bad feeling going into that appointment and my fears were realised. It was the people around me that I felt worst for. Nathan Charles playing for the Western Force against the Chiefs in 2014. Getty Images “My first question was, ‘How long have I got?’ I really only know what you see and hear [about MND]. I know that every person with MND has a different journey and path, and it affects everyone differently. I know there’s no cure, and your physicality and body deteriorate, cutting your life short.



“I am already greatly impacted by it. I get around with mobility aids and struggle with many daily tasks. Putting on shoes and socks is a challenge.” According to MND Australia, the average life expectancy after diagnosis is two to three years. Scientists don’t know the exact cause of MND, but believe it results from a mix genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors. “As far as I know, there is no connection with CF [cystic fibrosis], it’s just absolute rotten luck,” Charles said. “To be fair, if I’m a person of firsts, I’m taking it to the extreme.” “It has been extremely challenging and overwhelming, and at times quite cruel.” Nathan Charles on his MND diagnosis Given the spate of footballers who have been diagnosed with, or died from, MND, the role of concussion in the condition is also being scrutinised. Carl Webb, Rob Burrow, Doddie Weir, Neale Daniher and Joost van der Westhuizen are among others who have died from MND.



Charles says he agrees with Moody, who said in a recent interview he’d live the same life over, regardless. “Even if it did [contribute], would I change what I’ve done?” he asked. “Probably not, because rugby has given me a great life. I’ve been able to do things that less than 1 per cent of the population have the opportunity to do.” Now walking with the help of crutches, Charles this week shared his story with the Herald and in an interview with Justin Harrison on Stan Sport. Nathan Charles is planning to launch a foundation in his name to help young people overcome challenges and build resilience. Audrey Richardson Friends are rallying from all corners of the globe for a hugely popular figure.



A GoFundMe has been created to help Charles and his family with the costs of future care and mobility challenges, and there are also plans to launch the Nathan Charles Foundation. Related Article Illness Is there a link between head knocks and motor neurone disease? “We want to create something that supports and empowers young people around resilience, while helping people access opportunities they may have thought were out of reach,” he said. The news is still raw, but Charles is focused on moving past the shock and grief, and living a full life. “I woke up one morning, a couple of days afterwards, and thought, ‘This is a bad dream’,” Charles said. “But after that, I realised I can’t keep thinking like this.



“My initial mindset was, ‘I’m now doing things for the last time’. Instead, I really want to flip the script and say, ‘I want to start doing things for the first time’.” The fights against CF and MND are different, Charles says, but the mindset is the same. “You’re going to have your challenging days, and understanding that allows you to reset and say, ‘Righto mate, today is today, what are you going to with it?’ ” Watch the full interview between Nathan Charles and Justin Harrison on Stan Sport. To contribute to the GoFundMe for Charles, click here.

World.title: US forces have finally quit Iraq. What happens now?
World.content:
Analysis WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US forces have finally quit Iraq. What happens now? Mustafa Salim and Alex Horton October 1, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Baghdad: US military forces pulled out of Iraq on Wednesday following two decades of American involvement that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Iraqi civilians and thousands of US troops, and now leaves a battered but increasingly influential Iran at the centre of the region’s future. The withdrawal concludes a Biden administration agreement made in 2024 to zero out US military personnel in Iraq by this year. Recently, there were about 1500 combined US personnel and anti-Islamic State coalition members in Iraq, a US official said, as forces consolidated and departed ahead of the September 30 deadline. That mission will continue in Jordan, from where the Pentagon says it can target militants who pose a threat to US personnel and interests, the official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss military planning. A US Air Force C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft prepares for takeoff from Camp Victory on the outskirts of Baghdad International Airport. AFP The redeployment of US forces has been a muted event in Washington. The 2003 invasion triggered a significant human and financial toll that will be felt for generations. As many as 210,000 Iraqi civilians were killed between the invasion and 2023, along with 4599 US service members, according to figures from Brown University’s Cost of War Project.



Roughly 170,000 US troops were in the country at the height of the war in 2007, when sectarian violence spiralled out of control. President Barack Obama vowed to end the unpopular conflict after he was elected in 2008. He declared an end to combat operations and an eventual pullout in 2011. The Islamic State, born of al-Qaeda militants and other extremists, blitzed across Iraq and Syria in 2014, prompting Obama and an international coalition to re-enter the region in a campaign that lasted into the first Trump administration. The decades of conflict has cost US taxpayers more than $US2.8 trillion ($4 trillion), Brown estimated, including related veterans care and operations in Syria. Iraq emerged from the conflict with the Islamic State with a growing economy and a quasi-democracy that has been tested by religious sects in the government, particularly those with close ties to Tehran.



The US departure has been celebrated as a victory in Iran, which remains in an uneasy ceasefire with the US and Israel following months of war. Iran has long taken advantage of Iraq’s destabilisation, seeding the government with friendly officials and arming militia groups that have expanded Tehran’s influence. Iraqi security officers flash victory signs as they celebrate the complete withdrawal of US troops. AP Photo/Hadi Mizban Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary Speaker, remarked on the US withdrawal last month during a diplomatic visit to Baghdad that included a visit to the site where Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani was killed in a US strike in 2020. “The resistance front is the one prevailing now,” he said at a news conference, referring to cross-border Iranian political and military groups.



The fighters were organised under an umbrella group called the Popular Mobilisation Forces to confront the Islamic State. They are on Iraqi military payrolls but serve as Iranian proxy forces, numbering more than 200,000, analysts have said. They have fielded one-way attack drones and missiles to attack US troops and other adversaries. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump chose to go it alone against Iran. Now he’s learning the value of friends Rodger Shanahan Middle East and security analyst The September 30 departure of US forces was meant to coincide with the disarmament of those Iranian-backed militia groups, which have largely ignored or defied the calls to disband. The timeline for the militias to disarm has been extended to June 2027, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said. Iran might be boosted by the US withdrawal, but its recent behaviour in the region had also created unlikely alliances against Tehran that challenged its power, said Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Centre for Strategic and International Studies think tank. The 2003 operation that toppled Saddam Hussein threw Iraq into chaos, eliminating Tehran’s adversary on its western border, Cancian said. But its targeting of countries that house US troops during the Iran war had pushed some nations such as Saudi Arabia closer to Israel, Cancian said, creating a bulwark that was “unimaginable” decades ago.



“That’s a great help for the United States,” he said, “because we always had difficulty in balancing the Arabs and the Israelis.” US forces in Jordan will focus on Islamic State militants. If the group “metastasises to something beyond [Iraq and Syria’s] control, and they want our help, then we’ll come in and help them,” the US official said. A billboard in downtown Baghdad celebrating the end of the US military presence in Iraq. Getty Images Iranian-allied militias in Iraq have for years targeted Americans in the region, escalating attacks after Israel launched its devastating campaign in Gaza. Three US soldiers were killed in one such attack in Jordan in 2024. “We only went after [Iranian-backed militants] in response to attempted attacks on our people,” the US official said. But overall, contending with those groups would henceforth be an “Iraqi responsibility”.



Iran’s hard-line Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has recently evolved its paramilitary operations in Iraq, which may pose difficulties for Baghdad, according to a senior official in the Iraqi prime minister’s office. Related Article Middle East at war Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech The IRGC had focused its resources in Iraq on smaller cells outside the larger militia networks to evade detection and deterrence, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters. The recent disarmament process has highlighted concerns about splinter groups. The Iraqi official said, for instance, that the Iranian-backed militia group Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq turned over only about half the arsenal it was estimated to have, with its leaders saying the rest had been claimed by defectors who formed a new militia. That new organisation received substantial Iranian support, had co-operated with Houthi allies in Yemen and was involved in recent attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the official said.



The Washington Post Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Can’t afford to buy a house in Tuscany? These TV shows will let you dream about it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most reality shows rely on jeopardy or some kind of life-changing quest. They feature lucky contestants hoping to be recognised for their cooking or singing talents. Or average folk renovating a home or searching for a soulmate. The higher the stakes, the more relatable the challenge, the better. Editor's pick Streaming Netflix’s new Wonka series is bonkers. It was even crazier in real life But a spate of recent shows have upped the ante on a stalwart TV genre: the home renovation. They’ve set their sights on something more ambitious than plumping the cushions or installing the latest must-have kitchen gadget. What if you could up sticks, leave the nine-to-five grind behind and start a new life on the other side of the world? Say, in a hilltop town in Tuscany; in a fairytale-worthy chateau in France; bottling your own wine in Spain; capping off a day on the tools with an Aperol spritz on a beach in Sicily? Producers are always looking for a good hook and a bargain. So when a number of European nations introduced “one Euro schemes” several years ago, TV-makers were quick to see the possibilities. These schemes, which have been flooded with interest, allow non-residents to purchase rundown and abandoned houses in remote villages that are at risk of becoming ghost towns. For a token sum, the houses can be purchased on the condition that they are renovated, to be used by foreigners looking for a life change, a holiday house or the chance to turn a tidy profit when the house is flipped. Admittedly, the appealing proposition masks some sobering facts. Across Europe, traditional villages are dying because of declining birthrates and ageing populations, inheritance laws, poverty, unemployment and industrialisation.



The TV shows these initiatives have spawned don’t make too much mention of this. But as armchair adventures go, they have an irresistible appeal. Shaynna Blaze and Darren Palmer host new series 1 Euro House. Nine 1 Euro House (Nine*, October 6) The Block judges Shaynna Blaze and Darren Palmer are getting their hands dirty. Blaze has purchased a €1 home, sight unseen, in a remote village in Sicily and enlisted Palmer to help make it habitable. Editor's pick Australian TV He respects Hughesy’s ‘passion’, but Peter Helliar is staying on the silly side It begins with a small, abandoned stone terrace in Castronovo, a hilltop village with a population of 2800. With a budget of €210,000 ($342,000), they set to work with an ex-pat British builder (who also appears in Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job). A can-do spirit pervades this show, which doesn’t sugar-coat what’s in store for the intrepid and aspirational €1 renovator and sees the presenters finding thrifty solutions to design and decorating tasks rather than sponsored products. It feels like a fun vacation job for the duo, though their tricks from The Block – such as a room reveal and confected shock when a building problem is uncovered – seem unnecessary.



Amanda Holden and Alan Carr in Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job. Voltage TV Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job (ABC iview), Amanda and Alan’s Greek Job (Binge), Amanda and Alan’s Spanish Job (Binge) British TV personalities Amanda Holden and Alan Carr have spent the past few European summers renovating rundown houses in Spain, Italy (twice) and most recently Greece. Their shows follow a familiar template as they inevitably realise they under-estimated the scope of the tasks they face, call in local trades, explore the local sights and visit compatriots who have made the big move, then eventually congratulate themselves on their achievements. The main selling point of the hugely popular franchise is their easy camaraderie. Their on-screen chemistry is raucous and blue. Despite the dust and racket, Holden always looks like she just stepped out of hair and make-up, while Carr constantly reminds us that he has no practical skills and will never waste the chance for a snarky pun or campy innuendo. It’s naff as hell and forgets at times that it’s actually a renovation show, but that doesn’t seem to bother its legion of fans in the UK and Australia. Australians Banjo Beale and Rohan Christopher star in Banjo and Ro’s Grand Island Hotel. Nine Banjo and Ro’s Grand Island Hotel (9Now) Banjo Beale and Rohan Christopher are a couple of Australians who ended up in Scotland’s remote Hebrides after years of backpacking adventures and travel. In this series, they are turning a dilapidated 27-room mansion with no running water or electricity into a hotel on the tiny island of Ulva. The island has been owned since 2018 by local residents who want to bring life back to the remote backwater, the building overseen by a charitable trust.



This isn’t a cookie-cutter makeover show. Beale, who looks after the decorating side of things while Christopher tends to the tools, has a taste for the esoteric and unconventional. And Ulva, with just 16 residents and accessible only by ferry from the island Mull, is as far off the beaten track as renovation porn has ever travelled. Their show is less an extended ad for the boutique hotel it is destined to become than a portrait of a remote farming community perched at the very edge of the world. When Australians are described as individualists with an adventurous streak, think of Beale and Christopher. Angel and Dick Strawbridge from Escape to the Chateau. Escape to the Chateau (7Plus, 9Now, Binge) This sprawling lifestyle show falls outside €1 schemes, but it nails the escapist fantasy that those other series play with. Dick Strawbridge, an engineer and former lieutenant in the British army, and his flame-haired wife Angel purchased a derelict 45-room chateau in France. In between restoring the magnificent pile (which is partly used as a high-end wedding venue) and raising two children, the couple indulge in their various and many hobbies, from tinkering and practical building to crafting, dressmaking and cookery. Want some unvarnished truth? Try The One Euro House Dream – Italy (ABC iview) This 2024 episode of Foreign Correspondent looks at Italy’s €1 scheme, via a hilltop town in Sicily called Mussomeli. But it presents a far less telegenic vision of la dolce vita than what’s served up in Amanda and Alan. This is a village in decline, where houses are being bought not by cashed-up holiday-homeowners but by people priced out of more expensive European cities and the children of families who moved away. *Nine owns this masthead.

World.title: TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch Paul Kalina October 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

70 Up ★★★★ 70 Up brings to a close one of the most fascinating – and arguably the longest-running – shows in the annals of TV history. It started in 1964 with a group of 14 children from a cross-section of English society in the documentary Seven Up! It was there we met Cockney lad Tony, who at age seven planned to be a jockey; headstrong Jackie, who said she would marry a boy with money; and Symon, the only non-white participant, who was raised in a boy’s home and in reply to a question about his future education replied, “What’s a university?” Every seven years since, director and behind-the-camera interviewer Michael Apted returned to see how these playful children became feisty teenagers, then parents and eventually grandparents; how marriages were made and unmade; how hopes soared and were sometimes extinguished. John, Bruce, Symon, Andrew, Suzy, Jackie, Tony, Sue, Peter, Paul and Neil all return for 70 Up, reportedly the final instalment of this famous documentary series. ITV The original concept was to test the Jesuit adage, “Give me a child until he is seven and I will give you the man” – a window into how class and socioeconomic circumstances determine the chances and opportunities that shape their (and our own) lives. But what it’s mostly remembered for today is the front-row seat it offered to the daily dramas of life and how each of the participants was forged into the person that they became.



Now, here they are as 70-year-olds looking back, but also forwards, in what is touted to be the last instalment of the show. Related Article Review 63 Up's Aussie battler Paul Kligerman on the call he dreads every seven years In the two-part 70 Up, we see where the 13 surviving people have ended up (Lynn, the librarian, died in 2013). For the most part, they’re fulfilled, contented and self-aware – which may be surprising given the challenges some have faced. They are also deeply contemplative and ruminative, not only about how their lives have unfolded but how they’ve been depicted in the films. Directed by Asif Kapadia (Amy, Senna, Diego Maradona), 70 Up is very much about legacy (Apted died in 2021). At stake is not only the personal legacies of the participants, but the legacy of the series itself. Several talk about how the show has turned them into celebrities, and we are poignantly reminded that as seven-year-olds they never really consented to be part of a program that has come to define them. They all return, however, for this last hurrah – even some who opted not to participate in earlier instalments. Their humility and, ultimately, gratitude are truly heartrending.



Sue and Claire reflect on their past selves. SBS/ITV Indeed, 70 Up raises many valid questions about Apted’s agendas and preconceived ideas, such as the sexist questions he put to the female participants, as well as setting up the posh schoolboys to look like undeserving twits. “Sneering and supercilious” is how one of the participants remembers him. Hearing some of Apted’s loaded and insulting questions from earlier chapters is cringe-making. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight That’s one part of the legacy that 70 Up wants to correct. The other is that the series’ focus on outdated notions of class and society meant it wasn’t always asking the right questions. It’s here that 70 Up, its second episode in particular, delivers an emotional punch to the gut. There’s Neil, the sunny daydreamer in Seven Up! who now talks with admirable candour about his lifelong mental health battles. And Symon, who still rues having never met his father, and has gone on to foster more than 100 children. What we take away isn’t the fairness of the cards they were dealt but how they faced the unpredictable twists and turns that life put in their paths. It’s impossible not to be moved by this remarkable endeavour.

World.title: ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save Flight FZ1073
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastAviation ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save Flight FZ1073 David Crowe Updated October 1, 2026 — 7:28am ,first published 7:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A gruesome brawl was underway at the front of Flight FZ1073 when one passenger chose to force his way into the cockpit to prevent a disaster. That passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, is now recognised as a hero who stopped one of the pilots from sending the flydubai Boeing 737 MAX crashing to the ground. Yaniv Hayoun says he learned how to pull the plane out of a nosedive by watching a Canadian documentary series. AP Photo/Tomer Appelbaum Yaniv Hayoun says he confronted the co-pilot in the cockpit. AP Photo/Tomer Appelbaum He did not act alone: several others joined him in a fight that lasted at least 20 minutes to defeat the co-pilot, who is now under arrest over a suspected act of terrorism.



Related Article Updated

Aviation Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster But Hayoun’s account reveals how close things came to a catastrophic mass murder of 174 passengers and crew, almost all of them Jewish. “When I went in, I saw the terrorist on the controls, between the two seats. There were no pilots in the seats,” Hayoun said. “I grabbed the terrorist, put him in a hold, and first of all pulled him outside.” Loading



The aircraft cabin was a scene of chaos at this time. The flight had left Dubai about two hours earlier and was above Saudi Arabia on its way to Tel Aviv. Israeli authorities say the key suspect, an Omani man working as the co-pilot, had turned on the lead pilot with a knife and begun stabbing him. Witnesses said the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of the wounds took effect. The plane’s captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of his wounds took effect. Hayoun described what happened in several accounts including a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when the passengers and crew finally made it to Tel Aviv on a second flight.



He saw what the pilot with the knife was attempting to do: “He was trying to destroy the controls in order to disable the plane.” The aircraft was racing toward the ground at this point. Flight tracking sites, including Flightradar24, show that the plane dropped 14,000 feet (4300 metres) in less than 30 seconds. “I jumped back in there, grabbed the controls, started pulling the controls,” Hayoun said in his meeting with Netanyahu. He mimed his action with the controls as he gave his account. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayoun. AFP How did he know what to do? “I watch Mayday,” he said. This is a Canadian television documentary series that examines air crashes, hijackings and bombings.



Another passenger, Assaf Rajwan, joined Hayoun in confronting the co-pilot. In an interview with Israeli news outlet Channel 12, he said he heard shouting from the cockpit when the plane was in its dive. “We kept the terrorist neutralised for 55 minutes,” Rajwan said, in an account reported by The Times of Israel. “I can’t believe I was in Thailand a few hours ago on a family vacation. “Life is stronger than everything, and we decided to fight for it.” Passengers who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, during a flight on FlyDubai plane, arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



Assaf Regavim, one of the passengers who helped to overpower the co-pilot. Getty Images A third passenger, Tzvika Manes, said his wife and young daughter were at the bathroom when the struggle began in the cockpit. Manes said the captain fell out into the cabin as the co-pilot was stabbing him, while the aircraft was falling rapidly and passengers were thrown about in the turmoil. Manes described his daughter screaming: “We don’t want to die.” He moved out of his seat to get to the cockpit. He said it took about 20 to 25 minutes for the three men to subdue the co-pilot. They used headphone cords to tie him up.



In a video shared by one person on the flight, the captain is covered in blood as some passengers support him and praise him for saving the aircraft from disaster. The co-pilot is seen tied up nearby and apparently unconscious. The wall of the cabin is splashed in blood. The flight tracking sites show it took another 90 minutes for the aircraft to land at Tabuk Airport in the far west of Saudi Arabia. Another stroke of luck saved the passengers and crew. On board were two pilots. They joined the passengers at the front of the aircraft and took control. While these two pilots have not been named, some reports have described them as a South African and a New Zealander.



One passenger, Daniel, told Channel 12 that he thought the aircraft would be destroyed in a repeat of the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington DC in 2001. When the off-duty pilots took over, Daniel said, they kept to the cockpit and focused on securing the aircraft. Israeli passenger Haim Lazarovich celebrates a safe return home. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit People celebrate the arrival of the replacement aircraft in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit “The pilots locked themselves in the cockpit, and we had no contact with the pilots,” he said. He added that two of the flight attendants were of no help.



“All kinds of thoughts were running through our heads, but [then] we heard the pilot start speaking to the passengers and telling them that they were going to land.” At that point, he said, things calmed down. Once on the ground, the passengers and crew were helped by Saudi healthcare workers. “We immediately felt safe because they were really amazing and generous. So many soldiers and nurses and doctors,” said Lital Shahar, a passenger travelling with her four daughters. A plane carrying passengers from an earlier Flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport. Getty Images Passengers embark on a Flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



Shahar told The Times of Israel the passengers and crew survived due to two miracles. “I felt sick. There are no words to describe what we experienced,” she said. “There were two miracles – that Israelis were on the plane who heroically went into the cockpit. And that there were off-duty pilots onboard who could land the plane in Saudi Arabia.” The captain of the flight is being hailed as a hero for resisting the co-pilot and opening the cockpit door. A photo showing Yaniv Hayoun on flydubai FZ1073 with blood on his shirt. Amichai Stein/Twitter



Captain Machchhar was helped by an Israeli dentist, Doctor Shota Musayev, who went to the cockpit. “When I heard screaming, after 10 seconds I ran – I didn’t wait,” Musayev told The Times of Israel. “When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape, with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head. “I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure.” Netanyahu praised Captain Machchhar for his bravery.



The flight making its safe landing back in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” the Israeli prime minister said. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals. I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery. He is a true hero.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

A pedestrian has been hit and killed by a car in the suburbs of Brisbane late on Wednesday.

Police were called to reports a 30-year-old man had been struck by a Volkswagen Golf at the intersection of Beaudesert Road and Paradise Road in Acacia Ridge about 6.25pm.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Chalmers says inflation still lower than expected after rise, but another rate hike on horizon; Crew members, passengers intervene after midair pilot stabbing
World.content:
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie says there is a “deep level of denial and contempt” in Labor’s approach to economic management after the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates to a 15-year-high this week and inflation increased through August.

McKenzie accused the Albanese government of failing to accept responsibility for its role in driving up inflation through high levels of government spending.

“Everyone watching this has seen real wages go backwards, the largest drop in living standards in the developed world, and highest interest rates of industrial countries other than Iceland. They are the real economic indicators of the level of incompetence of this Labor government,” she told Nine’s Today show this morning.

Senator Bridget McKenzie. Alex Ellinghausen

Appearing alongside the Victorian senator on a regular panel was Environment Minister Murray Watt, who noted Labor reported a lower deficit in its final budget outcome than it had inherited when it came to office.

“It’s also far lower than was predicted when we first came to office, so that’s the result of the changes that we’ve been making and the savings that we’ve made,” he said.

“The great bulk of spending that is happening in the economy at the moment is not from government; it’s actually coming from the private sector, and that is because we are continuing to reduce government spending.”

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street falls late as bond market ramps up pressure
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street falls late as bond market ramps up pressure Stan Choe Updated October 1, 2026 — 6:51am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of the US stock market fell as Wall Street contended with the downside of a US economy that keeps powering through its many challenges. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent to close out its third losing month in the last four. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 443 points, or 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.2 per cent. Wall Street slid lower to wrap up a losing September. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 6.36am AEST pointing to a loss of 51 points or 0.6 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US69.58¢. US stocks turned lower after data reports suggested the US economy was even stronger during the spring than earlier thought. That helped yields remain high in the bond market, which in turn kept up the pressure weighing on stocks and all financial markets.



The day began with gains for stocks following an encouraging report that said inflation wasn’t as bad across the United States last month as economists expected. It said the cost of living for US consumers was 3.4 per cent higher overall in August than a year earlier. That was not as high as the 3.7 per cent inflation rate that economists expected, even if it remained worse than the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The report followed others from earlier in the month about inflation during August, but it’s the one that the Federal Reserve prefers to use. Shorter-term Treasury yields fell as traders pared bets that the Fed will raise its main interest rate next month to get inflation further under control. They now see just a 37 per cent chance of that, down from the coin flip’s chance seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. That helped the yield on the two-year Treasury briefly fall toward 4.83 per cent before it pulled back to 4.89 per cent, where it was late Tuesday. But longer-term yields rose in the bond market. That’s in part because worries about high inflation are just one of the reasons longer-term yields have jumped in the United States and around the world.



Related Article Mergers & acquisitions Giant gold miner eager to keep $38b Australian mega-deal alive The seemingly solid US economy is another. Besides Wednesday’s better-than-expected report on the overall US economy, another update said growth in business activity in the Midwest was also stronger than economists expected. Much of the strength in the US economy is due to consumers, who are increasing their spending by more than their incomes are rising. “The consumer remains resilient, in a much better position than previously thought,” according to Gary Schlossberg, global strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Other factors sending Treasury yields higher are also continuing to churn, including worries about the big debt loads that Washington and other governments worldwide are supporting.



Oil prices, meanwhile, rose in their latest swings amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the flow of crude to be fully restored. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 1.9 per cent to settle at $98.03 per barrel. It all helped the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the bond market, drop as low as 5.20 per cent in the morning before rising to 5.29 per cent. That’s up from 5.26 per cent late Tuesday, and it’s back to where it was more than two decades ago in 2002. The 30-year Treasury yield, which takes into account expectations for inflation and economic growth many years down the line, climbed to 5.64 per cent from 5.59 per cent late on Tuesday. Higher yields slow the overall economy by making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while undercutting prices for all kinds of investments. On Wall Street, Cal-Maine Foods dropped 0.7 per cent after the country’s largest egg company reported a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected. With plenty of eggs available in the market, Cal-Maine Foods saw a sharp drop in prices it could charge, compared with a year earlier.



Helping to limit the market’s losses was Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which rose 3.9 per cent. It increased its forecast for revenue from its networking business, which is benefiting from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist MongoDB climbed 3.4 per cent after the database company’s board boosted its program to send cash to shareholders by $US1 billion ($1.44 billion) through buybacks of its own stock. That helped MongoDB recover some of its sharp loss from earlier in the week, after it said Chirantan “CJ” Desai was stepping down as CEO for a senior role at Meta Platforms. All told, the S&P 500 fell 19.30 points to 7,651.54. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 443.87 to 50,906.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 63.52 to 26,861.06. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 1.9 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 fell 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.

World.title: He beat cystic fibrosis and became a Wallaby. Now Nathan Charles is fighting another cruel disease
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby He beat cystic fibrosis and became a Wallaby. Now Nathan Charles is fighting another cruel disease Iain Payten October 1, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nathan Charles’ voice breaks momentarily before he steadies himself and gets back to a lifelong routine, sizing up the next wave of adversity and figuring out how to manoeuvre. “I find it strange – I won’t use the word funny – but it’s ironic I was born with a life-threatening illness, and gave that a red-hot crack, and now this other thing comes along,” Charles said. “Something else is striking me down, rather than what I’ve been dealing with my whole life.” Former Wallaby Nathan Charles, pictured at home after revealing his motor neurone disease diagnosis. Audrey Richardson After being diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at three months of age, Charles made history by overcoming the condition and playing rugby for the Wallabies in 2014. He is believed to be the only cystic fibrosis sufferer in the world to ever play a contact sport professionally. Last month, however, Charles and his family received a second devastating blow.



After a steady decline in his health, the 37-year-old was diagnosed with motor neurone disease, the same crippling condition NRL star Jai Arrow and former England rugby player Lewis Moody are fighting. MND has no cure. Nathan Charles playing for Wallabies during a 2014 Bledisloe Cup Test in Sydney. Cameron Spencer “It has been extremely challenging and overwhelming, and at times quite cruel,” Charles said. “But I’ve got a lot of great people around me. It is what it is, and you’ve got to get on with it, so that’s what I’m trying to do.” Charles has already had more than his fair share of difficulties in life.



After being diagnosed with cystic fibrosis – a genetic disorder that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system – Charles’ parents were told he may not survive past his 10th birthday. But after a regimen of blowing up balloons as a toddler, medication and playing lots of sport, Charles thrived and became a talented footballer. He was chased by the Bulldogs but chose rugby, and after working his way through the ranks with Sydney Uni and the Western Force, Charles played for the Wallabies in four Tests in 2014. He started at hooker for Australia against the All Blacks in 2014 in front of 68,000 people at Accor Stadium. After a 10-year career, Charles retired in 2018 and later worked as chief executive of Rugby WA and helped run Sydney Uni rugby. He is also a tireless ambassador for cystic fibrosis charities. Loading In December last year, however, Charles started feeling “a bit off” at the gym. Medical checks showed nothing.



“It was probably when I went to the neurologist for the first time in March and, naturally, you type in your symptoms and the first thing that comes up is MND,” Charles said. “At that point, I didn’t believe it was that, but in July, when things were getting worse, I definitely had a bad feeling in my gut.” Charles was diagnosed with MND on September 13. His first thoughts were concern for his fiancée, Steph Bailey, parents, David and Heike, and his brother, Matthew, sister-in-law Andy and niece Oakley. “Because I felt as though this would impact them greater than it would me,” he said. “I had a bad feeling going into that appointment and my fears were realised. It was the people around me that I felt worst for. Nathan Charles playing for the Western Force against the Chiefs in 2014. Getty Images “My first question was, ‘How long have I got?’ I really only know what you see and hear [about MND]. I know that every person with MND has a different journey and path, and it affects everyone differently. I know there’s no cure, and your physicality and body deteriorate, cutting your life short.



“I am already greatly impacted by it. I get around with mobility aids and struggle with many daily tasks. Putting on shoes and socks is a challenge.” According to MND Australia, the average life expectancy after diagnosis is two to three years. Scientists don’t know the exact cause of MND, but believe it results from a mix genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors. “As far as I know, there is no connection with CF [cystic fibrosis], it’s just absolute rotten luck,” Charles said. “To be fair, if I’m a person of firsts, I’m taking it to the extreme.” “It has been extremely challenging and overwhelming, and at times quite cruel.” Nathan Charles on his MND diagnosis Given the spate of footballers who have been diagnosed with, or died from, MND, the role of concussion in the condition is also being scrutinised. Carl Webb, Rob Burrow, Doddie Weir, Neale Daniher and Joost van der Westhuizen are among others who have died from MND.



Charles says he agrees with Moody, who said in a recent interview he’d live the same life over, regardless. “Even if it did [contribute], would I change what I’ve done?” he asked. “Probably not, because rugby has given me a great life. I’ve been able to do things that less than 1 per cent of the population have the opportunity to do.” Now walking with the help of crutches, Charles this week shared his story with the Herald and in an interview with Justin Harrison on Stan Sport. Nathan Charles is planning to launch a foundation in his name to help young people overcome challenges and build resilience. Audrey Richardson Friends are rallying from all corners of the globe for a hugely popular figure.



A GoFundMe has been created to help Charles and his family with the costs of future care and mobility challenges, and there are also plans to launch the Nathan Charles Foundation. Related Article Illness Is there a link between head knocks and motor neurone disease? “We want to create something that supports and empowers young people around resilience, while helping people access opportunities they may have thought were out of reach,” he said. The news is still raw, but Charles is focused on moving past the shock and grief, and living a full life. “I woke up one morning, a couple of days afterwards, and thought, ‘This is a bad dream’,” Charles said. “But after that, I realised I can’t keep thinking like this.



“My initial mindset was, ‘I’m now doing things for the last time’. Instead, I really want to flip the script and say, ‘I want to start doing things for the first time’.” The fights against CF and MND are different, Charles says, but the mindset is the same. “You’re going to have your challenging days, and understanding that allows you to reset and say, ‘Righto mate, today is today, what are you going to with it?’ ” Watch the full interview between Nathan Charles and Justin Harrison on Stan Sport. To contribute to the GoFundMe for Charles, click here.

World.title: US forces have finally quit Iraq. What happens now?
World.content:
Analysis WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US forces have finally quit Iraq. What happens now? Mustafa Salim and Alex Horton October 1, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Baghdad: US military forces pulled out of Iraq on Wednesday following two decades of American involvement that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Iraqi civilians and thousands of US troops, and now leaves a battered but increasingly influential Iran at the centre of the region’s future. The withdrawal concludes a Biden administration agreement made in 2024 to zero out US military personnel in Iraq by this year. Recently, there were about 1500 combined US personnel and anti-Islamic State coalition members in Iraq, a US official said, as forces consolidated and departed ahead of the September 30 deadline. That mission will continue in Jordan, from where the Pentagon says it can target militants who pose a threat to US personnel and interests, the official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss military planning. A US Air Force C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft prepares for takeoff from Camp Victory on the outskirts of Baghdad International Airport. AFP The redeployment of US forces has been a muted event in Washington. The 2003 invasion triggered a significant human and financial toll that will be felt for generations. As many as 210,000 Iraqi civilians were killed between the invasion and 2023, along with 4599 US service members, according to figures from Brown University’s Cost of War Project.



Roughly 170,000 US troops were in the country at the height of the war in 2007, when sectarian violence spiralled out of control. President Barack Obama vowed to end the unpopular conflict after he was elected in 2008. He declared an end to combat operations and an eventual pullout in 2011. The Islamic State, born of al-Qaeda militants and other extremists, blitzed across Iraq and Syria in 2014, prompting Obama and an international coalition to re-enter the region in a campaign that lasted into the first Trump administration. The decades of conflict has cost US taxpayers more than $US2.8 trillion ($4 trillion), Brown estimated, including related veterans care and operations in Syria. Iraq emerged from the conflict with the Islamic State with a growing economy and a quasi-democracy that has been tested by religious sects in the government, particularly those with close ties to Tehran.



The US departure has been celebrated as a victory in Iran, which remains in an uneasy ceasefire with the US and Israel following months of war. Iran has long taken advantage of Iraq’s destabilisation, seeding the government with friendly officials and arming militia groups that have expanded Tehran’s influence. Iraqi security officers flash victory signs as they celebrate the complete withdrawal of US troops. AP Photo/Hadi Mizban Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary Speaker, remarked on the US withdrawal last month during a diplomatic visit to Baghdad that included a visit to the site where Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani was killed in a US strike in 2020. “The resistance front is the one prevailing now,” he said at a news conference, referring to cross-border Iranian political and military groups.



The fighters were organised under an umbrella group called the Popular Mobilisation Forces to confront the Islamic State. They are on Iraqi military payrolls but serve as Iranian proxy forces, numbering more than 200,000, analysts have said. They have fielded one-way attack drones and missiles to attack US troops and other adversaries. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump chose to go it alone against Iran. Now he’s learning the value of friends Rodger Shanahan Middle East and security analyst The September 30 departure of US forces was meant to coincide with the disarmament of those Iranian-backed militia groups, which have largely ignored or defied the calls to disband. The timeline for the militias to disarm has been extended to June 2027, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said. Iran might be boosted by the US withdrawal, but its recent behaviour in the region had also created unlikely alliances against Tehran that challenged its power, said Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Centre for Strategic and International Studies think tank. The 2003 operation that toppled Saddam Hussein threw Iraq into chaos, eliminating Tehran’s adversary on its western border, Cancian said. But its targeting of countries that house US troops during the Iran war had pushed some nations such as Saudi Arabia closer to Israel, Cancian said, creating a bulwark that was “unimaginable” decades ago.



“That’s a great help for the United States,” he said, “because we always had difficulty in balancing the Arabs and the Israelis.” US forces in Jordan will focus on Islamic State militants. If the group “metastasises to something beyond [Iraq and Syria’s] control, and they want our help, then we’ll come in and help them,” the US official said. A billboard in downtown Baghdad celebrating the end of the US military presence in Iraq. Getty Images Iranian-allied militias in Iraq have for years targeted Americans in the region, escalating attacks after Israel launched its devastating campaign in Gaza. Three US soldiers were killed in one such attack in Jordan in 2024. “We only went after [Iranian-backed militants] in response to attempted attacks on our people,” the US official said. But overall, contending with those groups would henceforth be an “Iraqi responsibility”.



Iran’s hard-line Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has recently evolved its paramilitary operations in Iraq, which may pose difficulties for Baghdad, according to a senior official in the Iraqi prime minister’s office. Related Article Middle East at war Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech The IRGC had focused its resources in Iraq on smaller cells outside the larger militia networks to evade detection and deterrence, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters. The recent disarmament process has highlighted concerns about splinter groups. The Iraqi official said, for instance, that the Iranian-backed militia group Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq turned over only about half the arsenal it was estimated to have, with its leaders saying the rest had been claimed by defectors who formed a new militia. That new organisation received substantial Iranian support, had co-operated with Houthi allies in Yemen and was involved in recent attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the official said.
