World.title: Can’t afford to buy a house in Tuscany? These TV shows will let you dream about it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most reality shows rely on jeopardy or some kind of life-changing quest. They feature lucky contestants hoping to be recognised for their cooking or singing talents. Or average folk renovating a home or searching for a soulmate. The higher the stakes, the more relatable the challenge, the better. Editor's pick Streaming Netflix’s new Wonka series is bonkers. It was even crazier in real life But a spate of recent shows have upped the ante on a stalwart TV genre: the home renovation. They’ve set their sights on something more ambitious than plumping the cushions or installing the latest must-have kitchen gadget. What if you could up sticks, leave the nine-to-five grind behind and start a new life on the other side of the world? Say, in a hilltop town in Tuscany; in a fairytale-worthy chateau in France; bottling your own wine in Spain; capping off a day on the tools with an Aperol spritz on a beach in Sicily? Producers are always looking for a good hook and a bargain. So when a number of European nations introduced “one Euro schemes” several years ago, TV-makers were quick to see the possibilities. These schemes, which have been flooded with interest, allow non-residents to purchase rundown and abandoned houses in remote villages that are at risk of becoming ghost towns. For a token sum, the houses can be purchased on the condition that they are renovated, to be used by foreigners looking for a life change, a holiday house or the chance to turn a tidy profit when the house is flipped. Admittedly, the appealing proposition masks some sobering facts. Across Europe, traditional villages are dying because of declining birthrates and ageing populations, inheritance laws, poverty, unemployment and industrialisation.



The TV shows these initiatives have spawned don’t make too much mention of this. But as armchair adventures go, they have an irresistible appeal. Shaynna Blaze and Darren Palmer host new series 1 Euro House. Nine 1 Euro House (Nine*, October 6) The Block judges Shaynna Blaze and Darren Palmer are getting their hands dirty. Blaze has purchased a €1 home, sight unseen, in a remote village in Sicily and enlisted Palmer to help make it habitable. Editor's pick Australian TV He respects Hughesy’s ‘passion’, but Peter Helliar is staying on the silly side It begins with a small, abandoned stone terrace in Castronovo, a hilltop village with a population of 2800. With a budget of €210,000 ($342,000), they set to work with an ex-pat British builder (who also appears in Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job). A can-do spirit pervades this show, which doesn’t sugar-coat what’s in store for the intrepid and aspirational €1 renovator and sees the presenters finding thrifty solutions to design and decorating tasks rather than sponsored products. It feels like a fun vacation job for the duo, though their tricks from The Block – such as a room reveal and confected shock when a building problem is uncovered – seem unnecessary.



Amanda Holden and Alan Carr in Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job. Voltage TV Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job (ABC iview), Amanda and Alan’s Greek Job (Binge), Amanda and Alan’s Spanish Job (Binge) British TV personalities Amanda Holden and Alan Carr have spent the past few European summers renovating rundown houses in Spain, Italy (twice) and most recently Greece. Their shows follow a familiar template as they inevitably realise they under-estimated the scope of the tasks they face, call in local trades, explore the local sights and visit compatriots who have made the big move, then eventually congratulate themselves on their achievements. The main selling point of the hugely popular franchise is their easy camaraderie. Their on-screen chemistry is raucous and blue. Despite the dust and racket, Holden always looks like she just stepped out of hair and make-up, while Carr constantly reminds us that he has no practical skills and will never waste the chance for a snarky pun or campy innuendo. It’s naff as hell and forgets at times that it’s actually a renovation show, but that doesn’t seem to bother its legion of fans in the UK and Australia. Australians Banjo Beale and Rohan Christopher star in Banjo and Ro’s Grand Island Hotel. Nine Banjo and Ro’s Grand Island Hotel (9Now) Banjo Beale and Rohan Christopher are a couple of Australians who ended up in Scotland’s remote Hebrides after years of backpacking adventures and travel. In this series, they are turning a dilapidated 27-room mansion with no running water or electricity into a hotel on the tiny island of Ulva. The island has been owned since 2018 by local residents who want to bring life back to the remote backwater, the building overseen by a charitable trust.



This isn’t a cookie-cutter makeover show. Beale, who looks after the decorating side of things while Christopher tends to the tools, has a taste for the esoteric and unconventional. And Ulva, with just 16 residents and accessible only by ferry from the island Mull, is as far off the beaten track as renovation porn has ever travelled. Their show is less an extended ad for the boutique hotel it is destined to become than a portrait of a remote farming community perched at the very edge of the world. When Australians are described as individualists with an adventurous streak, think of Beale and Christopher. Angel and Dick Strawbridge from Escape to the Chateau. Escape to the Chateau (7Plus, 9Now, Binge) This sprawling lifestyle show falls outside €1 schemes, but it nails the escapist fantasy that those other series play with. Dick Strawbridge, an engineer and former lieutenant in the British army, and his flame-haired wife Angel purchased a derelict 45-room chateau in France. In between restoring the magnificent pile (which is partly used as a high-end wedding venue) and raising two children, the couple indulge in their various and many hobbies, from tinkering and practical building to crafting, dressmaking and cookery. Want some unvarnished truth? Try The One Euro House Dream – Italy (ABC iview) This 2024 episode of Foreign Correspondent looks at Italy’s €1 scheme, via a hilltop town in Sicily called Mussomeli. But it presents a far less telegenic vision of la dolce vita than what’s served up in Amanda and Alan. This is a village in decline, where houses are being bought not by cashed-up holiday-homeowners but by people priced out of more expensive European cities and the children of families who moved away. *Nine owns this masthead.

World.title: TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch Paul Kalina October 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

70 Up ★★★★ 70 Up brings to a close one of the most fascinating – and arguably the longest-running – shows in the annals of TV history. It started in 1964 with a group of 14 children from a cross-section of English society in the documentary Seven Up! It was there we met Cockney lad Tony, who at age seven planned to be a jockey; headstrong Jackie, who said she would marry a boy with money; and Symon, the only non-white participant, who was raised in a boy’s home and in reply to a question about his future education replied, “What’s a university?” Every seven years since, director and behind-the-camera interviewer Michael Apted returned to see how these playful children became feisty teenagers, then parents and eventually grandparents; how marriages were made and unmade; how hopes soared and were sometimes extinguished. John, Bruce, Symon, Andrew, Suzy, Jackie, Tony, Sue, Peter, Paul and Neil all return for 70 Up, reportedly the final instalment of this famous documentary series. ITV The original concept was to test the Jesuit adage, “Give me a child until he is seven and I will give you the man” – a window into how class and socioeconomic circumstances determine the chances and opportunities that shape their (and our own) lives. But what it’s mostly remembered for today is the front-row seat it offered to the daily dramas of life and how each of the participants was forged into the person that they became.



Now, here they are as 70-year-olds looking back, but also forwards, in what is touted to be the last instalment of the show. Related Article Review 63 Up's Aussie battler Paul Kligerman on the call he dreads every seven years In the two-part 70 Up, we see where the 13 surviving people have ended up (Lynn, the librarian, died in 2013). For the most part, they’re fulfilled, contented and self-aware – which may be surprising given the challenges some have faced. They are also deeply contemplative and ruminative, not only about how their lives have unfolded but how they’ve been depicted in the films. Directed by Asif Kapadia (Amy, Senna, Diego Maradona), 70 Up is very much about legacy (Apted died in 2021). At stake is not only the personal legacies of the participants, but the legacy of the series itself. Several talk about how the show has turned them into celebrities, and we are poignantly reminded that as seven-year-olds they never really consented to be part of a program that has come to define them. They all return, however, for this last hurrah – even some who opted not to participate in earlier instalments. Their humility and, ultimately, gratitude are truly heartrending.



Sue and Claire reflect on their past selves. SBS/ITV Indeed, 70 Up raises many valid questions about Apted’s agendas and preconceived ideas, such as the sexist questions he put to the female participants, as well as setting up the posh schoolboys to look like undeserving twits. “Sneering and supercilious” is how one of the participants remembers him. Hearing some of Apted’s loaded and insulting questions from earlier chapters is cringe-making. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight That’s one part of the legacy that 70 Up wants to correct. The other is that the series’ focus on outdated notions of class and society meant it wasn’t always asking the right questions. It’s here that 70 Up, its second episode in particular, delivers an emotional punch to the gut. There’s Neil, the sunny daydreamer in Seven Up! who now talks with admirable candour about his lifelong mental health battles. And Symon, who still rues having never met his father, and has gone on to foster more than 100 children. What we take away isn’t the fairness of the cards they were dealt but how they faced the unpredictable twists and turns that life put in their paths. It’s impossible not to be moved by this remarkable endeavour.

World.title: National promises to make trans-Tasman travel easier
World.content:
National wants to progress a more seamless trans-Tasman travel experience.

If re-elected, the party says it will "work with" Australia on a fully digital trial, in time for the next men's T20 World Cup.

It could mean paper passports are no longer required at the gates, with Australian and New Zealand citizens providing their details digitally before departure, and then relying on smartphones, digital credentials, and biometric technology in their journeys through the airports.

National's tourism spokesperson Louise Upston said it is the "next logical step" in the relationship.

"Today's announcement is in the spirit of the long-standing and close relationship between our two countries and will make passage between them as seamless as possible, whilst still maintaining the security and integrity of New Zealand's border."

It would not mean bypassing biosecurity, however, with travellers still having to make declarations and potentially getting their bags inspected.

Upston said National intends to trial it in time for the 2028 ICC Men's T20 World Cup, which is being joint-hosted by Australia and New Zealand.

There have been a few steps to make crossing the ditch easier in recent years. In 2009, SmartGates were brought in for trans-Tasman passengers.

In 2023, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and then-prime minister Chris Hipkins committed to simplifying travel, and established an expert taskforce to explore how to do it.

Tuvalu appoints first woman Governor-General ahead of 48th Independence Day
World.content:
Temukisa Auina Penehuro Hauma, 71, has become the first woman to be appointed the Governor-General of one of the world's smallest nations.

Tuvalu has had 10 substantive governors-general - all of them men - since gaining independence on 1 October 1978.

Hauma, who will be King Charles III's representative for Tuvalu, took the oath of office and oath of allegiance in the capital Funafuti on the eve of the country's 48th Independence Day on Wednesday.

"I look forward to leading the nation and empowering our people, especially the women of Tuvalu," Hauma was quoted as saying Tuvalu Government Media statement.

Hauma is from Vaitupu and Nanumaga and brings more than three decades of experience in education, including 12 years as a headmistress, the statement read.

It said Hauma has served as president of the Tuvalu National Council of Women since 2016 and contributed to important national initiatives, including the review of the Constitution and work towards establishing a Tuvaluan dictionary.

World.title: Wellington City Council, Tiaki Wai prosecuted over Moa Point plant disaster
World.content:
Greater Wellington Regional Council is prosecuting Wellington City Council and Tiaki Wai over the catastrophic failure at Moa Point wastewater treatment plant.

Billions of litres of raw sewage have spilled into the city's south coast since the plant flooded in February.

Wellington City Council says it anticipated the prosecution.

It acknowledges the seriousness of the impact on the environment, residents and businesses on Wellington's south coast.

The council says it's co-operating fully.

Wellington City Council chief executive Matt Prosser. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Greater Wellington said Tiaki Wai and Wellington City Council could face tens of millions in fines if convicted.

In a statement, it said each organisation faced 10 charges related to what it claims are unlawful sewage discharges from the plant.

The charges covered two periods; between October 2025 and January 2026 when the plant's ultraviolet system was being upgraded, and the failure at the plant in early February 2026 and ongoing discharges of sewage connected to it.

Greater Wellington director strategy, policy and regulation Fathima Iftikar said the decision to prosecute followed a detailed investigation into events, the roles of the parties involved and the environmental consequences.

She said it was not taken lightly.

Tiaki Wai chief executive Michael Brewster. RNZ

"As an independent regulator, Greater Wellington is responsible for enforcing compliance with the Resource Management Act (RMA), including compliance with resource consents and the regional plan," Iftikar said.

Each party faced 10 charges, five related to what Greater Wellington said were unlawful discharges, and five for breaches of an abatement notice.

Under the RMA, if convicted Tiaki Wai and Wellington City Council each faced a maximum fine of $10 million per charge, Iftikar said, however that would be up to the court.

"No matter how important the service, or who owns or operates it, the obligation to comply with environmental law remains the same."

Iftikar said Greater Wellington was separately considering if regulatory measures were needed to ensure the plant returned to full compliance.

World.title: Farmers warn Opportunity's land tax has risks
World.content:
Farming groups have been critical of the Opportunity Party's agriculture policies on climate and tax, fearing it will see farmers walk off the land.

The party's proposed an annual tax of 1.75 percent for urban land, and 0.5 percent for rural land to help make land ownership more affordable for future generations and raise funds for its Citizen's Income policy.

However, Federated Farmers meat and wool chair Richard Dawkins said it taxed an asset, which didn't reflect the farm's profitability or farmers' ability to pay.

He saw it as an added cost, and a burden for existing farmers and anyone coming into the industry, too.

"When you consider the profitability of our sector, I mean the average 0.5 percent tax that they've proposed - you're talking about $40,000 for your average sheep and beef farm, $27,000 for dairy.

"Taxes like that, it's not related to income - it's simply related to the value of your land and it would see a lot of people become unprofitable."

Beef and Lamb New Zealand modelled the tax package across more than 500 of its survey farms - using farm values, which include infrastructure like woolsheds and fences that would be excluded under the policy, meaning the overall impact would be slightly lower.

The Opportunity Party's proposed a 0.5 percent annual land value tax for rural land. RNZ/Sally Round

It found some farm types came out ahead once the Citizen's Income of over $19,000 a year for most adults was counted, while others face a sizeable net cost - depending on farm specifics.

Overall, the analysis estimates the land value tax would raise about $395 million from the sheep and beef farm classes assessed, while the Citizen's Income payments to farmers would total about $355m if all farms received a couple Citizen's Income.

It estimated the land value tax would add an additional tax of $4500 to $23,655 on top of income tax, depending on whether a single or married couple.

The impacts varied though, with high country farms in the South Island bearing the brunt.

For that class, the estimated land value tax is about $80,100 per farm, while the Citizen's Income for a couple is estimated at $38,800. That leaves a net annual impact of about minus $41,300 per farming couple.

Meanwhile, South Island hill country, North Island hard hill country and South Island finishing-breeding farms also showed negative results, with estimated net impacts ranging from about minus $11,600 to minus $18,500 per farm.

North Island hill country farms showed a small positive impact of about $2200 per farm, while South Island finishing farms showed a larger positive impact of about $12,000 per farm. This was based on the farmer receiving a couple Citizen's Income, and would be negative if only a single income.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Opportunity Party deputy leader and agriculture spokesperson Daniel Eb said there would be exemptions for things like conservation land on farms, as well as years of drought or low commodity prices - something not factored into the industry modelling.

"The land value tax itself is quite neatly balanced with another party policy which is our Breakthrough Economy Policy, which is a generational uplift in our ability to innovate and be productive on the land. That includes things like a 25 percent rebate on any investment that farmers make in new technology.

"Basically our vision is on the most productive parts of your farm we want to see more intensification, more productivity out of those areas; and the least productive parts of your farm, we want to see those go out of production and go into native restoration."

He said it was about starting a conversation for a new tax system to replace one that was over 40 years old.

Similarly, he said the party would work with the sector on proposed policies to reduce emissions. It wanted to back farmers to cut their emissions through technology, and wants to explore a "cap-and-trade market or levy structure" to reduce biogenic methane emissions.

It's set a methane reduction target of 35 to 47 percent below 2017 levels by 2050 - in line with the Climate Change Commission's recommendation.

It's also proposing changes to the existing emissions trading scheme (ETS), to prioritise cutting emissions at their source rather than offsetting them through forestry.

Dawkins said it was disappointing to see a return to "blunt instruments" being used to address agricultural emissions.

He said the proposal went beyond the scrapped He Waka Eke Noa targets, which he said would have forced about 20 percent of sheep and beef farmers and 5 percent of dairy farmers out of the industry.

"Pricing agricultural emissions, it really saw the industry to one of its lowest points in terms of morale and that coincided with a real challenge around profitability at that time as well.

"We're not going back, we're not retracing those footsteps. There's far more effective ways of making progress together than simple taxation."

The Party's also proposed exploring means to price agricultural emissions. RNZ / Alexander Robertson

Dawkins said the Climate Change Commission found New Zealand was projected to reduce biogenic methane by almost 8 percent by 2030 - missing the statutory 10 percent reduction target.

However, he said emissions reductions through land use change, improved genetics and pastures, and other tools being developed by AgriZero will help close the gap.

Eb said targets shouldn't be set by politicians, but by experts like the Climate Change Commission. He said the policy aimed to accelerate adoption of the technologies being developed by the likes of AgriZero.

"We believe that technology and innovation is gonna get us part of the way there, but often when it comes to these kinds of problems it's not just about the what or the how.

"Like the tech, it's also about adoption and the pace at which farmers jump into these technologies, start experimenting with them and making them work within their systems.

"And without something like a cap and trade there's no incentive for those leading farmers to grab that technology ... and there's equally no disincentive for those later followers to actually move along."

EcoPond is one of several new technologies being developed to reduce methane emissions. Supplied / Fonterra

Beef and Lamb supported the Opportunity Party's proposals to restrict pine trees in the ETS, reward farmers for on-farm sequestration and biodiversity, support trade, and increase investment for research and development.

Meanwhile Greenpeace has largely welcomed the party's climate policy and its promise to cut agricultural methane.

Nearly half of New Zealand's total emissions come from agricultural methane.

Last year the government lowered its 2050 methane reduction target from 24 to 47 percent to 14 to 24 percent below the 2017 levels, and ruled out any future methane tax.

World.title: Heartland shareholders vote to proceed with $620m TSB takeover
World.content:
Heartland Group Holdings shareholders have given the go-ahead to the $620 million takeover and merger of its Heartland Bank with TSB.

Shareholders voted on the proposed TSB merger at a special meeting yesterday, with 94.8 percent of the votes cast in favour.

Heartland Group Holdings is the parent of the Heartland Bank.

CEO Andrew Dixson said Heartland shareholders' approval reflected confidence in Heartland's ability to deliver the merger successfully.

"Yesterday's approval is a strong endorsement from our shareholders of the strategic rationale for this transaction and the long-term value it is expected to create."

It would create a stronger bank, Dixson said.

"It marks an important milestone towards bringing together two complementary banks to create a larger, more competitive New Zealand bank, with greater capacity to invest in future growth."

The Heartland Group shareholders' approval follows a vote in favour of the merger by TSB's shareholder, the Toi Foundation, in August.

Dixson stressed that Heartland would keep up TSB's strong connection and longstanding commitment to Taranaki.

"Subject to the remaining conditions being satisfied and the Proposed Transaction completing, Taranaki would remain a key operational hub for customer banking services, including through its local branch network and customer-facing roles."

He said the merged bank would also retain Heartland Bank's existing nationwide network, creating a national bank with a clear regional commitment.

Last week, the Reserve Bank announced it had requested an independent report into TSB, after the Taranaki-based bank reported issues concerning its capital and liquidity ratios.

Consultancy firm Deloitte was appointed to carry out the independent report, with the findings due in November.

World.title: Veteran sports journalist Phil Gifford dies, aged 79
World.content:
Veteran sports journalist Phil Gifford has reportedly died, ending a varied career that spanned more than half a century.

The New Zealand Herald reported Gifford died in Auckland on Tuesday and is survived by his wife Jan and four children.

As a teenager, Gifford took up a journalism cadetship at The New Zealand Herald in 1965 and emerged as an accomplished writer.

He rose to further prominence in the early 1970s by creating the satirical rugby character "Loosehead Len", who offered anti-establishment commentary on the sport and its culture.

Phil Gifford and Graham Henry. Men’s Health Trust New Zealand (You) Charity Dinner and Auction with The Blues Super Rugby Team at Eden Park in 2012. Andrew Cornaga

As an author he wrote more than 25 books, mostly sport-related, and often focused on his primary interest of rugby.

Blessed with a laconic turn of phrase and insightful wisdom, he was twice named New Zealand sportswriter of the year, and three times won the sports columnist prize.

He covered numerous rugby internationals and Olympic and Commonwealth Games and developed into a quality broadcaster, both in the sporting sphere and, latterly, as a general talkback host.

World.title: Multi-viral RATs in GPs cut unnecessary antibiotics and hospital referrals, study finds
World.content:
Audio player for " Study examines impact of RATs on winter illness treatment " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1667568%2Fmulti-viral-rats-in-gps-cut-unnecessary-antibiotics-and-hospital-referrals-study-finds

Study examines impact of RATs on winter illness treatment Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Multi-viral rapid antigen tests (RATs) at GPs could cut unnecessary antibiotics and, in some cases, avoid hospital referrals, according to a new study.

Researchers were investigating the impact of administrating the tests to detect not only Covid-19, but Influenza A and B and RSV as well.

Otago University professor and co-author of the study, Maria Stubbe said they trialled the single-swab tests at five different GPs, including an after-hours practice in Wellington, and before the tests were publicly available through pharmacies.

They were very popular with both the health professionals and with the patients that were part of that pilot, she said.

"We did about 1700 swabs, so it was a small-scale study in that regard, but the doctors and nurses said that having these results right there and then, in the moment with the patients in front of them, made it less likely that they'd need to order further tests or procedures like x-rays and blood tests, in some cases avoiding referrals to hospital.

"It's reduced their prescription of antibiotics because if you have a virus, antibiotic isn't going to work for that.

"That was really positive because there's always attempts in our healthcare system to reduce the unnecessary use of antibiotics because we have some rising antibiotic resistance."

Stubbe said patients liked knowing what they had and it made them feel quite empowered in terms of dealing with the illness and knowing what they could do to avoid transmitting it to others.

"I think we've seen this year just how important that is if we can avoid transmitting influenza and it just slams the EDs and the primary care practices.

"Anything that we can do that's essentially not that expensive or difficult to do would be a really huge benefit both to the health of people and their households, but also reducing the burden on our rather overstretched health system in the winter months."

Stubbe said people were now able to walk into any pharmacy and buy a test, which typically cost around $10.

For some, particularly entire households who wanted to test themselves, the costs could mount quickly.

GPs weren't funded to provide them, and often needed to pass the cost onto the patients, Stubbe said.

People underestimated the harms of the flu, and the tests could help combat that.

"It's just an opportunity to make a real difference to the transmission of flu, and flu is a really serious illness. I think people underestimate it," Stubbe said.

"Covid hit the headlines for a couple of years there, but flu regularly kills four, five, six hundred people a year in New Zealand.

"So, it's a good target to go for to reduce that."

World.title: The AFLW is speeding up and these numbers prove it
World.content:
Ask a regular punter down the street what they think of AFLW and there's a good chance you'll get some version of "it's improving every year".

While this is not intended to be dismissive of those pioneers who helped lay the groundwork for the league a decade later, there is clear evidence that games are faster, more competitive, and more entertaining than ever.

And yes, there are teams still dwelling down the bottom, struggling to grow alongside the rest of the competition, but there is increasing pressure on those clubs to make adjustments in order to catch up.

The numbers are stark. Average scores are the highest they've ever been as metrics across the competition indicate increasing strategic control, and a growing desire to move the ball to attack, rather than focus wholly on defending the opposition.

Over the opening seven rounds of the 2026 season, teams are kicking an average of 45.6 points per game. This is an increase of 4.6 points compared to the previous all-time high of 41.1 points struck last year.

Of the 18 clubs, only four have failed to average a higher score in 2026 compared to 2025: Brisbane (-9.8 points per game), North Melbourne (-5.2), Port Adelaide (-18.5), and St Kilda (-7.2).

In line with this, inside 50s (avg. 35.1) and shots on goal (avg. 15.4) are at an all-time high, as are goal assists (avg. 4.2), all suggesting greater nuance in the attacking style employed by clubs.

Scoring is ultimately the end product of the way sides are moving the ball down the ground. Early days of AFLW were stoppage and tackle-heavy, keeping things caught in a rolling maul for extended periods of time.

But as we've seen fitness, skill, and strategy develop, the capacity to move the ball on the outside has become a weapon for a host of sides.

Rule changes last year — specifically, the adjudication of holding the ball — forced stoppages down from an average of 67 per game in 2024, to 44 in 2025.

That number has dropped again by 2.9 per game, which is another indicator of that desire to spread away from contest and use the ball in a more productive way.

Fewer sides are relying on resetting the ground via a stoppage in order to regain control.

Fremantle has been the clearest proponent of this shift. In 2025 it was caught out, relying heavily on a contested possession game, the late news that the holding the ball interpretation had been changed throwing the club out of sorts. No longer could heavy contest be the solution, and adjusting on the run was tough work.

This year, the Dockers have moved away from that contested game, averaging a positive uncontested possession differential for the first time in their 11-season history, and are reaping the benefits of the shift.

Slick ball movement by hand is now a strength for many AFLW teams. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

It is just one example of increased reliance on outside ball, with uncontested possession at an all-time high of 142.4 per game, up 10.2 on last year's record, while contested possession has marginally dropped. Disposal efficiency has also shot up to a record 63.6 per cent.

Teams are establishing far more control in game with ball in hand and enjoying a greater connection between lines.

Transition the key for improving sides

Clubs have opted to go one of two ways with their ball movement this year. The likes of Richmond, Hawthorn, and Adelaide have leaned into kick-mark football, choosing to control play with systematic build up. Whereas teams like Geelong, Gold Coast, and Carlton have taken the AFLW by storm with aggressive run and carry, moving the ball by hand and at speed.

Both methods have been beneficial in the increase in end-to-end transition throughout the season, with defensive half to inside 50 movement up to 20.6 per cent from 18.6 per cent last year, and defensive 50 to inside 50 movement also up by two per cent. This is combined with effective metres gained rising by 120 per game as well.

There has been AFLW-wide growth in handball metres gained with the average going from 160.7 last year to 224.5 this year, led by the Suns (+197) and Geelong (+130). A shift in Collingwood's game style has also seen it grow in this area (+119) and Carlton (+90) has doubled down on this after making its big move in this area last year.

The rolling mauls that characterised the early years of AFLW are decreasing. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Morgan Hancock)

It's hard to quantify the increased trust teams have in their system and willingness to attack, rather than simply rely on defence. With long kicks down the line marginally down — an indicator of the preference to build the ball up rather than opt for a bail out kick — and the aforementioned uncontested possession and stoppage metrics, there has been a clear move toward system, structure, and attack.

It requires teams to go into matches with faith that their system will do the job, rather than simply planning for how to stymie the opposition's style of play.

So, when that punter says that the AFLW is improving every year, they are correct, but this year more than ever. And the numbers back it up.

World.title: Nathan Cleary has no worlds left to conquer after Dally M win
World.content:
As Nathan Cleary sat on his couch, in between surgeries with his first Dally M medal around his neck on Wednesday night, the secret of his victory was that he didn't need it to prove his greatness.

That has been beyond dispute for some time now. It's very hard to argue otherwise against Cleary's four-straight premierships, five grand final appearances and two Clive Churchill Medals.

He and Cooper Cronk are the only halfbacks this century to win four titles, and he's the only halfback in history, and one of just three players, to win multiple man of the match awards in grand finals.

Dally M live Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has claimed his maiden Dally M Medal, with Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton taking the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.

It's the same in rep football. His record for Australia is perfect, literally — the Kangaroos have won all eight games Cleary's played for them.

Cleary's time with New South Wales hasn't always been as smooth, and before this season it was the last thing his critics could point to because it was the only frontier left he had not totally dominated.

But if those same critics are still holding on, they're the rugby league version of the Japanese soldiers who hid out in the jungle for decades after World War II, refusing to admit the war was lost.

After his play in this year's series, where he became the third player ever — after Cameron Smith and Wally Lewis — to win two man of the match awards in one series en route to masterminding the Blues win in the Lang Park decider and claim his first player of the series award, his play for the Blues is now also beyond rebuke.

If all that wasn't enough, a Dally M wasn't going to make a difference either, even if it is richly deserved and now gives Cleary a complete set of all the major individual awards the NRL has to offer; at 28, he has no worlds left to conquer.

Cleary's record of success is astounding. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Cleary's 29 try assists this season marked a new career high as were his 14 line breaks, way up from his prior best of nine.

His 62 tackle busts were also his best-ever mark, and he led the league in goal-kicking percentage among full-time kickers while all the other heralds of his game — the boot that alternates between booming and clever, the roughneck physicality and on-field generalship — were constantly at the fore as Penrith stormed to the minor premiership.

When a player has been as good at club level for as long as Cleary has, it can be hard for individual seasons to stand out, but there's a reason nobody dared predict that anyone but him would take the medal home on Wednesday night.

Cleary was the runaway favourite to win the Dally M medal almost all season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Simply put, it's been the best year of his NRL career, and given he's been counted as one of the best players in the league for more than half a decade now, that's really saying something.

That first year he proved himself worthy of such a title also marked the closest he'd come to the Dally M before.

Back in 2020, when he and Penrith were first ascending via a regular season of 19 wins and one loss, Cleary was the hot favourite to win the medal but finished third behind Clint Gutherson and winner Jack Wighton.

Wighton won the award with Canberra's penultimate game of the season, where he earned three votes in a 26-14 win over the Warriors.

Blues write a new fate in blood Against all odds and with most of their state doubting them, Laurie Daley's New South Wales side has pulled off one of the greatest wins in Blues history.

Wighton set up a try but did little else of note besides being sin-binned. Elliott Whitehead, who was forced to play in the halves when Canberra halfback George Williams was sidelined due to an HIA and Wighton was in the bin, was the clear choice for best on ground but only received two votes.

Likewise, Gutherson was awarded two points in Parramatta's Round 1 over Canterbury, an 8-2 struggle where he did not score a try, set one up or make a line break.

He worked hard, running for over 200 metres, but in a game of such fine margins it would have been easy for the vote to go another way.

The details of forgotten Raiders and Eels wins from years past — the Parramatta match was so long ago it still had two referees and predates the set restart rule — seemingly have little to do with Nathan Cleary's story, but this is how the Dally M's work.

The six types of Dally M winners This week is the final round for NRL players to accumulate Dally M votes. Here are the six types of stars who can win the award.

The 3-2-1 voting system invites inconsistency, especially since an extra judge was appointed for each game and, given that said judges are anonymous, accountability is impossible.

One bad decision from one voter, just once, can decide the award and dictate how we talk about a player's legacy and place in history.

The flip side is a player doesn't need a Dally M to be considered an all-time great. Darren Lockyer, Brad Fittler, Allan Langer and Benji Marshall all never won one and because it's only been the official player of the year award since 1998, Andrew Johns is the only Immortal who's ever won it.

Even before Wednesday night, Cleary could exist in that mighty company and not feel ashamed.

He has achieved as much as any of them and more than some, and can match accolades with any player of modern times, including Johnathan Thurston (who won four Dally M's) and Johns himself (who won three).

This medal is not a validation or culmination. It is an affirmation, a glittering reminder of a truth we all knew already.

There's a reason Cleary's fitness dominated the talk leading into the preliminary final against Newcastle. There's a reason his every move on the bench was dissected like it was the Zapruder film.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

There's a reason the world seemed to stop when he suffered a compound fracture to his ankle following Phoenix Crossland's hip drop tackle and there's a reason his absence was felt so keenly, first through the final 45 minutes of Penrith's upset loss and right to the Dally M ceremony on Wednesday night.

He has the rugby league world in his hands, and he has for many years now. This era belongs to him more than it does to anybody else.

That was true before he was a Dally M winner and will remain true wherever his career goes next as he returns from his shocking ankle injury.

Where that is and what he does when he gets there remains to be seen.

All that's certain is that now he's ticked this final box: whatever spoils of war come his way are repeats.

There's long been nothing left to prove; now there's nothing new left to win.

The Dally M is one more thing on the pile of gold, a pile so large the medal could be lost amongst the glittering.

World.title: Jai Arrow told 'nothing' about pre-grand final tribute
World.content:
Jai Arrow says he has been told "nothing" about a tribute awaiting him ahead of Sunday's NRL grand final.

It was widely reported today that Arrow would do a lap of Stadium Australia while a selection of Australian musicians perform Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Earlier this year, Arrow retired from the NRL after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).

Speaking to the ABC at this evening's Dally M Awards in Sydney, Arrow said he was unsure of the details of the ceremony.

"[I know] nothing yet, apparently I'm going around … but I don't know anything," Arrow said.

"So it'll be interesting. It won't just be for me, it'll be for everyone fighting MND."

Loading...

Arrow was honoured with the Provan-Summons Medal at the awards night for embodying the spirit of the game, which is measured against the values of respect, honesty, bravery and sportsmanship.

He said the proposed pre-game tribute on Sunday would be an opportunity to continue raising awareness of MND.

"I can use my platform to spread awareness," he said.

Meanwhile, NRL executive chairman Peter V'landys was tight-lipped about the tribute but promised fans they would be "happy and impressed" with the performers selected.

"You'll see, there'll be superstar Australian performers, that's all that we'll say, and everyone will be very happy and impressed with what we've got," he said.

"But it's not about them; it's about Jai, it's about what Jai does; he inspires people.

"We've received a lot of correspondence at the NRL about how his inspiration has made them see their illnesses through."

V'landys also said the league will be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, as well as $1 million to a "fund for underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league".

"If we can lift a lot of other people with Jai's courage and leadership, that's what we're going to do on Sunday night," V'landys said.

The NRL was left without pre-match entertainment for the grand final after talks with Australian artist Tones and I broke down earlier this month.

World.title: Stawell Gift winner suspended for 12 months after positive drug test
World.content:
This year's Stawell Gift men's winner, Olufemi "Femi" Komolafe, has been suspended for 12 months after testing positive for ADHD medication.

The 21-year-old set a new personal best to claim his first major title in April this year, and also claimed the $40,000 prize for placing first in the annual 120-metre handicapped sprint.

Komolafe was given a 5-metre handicap in this year's race, starting behind all but one of his opponents in the final.

But Sports Integrity Australia has handed down a 12-month ban, confirming Komolafe had tested positive for the banned medication.

ADHD medications are banned in sport for their potential performance-enhancing effects, with athletes only able to use them if they have a medical diagnosis and it is part of treatment.

Stawell Gift organisers have not confirmed whether Komolafe will be asked to return his winnings or whether he will be stripped of his title.

The ban comes as Sports Integrity Australia expresses concerns over the prevalence of athletes using ADHD medications without a formal diagnosis.

In July, its chief executive, Sarah Benson, said she was seeing a "significant number" of inadvertent doping violations from high-level Australian athletes using ADHD medication.

Dr Benson said the consequences are severe for athletes found breaching the rules.

"Since these medications could be abused by athletes for performance improvement reasons, the tough reality is that they are banned under the World Anti-Doping Code if the athlete does not have a formal diagnosis," Dr Benson said.

"Under the Code, this is true even if they establish their diagnosis after the positive test, and they face a ban of one to four years."

World.title: Nathan Cleary accepts maiden Dally M Medal from his dad's couch
World.content:
Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has accepted his maiden Dally M Medal from his couch, while Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton took out the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.

After years of being the consensus best player in the men's game, Cleary finally made it official by romping clear in the Dally M count, securing the award with two rounds remaining and ultimately finishing 14 votes clear — 67 to Braydon Trindall's 53.

Trindall made a late push to cause a major upset before injuring his shoulder in round 24, while the rest of the top five — Dylan Edwards, Haumole Olakau'atu and Scott Drinkwater — failed to poll in round 25, when Cleary got a maximum six votes in a 22-14 win over Melbourne.

Having suffered a gruesome compound fracture of his left leg in the Panthers' preliminary final loss on Sunday, Cleary was not at the awards ceremony on Sydney Harbour, instead accepting the award via video message.

"I want to start by saying how grateful I am for everyone's support the past few days," he said from a couch with his injured leg propped up in a cast.

"I can't thank everyone enough for the messages they've sent through."

He thanked his parents, who he has been living with this year while his house has been being renovated.

He credited his Panthers teammates for making him a "10,000 times" better player, while he also paid tribute to girlfriend Mary Fowler, who is currently playing for Manchester City in England.

"It's tough doing the long distance but she always makes me feel supported and loved. That's all I could ever ask for," he said.

Tamika Upton will play for her sixth NRLW premiership on Sunday. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The NRLW count was much closer, with 2022 winner Raecene McGregor pushing Upton to the 11th and final round of the season, but the Broncos gun finished with 31 votes to McGregor's 29.

Upton is preparing to play for her sixth NRLW premiership when the Broncos face the Roosters for a second straight year on Sunday, when the league will honour Jai Arrow after his MND diagnosis earlier this year.

The tribute is set to occur in place of traditional pre-game entertainment after negotiations with Tones and I fell apart.

NRL boss Peter V'landys on Monday promised "surprises" and said on Wednesday night that a number of Australian artists would be part of the tribute, although Arrow said earlier in the night that V'landys had told him "nothing yet".

Look back at every moment of the NRL Awards night in our live blog below.

World.title: Ten years after their lowest ebb, Newcastle are one win from salvation
World.content:
The outpouring of emotion following Newcastle's return to the grand final after 25 years is proof you can't understand how good winning can feel until you've lost a few times.

The Knights know it better than most because in the quarter-century since their glory days they've lost hard and lost plenty.

Before this season there'd been more wooden spoons than finals wins over the past two decades, survived financial turmoil that threatened the club's very existence and persevered through other struggles that proved there's more to life than football, even in Newcastle.

But on the field the times were never harder than ten years ago, when the club won just a single game for the entire 2016 season, the equal fewest victories for a team in the past 60 years.

There's two men left standing from that leanest of winters and while Jacob Saifiti will miss Sunday's grand final through suspension, Dane Gagai has the chance to bury the old pain under a mountain of grand final glory.

Dane Gagai is the only grand final player who appeared in the 2016 season for the Knights. (Getty Images: Ashley Feder )

The 2016 season was the lowest point amid three-straight last-placed finishes, but what Gagai remembers most is the indomitable hope of the faithful, against all odds and good sense.

"The fans still kept turning up. There was still 20,000 people at a game, Knights jerseys on, even after back-to-back spoons," said Gagai.

"To be able to be in this position now and give these fans what they deserve, I couldn't be more proud to be a Newcastle Knight."

It's a similar story for Trent Hodkinson, who captained the Knights that season after arriving from Canterbury as the incumbent New South Wales Origin halfback

"I was excited to get there, I really like that it was a one-team town, seeing how they got behind their team — I wanted to be a part of that," said Hodkinson.

"The first thing that comes to mind is the loyalty from the fans. No matter how tough we were doing it on the field they'd rock up in numbers.

"We were trying our best to win for them, we really were, but we were deep in that rebuilding phase. The times on the field were so tough but the fans got us through it."

Hodkinson joined the Knights from Canterbury as the incumbent New South Wales halfback. (Getty Images: Tony Feder )

Both men are right about the support never wavering given the Knights had higher average crowds that season than three teams who made the finals.

They also, somehow, experienced an overall lift in crowds from the year before and had a higher average attendance than the club did in their 1997 premiership season.

All the players and fans had was their faith, which is just another way of saying they had one another, and few teams have ever needed it more.

Only six of their games were decided by less than one score and they conceded 24 points or more in 19 of their 24 matches.

There were special horrors that would rear their heads up from time to time that made the campaign seem like less of a bad season and more of a divine punishment, like an ironic torture dreamed up in the sick mind of a wicked and vengeful God.

The Newcastle people still showed up in droves for their team. (Getty Images: Ashley Feder )

Their sole win came in Round 6 against Wests Tigers, when a fan threw a ball on the field and prop Korbin Sims toed it through to force an error from Tigers winger Jordan Rankin as he tried to field a bomb.

The Knights scored from the ensuing set to claim an 18-16 victory but the next month was a taste of hell, as if they were being tormented for their one day of good fortune, for daring to have one happy day.

They lost their next four games by a combined margin of 179-10 and were kept scoreless three times.

The final match, a 62-0 loss at home to Cronulla, was the second heaviest defeat in club history.

Gagai played despite his grandmother passing on the morning of the match and broke down in tears in Sims's arms afterwards after he was racially abused by a member of the crowd.

Tariq Sims, who began the season as one of the club's co-captains, left on a mid-season transfer to St George Illawarra a few weeks later and Jarrod Mullen, the club's most experienced player, had his NRL career end months later after testing positive to steroids.

Newcastle couldn't find a win to save themselves in 2016. (Getty Images: Matt Blyth )

There were some days that were closer than others, but only close enough to make it sting all the more and show there can be no true despair without a little piece of hope.

Newcastle took Canberra, who finished the regular season second and ended up in the preliminary final, to extra time twice. They did manage, as a squad, to outscore Raiders centre Jarrod Croker, who finished as that year's top point-scorer but given it was 306 to 296 it was a close run thing.

In their last game of the season, when a win might have meant most of all, the Knights conceded a last-second penalty to lose to St George Illawarra and confirm their status as one-win wonders.

There was talent enough on the Knights roster to be competitive — Gagai was a Queensland regular by that point and won the club's player of the year award, his first taste of being a stand-out soldier for a hopeless cause.

"Back then he was exactly like he is now — a true competitor who worked his backside off at training and always tried to help the young guys through," said Hodkinson.

It was a season of constant sorrow for the Knights. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan )

"He'd try so hard, he'd do whatever it took to try and get a win for the team and the town."

Gagai and Hodkinson were just two of 12 players on the roster who would play Origin or for Australia or New Zealand at some point in their careers.

But none of the timelines matched up. Some of them were too young — Mitch Barnett and the Saifiti twins were in their first year of first grade.

Others were too old — Kade Snowden, Jeremy Smith and Mullen were all in the final year of their NRL careers and under coach Nathan Brown the mix was never right.

"The new guys, they were up for it, they were next in line, but they were just young," Hodkinson said.

No end in sight for ageless wonder Gagai He has already played more NRL matches than any other outside back in the history of rugby league but ahead of yet another finals campaign Dane Gagai is certain there are still great days to come.

"They did everything they could and I feel for a few of them but some of them have gone on to great careers — Josh King down at Melbourne, Jack Cogger is going great at Penrith, both Saifiti's turned into great players.

"But when you have more youth than experience it makes it hard, especially when the roster and combinations keep changing."

Given the team was unable to give back to the community in glory, Hodkinson worked hard to find other ways to repay the love that meant so much.

His work in the community with ill children, including escorting 15-year old Hannah Rye to her high-school formal while she had terminal cancer in 2017, served as a constant reminder that rugby league could be bigger than winning and losing.

"That made some tough times on the field a lot easier, it put things in perspective when you know kids out there are doing it much, much tougher than anyone who's playing football for a living," said Hodkinson.

"The fans and the club were so great to me. In a tough time they were such a positive part of my life.

"Me and my wife still speak about it now, because we loved Newcastle, we loved the people. Off the field, we wouldn't change a thing."

It's been a winding way back for the Knights, who went to the finals and back to last place over the course of the next ten years.

Gagai is so close to the ultimate reward for his years of loyal service. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Hodkinson was released at the end of 2017, just before Kalyn Ponga arrived and the long march to Sunday began.

Saifiti is the only player on the roster who's been there all the way after Gagai eventually left for South Sydney at the end of 2017 in search of winning football.

His return four years later to the club he'll always call home was that of a prodigal son and a premiership would be a reward he's earned a thousand times over, just like it would be for the fans who were with the team during those darkest days.

Ten years after one win was all they had, one more win can mean everything and would prove that true salvation comes to they who can suffer the most without losing the faith.

"I want it. I want it bad. But that's the end product of what needs to be done," said Gagai.

"A lot of people have been putting us as the underdog. But we've never done that, we've had that belief throughout the whole year.

"To be able to come back and play in a grand final here, I couldn't be more proud to be a Novocastrian."

World.title: Neale set to join Magpies as Lions confirm exit
World.content:
Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it was confirmed the three-time premiership player is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Neale's departure was no secret, as he revealed he was going to miss the Lions "very much" when speaking immediately after Saturday's AFL grand final at the MCG.

This morning, the Lions confirmed the 33-year-old would leave the club as an unrestricted free agent.

"Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons," Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said in a club statement.

"We understand Lachie's reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career."

Lions break Dockers' hearts The Brisbane Lions launch an incredible fightback late in the grand final to edge Fremantle by seven points and win a third consecutive premiership.

The Lions said they would "further celebrate and recognise Neale's contribution to the club in the coming days".

The Magpies did not waste time announcing Neale's intention to move south.

"Three-time premiership player and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has decided to exercise his free agency rights with a move to Collingwood," a Magpies statement read.

"The club looks forward to welcoming him … when the AFL trade and free agency period commences on Friday."

The AFL is expected to confirm the suitable free agency compensation the Lions will receive during the trade and free agency period.

Speaking after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with a remarkable seven-point win over Fremantle in the grand final, Neale said he owed the club a lot.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in," Neale said on Saturday.

"I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life."

Neale moved to the Lions from the Dockers at the end of the 2018 season.

He won his two Brownlow Medals (2020 and 2023) while playing 186 senior matches for the Lions.

Neale, a four-time All-Australian selection, played 135 matches for the Dockers between 2012-18.

World.title: Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
World.content:
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.

Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.

A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.

He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.

Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.

Tupou has been making his mark in grand finals for more than a decade. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.

"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.

"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."

That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.

But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.

His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.

In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.

In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.

It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.

"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.

"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.

"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."

It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.

Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.

This Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026 Fresh off another act of blunt-force artistry, there can be no doubt that Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte has been the best forward in the NRL in 2026.

But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.

None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.

"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.

"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

Tech.title: Neon sticks it to A24 by announcing a Creative Commons SCP Foundation movie
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A24 pissed off one of the internet’s largest horror communities when it announced it was working on an SCP Foundation film, but apparently hadn’t bothered to contact the SCP Wiki team, nor did it commit to releasing it under a Creative Commons license as required. Seeing an easy PR win, Neon is cashing in by announcing it’s making its own SCP movie. But unlike A24, it proactively reached out to the SCP Foundation Wiki team and has pledged to release it under the Creative Commons ShareAlike (CC BY-SA) license.

This is not an “official” SCP film. None of the wiki’s staff is involved in the writing or production, it is not receiving compensation, and the team’s official position is not to endorse such projects.

Other than the licensing details, there is almost no information about the upcoming film. Neon says it will be released theatrically in 2027, suggesting that this will be a quick turnaround, potentially low-budget affair. That’s not shocking considering the challenges of making a profit on a film made under a ShareAlike license.

In a statement, the SCP Foundation Wiki admin team said that, “The staff of the SCP Foundation Wiki and our community appreciate NEON’s excellent communication and commitment to following the requirements of our license as well as the spirit of collaboration at the core of the SCP Foundation project.“

Tech.title: Google announces Gemini 4 and says it’s so capable that only ‘trusted cyber defenders’ can have it right now
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google today revealed its next AI frontier model, which it’s calling Gemini 4 Argon. The new model delivers “frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense,” according to chief AI architect and Google DeepMind SVP Koray Kavukcuoglu. But the company is limiting access at first to a “set of trusted cyber defenders,” and Kavukcuoglu says that Google is “actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access while we gradually expand access.”

Kavukcuoglu says Gemini 4 Argon is already powering Google’s “internal workflows,” highlighting how the model has helped with tasks like large-scale codebase migrations. Google also shared a big chart showing many benchmarks where Gemini 4 fares better than competing models from OpenAI and Anthropic. (The AI community was buzzing earlier this week on X over what appeared to be leaked benchmarks for the new model.) Google will be strengthening “critical frontier safeguards” before a broader rollout, including defending against misuse and prompt injection attacks and monitoring for misalignment.

The launch of Gemini 4 Argon comes just a day after OpenAI’s splashy DevDay conference, where OpenAI launched its Dots AI agent and GPT-6.1 Sol AI model. (OpenAI also said this week that it wouldn’t be releasing a planned GPT-6.1 Astra model due to worries about safety.) It’s also arriving soon after Kavukcuoglu’s appointment as the new boss of DeepMind in August.

Tech.title: The AI Tamagotchis are coming
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

While AI has made plenty of inroads on people’s phones and computers, it’s largely failed in dedicated devices. But over the next year, two major AI companies, Meta and OpenAI, will attempt to change that. And they’re apparently betting on a similar path: testing appetites for physical hardware with their cutesy software agents.

“Hardware is hard” is a tech industry mantra. Dedicated AI devices like the Friend and Humane AI Pin have inspired mainly frustration and backlash, which may only worsen as public anger toward AI grows. Meta and OpenAI, however, are both pushing ahead. OpenAI is working with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive and plans to ship no earlier than February 2027, per a public filing. Meta aims to launch a pendant-like device sooner, before this year’s holiday shopping season.

While OpenAI’s hardware didn’t make an appearance at this year’s DevDay, the company debuted a major new AI agent platform called Dots, complete with personalizable colored blobs with eyes. During a Q&A with reporters after the keynote, when asked whether Dots would make their way into a future physical hardware device, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman replied that that “seems like a very reasonable thing to assume we may do someday,” declining to offer further details.

Meta, meanwhile, is more directly tying its hardware to the recently released Muse agent. Compared by CEO Mark Zuckerberg to a keychain, the device is called the Muse Charm, and it bears a screen featuring its cuddly-looking Muse AI agent, giving it the air of a Tamagotchi. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” Zuckerberg said onstage. “So, if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.”

Both OpenAI and Meta have likely learned from other companies’ failed hardware rollouts, and their resulting strategy seems to be soft-launching AI agents before hard-launching the hardware. Their solution for hacking the hardware problem is to prime the market by getting people used to AI agents, hoping people will spread the word that “yes, they really work now.” Once people find value in — and even get attached to — the cutesy agents, they might want them in a more physical form. Other companies, like Friend, have taken similar software-first strategies, but Friend was positioned mainly as a companion chatbot, not a productivity tool.

When asked during the DevDay press Q&A whether Dots will likely become the primary interface for interacting with ChatGPT, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said the company would be “evolving ChatGPT in place to be this incredible personal assistant very soon” and that he believes that as people are able to reach their AI agents via email, text, or phone call, the point of interaction is “all going to blur at some point.” It’ll be a “natural part of your life,” Sottiaux said.

Altman is banking on the fact that Dots will be more useful for long-term tasks than previous iterations of agents on the market have been. “This feels like an always-on helper, collaborator … that you can give very large pieces of work to and it gets to know you and helps proactively over time,” he said during the Tuesday press Q&A.

Both companies’ main bet is that, after years of less-than-impressive AI agents, they can finally deliver a useful everyday tool that will break through to a broader public market. But after Muse’s concerning exploits in Facebook Marketplace, and a Dots voice demo that went awry at DevDay, there’s apparently still some work to do.

Tech.title: Reddit says it has to cut back access to ‘Old Reddit’ because of AI bots
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Reddit is further limiting who can use the “Old Reddit” experience as part of its efforts to combat scraping and automated traffic. Reddit recently started forcing users to log in to be able to use Old Reddit, but in the “next few months,” the company says that you’ll have to be logged in and have used Old Reddit within the last six months from when the change rolls out to be able to continue browsing the platform with the classic experience.

Reddit says the six-month window covers “the vast majority of all Old Reddit users.” The announcement didn’t go into detail, but it’s clearly aimed at blocking not just new account creation for bots, but also any bots that might access unused or abandoned accounts. As part of the changes, Reddit will stop supporting RSS feeds on November 13th because RSS is “now a common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse,” and suggested replacements like Discord Relay for moderation help.

Reddit:

If you use RSS for feeds outside of a community you moderate, there is no replacement. We know RSS has been a beloved part of the open web for a long time, and we’re grateful to everyone who used it to stay connected to Reddit.

The company has been waging war against unsanctioned access to its data for some time, including blocking the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine to prevent AI scraping, suing Anthropic over alleged unauthorized bot access, and striking deals with Google and OpenAI to use Reddit data for training. Reddit knows that Old Reddit is beloved by many users, and in May 2025, CEO Steve Huffman said the company would “keep it online as long as people are using it.” But this past August, Huffman said that Reddit had gotten to a point where “we need to make some changes” because the experience was being used by “everyone who spams, scrapes, or does anything bad on Reddit.”

In its announcement today, Reddit said that the recent login requirement for Old Reddit “helped reduce scraping and automated abuse” but “still allowed any logged-in account to access Old Reddit, including accounts with no prior Old Reddit use.” Logged-in moderators, however, will still be able to use Old Reddit without a recent usage requirement.

Reddit also shared updates for the previously announced transition moving apps and bots that use Reddit’s public data API to the company’s developer platform. Reddit will begin removing API access for users that haven’t registered their apps by January 12th, 2027, and all remaining public API access “will end in March 2027.”

Tech.title: Amazon’s delivery driver smart glasses will reportedly take photos ‘almost constantly’
Tech.content:
Amazon deliveries could soon come with a new catch: the delivery driver’s smart glasses will be snapping photos of anything they see while they’re in use, including people and private property. Bloomberg reports that the glasses could take “several thousand captures in a single driver’s typical shift,” which Amazon plans to upload to its AI Wellspring platform. When asked if customers will be able to opt-out of this, Amazon’s Viraj Chatterjee told Bloomberg, “We haven’t thought about that.”

Chatterjee claimed Amazon’s only using the data from the glasses to “enhance the delivery process,” adding, “The intent has never been stuff like surveillance.” The impact of surveillance tech won’t be new to Amazon’s delivery drivers, who have had AI cameras watching in their vehicles and complained about it failing to register secured seat belts, or forcing them to pull over to take a sip of coffee, or having footage from the cameras leaked online.

Chatterjee also told Bloomberg that Amazon’s systems will blur any people and license plates in the images before they’re passed along for human review. Bloomberg says Amazon confirmed that “images from the smart glasses could be obtained with a warrant,” but wouldn’t specify how long it plans to store the images for. There reportedly won’t be a way for customers to see any images Amazon has of them or their property, or ask Amazon to delete those photos.

The photos from the glasses will reportedly be of a similar quality to the quick pictures delivery drivers snap when they drop off a package. Amazon says it’s planning to put 20,000 more pairs of the glasses in the field by the end of 2027, and drivers wearing them in a pilot program have already made over 275,000 deliveries.

It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to and I was very proud to have that discussion with a number of our colleagues who I think are running great companies.
