Tech.title: Sick of Paying for Slow Unlimited Data? Readers Recommend This Mobile Carrier
Tech.content:
When’s the last time you looked at what you’re paying for in your phone bill? If you’ve had the same carrier for years, you may be used to paying a set amount every month, with a few occasional surprises. Or maybe you have your bill set up for autopay, so it’s set-and-forget. But now’s the time to take a look. Especially when it comes to how much you’re paying for data.

Some activities can suck up your data quickly without realizing it — like streaming video, music and built-in AI features. Switching to an unlimited data plan may mean worrying less about surprise overages and slower speeds in most cases, but not all. I’ll share more on that in a bit.

With the holidays fast approaching, upcoming travel and new smartphone releases, you may be looking for a new carrier that offers a good deal on a new phone, service and unlimited data at fast speeds — all without costing a fortune. But with so many carriers to choose from, which one is really the right one for you?

More from CNET

Is fast unlimited data really that big of a deal?

It is when you’re paying for data with unbearably slow speeds. For example, AT&T offers unlimited plans, but most have a limit on how much high-speed data you get before the rate is reduced. AT&T’s Value 2.0 includes 5GB of high-speed “premium” data, while the Extra 2.0 plan includes 100GB. (All carriers also reserve the right to deprioritize your device or deliver slower speeds in times of network congestion.) It’s also worth keeping in mind that your hotspot data and its speed also vary by plan, which can be another hurdle if you’re working away from home or need to send files quickly.

Readers recommend this mobile carrier for unlimited data

CNET polled readers to get their opinions about their mobile carrier through our People’s Picks community awards program. We asked about their overall satisfaction, pricing and data. When it comes to truly unlimited data, there’s one mobile carrier that readers rate highly.

Visible by Verizon wins CNET readers over for its unlimited data. J. Hazelwood/CNET

CNET readers say Visible by Verizon ranks highest with an average rating of 4.73 out of 5 for unlimited data, and 4.53 out of 5 for overall satisfaction. So I dug in to see what all of the readers’ hype is about.

Visible by Verizon’s plans with unlimited data start at $25 per month, and use Verizon’s 4G LTE and 5G networks. Sometimes, limited-time deals offer even lower rates, like the one I saw: $19 per month for new members who commit to a one-year term on any monthly Visible plan.

It’s worth noting that the unlimited data varies by plan. For example, the Visible plan offers unlimited data using Verizon’s network, but the Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro plans have unlimited premium data and cost $35 and $45 per month, respectively. So even if you have a phone capable of tapping into the fastest 5G speeds, the regular Visible plan doesn’t offer them. Visible also offers a mobile hotspot with unlimited data in each of its plans, but speeds vary by plan. For instance, the Visible Plus Pro’s hotspot speed is three times that of the Visible plan.

Download speeds range from 20 to 148Mbps, and upload speeds are 2 to 15Mbps for the Visible plan, but speeds are much higher for the premium plans (163 to 622Mbps for downloads and 9 to 48Mbps for uploads).

Another unlimited data contender to consider

If you’re looking for another option, CNET readers say US Mobile is a close runner-up. US Mobile’s Premium plans have unlimited data, but there’s a caveat. US Mobile’s Unlimited Starter plan has unlimited high-speed data, but you may not be at the head of the line to access it in congested areas. The Unlimited Premium plan, however, has unlimited priority data, ensuring you’re getting the best speeds all the time. The Unlimited Flex plan is cheaper, but only offers 10GB of high-speed data. US Mobile says it offers speeds of up to 250Mbps using 4G and 5G bands from different towers. Plans start at $16.58 per month.

US Mobile’s high-speed data is unlimited, but speeds may slow down due to network congestion and the network you’re connected to. Unlike most other providers, US Mobile lets you choose which network to use – AT&T’s, T-Mobile’s or Verizon’s – so you can get the best performance in your area. There are three download and upload speed ranges, so I’d recommend looking at US Mobile’s Broadband Facts for a full breakdown.

But overall, readers give US Mobile the highest average rating of 4.65 out of 5 for data speed; however, your download and upload speeds will depend on which cellular network you’re connected to. Comparatively, Visible by Verizon scores 4.23.

Unlimited data may not seem to matter much if you’re usually connected to Wi-Fi you trust, like at home or at your workplace. And if you don’t use cellular often, choosing a plan with a smaller amount of high-speed data could be a good way to save money. But if you’re constantly going over your limited data plan or experiencing slowdowns, it’s worth considering a new carrier to save money without worrying about slow data speeds or overpaying.

Tech.title: The Results Are In: CNET Readers Trust These Mobile Carriers More Than the Major Networks
Tech.content:
If you plan to upgrade your phone during upcoming early holiday sales, now is the time to think about how satisfied you are with your mobile carrier. Switching to a new carrier you may have never considered before could give you the best deals and service for your new phone.

Major network carriers, like AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile, are well known for having plenty of perks and programs, like the Apple Upgrade program that can come in handy if you’re considering the iPhone 18 Pro Max or iPhone Duo. But don’t overlook mobile virtual network operators. Many of them can be more affordable and flexible, while still offering top notch cellular service just like major network carriers.

CNET’s People’s Picks asked readers what they think about their mobile carrier, and they have a few favorites. Surprisingly, readers’ top picks aren’t among the big three major network carriers and may make you think twice about which mobile carrier you trust for cellular service.

More from CNET

CNET’s People’s Picks: Mobile carriers’ overall satisfaction rating

Overall winner: Mint Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

CNET readers chose Mint Mobile as CNET’s People’s Picks overall mobile carrier winner. It has a strong overall satisfaction average rating of 4.68 out of 5.

“Customer satisfaction in general is a fuzzy metric, and Mint Mobile has done an excellent job of reinforcing to its customers that they’ve made the right choice,” said Jeff Carlson, CNET senior editor. “I chalk a lot of that up to its marketing, led by actor and former part-owner Ryan Reynolds, which elevates Mint in a crowded market. But Mint remains affordable and reliable, which solidifies its customers’ choice.”

Value for money

Mint Mobile beats out other MVNOs and major network carriers, giving you the best bang for your buck. It offers flexibility without costing a fortune.

Mint Mobile offers several phone plans depending on your term and data needs. It offers three, six and 12-month plans starting at $15 per month for some plans, but an upfront payment is required. Mint Mobile also offers family plans that let you choose the data amount for each included line at one set price. You’ll also have the option to use your existing phone or buy one through Mint Mobile.

“The position of Mint Mobile and the other MVNOs on this list really shows how much people value simplicity in pricing and features,” said Carlson. “Yes, Mint requires up-front payment to get the best value, but customers can see what that is. They can budget a set amount for the next six months, pay it, and then not worry about fluctuations during that time.”

Carlson also noted that Mint Mobile isn’t trying to load up its plans with features to justify higher costs. It has core features such as 5G coverage and high-speed data, which is what most people are looking for.

Comparatively, major networks struggle in this category. For comparison, Verizon and AT&T are 2.98 and 3.05, respectively. It’s also worth noting that readers are happy with Mint Mobile’s pricing — 90% say their bill has remained consistent over the past year, and 5% say it has decreased.

Cellular data connection

Usually, if your carrier’s cellular data connection isn’t reliable enough, you’ll go looking for a Wi-Fi network. Most CNET readers with Mint Mobile service (70%) give the mobile carrier high ratings for how well they’re able to rely on Mint Mobile’s cellular data without connecting to a Wi-Fi network.

Over half (59%) of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service rarely have that problem, and for some, not at all. Eleven percent of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service say they leave Wi-Fi off entirely because their cellular data is faster.

Carlson said it is surprising that MVNOs, including Mint Mobile, win against major network categories for cellular data connection, but there are many reasons people connect to Wi-Fi instead of relying on their mobile carrier — like downloading files quickly or watching YouTube videos.

Runner-up: Consumer Cellular

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Consumer Cellular wins a few categories in CNET’s People’s Picks, including signal reliability, customer service and the mobile carrier that’s least likely to drop calls. It also comes close to winning in two categories: cellular data connection and unlimited data.

Signal reliability

Consumer Cellular wins in signal reliability, with the highest average rating of 4.60 out of 5. US Mobile and Mint Mobile trail closely behind, with averages of 4.56 and 4.53, respectively.

But that’s not the whole story, because all the MVNOs use the big carriers’ infrastructure – they don’t have their own cell towers. Most are tied to a single carrier, like Mint Mobile, which uses T-Mobile’s network. On its website, Consumer Cellular says, “When you 

If you’re curious about coverage, Consumer Cellular has an interactive map that shows which areas are covered based on your zip code or address. Most areas have 5G or 4G LTE, and Wi-Fi calling is also available.

Least likely to drop calls

If you’re constantly dealing with dropped calls, CNET readers with Consumer Cellular give it high marks compared to other mobile carriers. Most (70%) of Consumer Cellular readers say they rarely or never lose service. Close to 23% experience call drops in rural areas and on road trips — the lowest among mobile carriers. Even fewer experience call drops inside their home. Carlson said that could be because CNET readers with the service are getting the best coverage in their area, which is also why readers have high signal reliability ratings.

Customer service

Consumer Cellular also wins in customer service, with an average rating of 4.72 out of 5, compared to US Mobile’s 4.34. There are two ways to reach Consumer Cellular for assistance: call (888) 345-5509 or use its online chat feature. Consumer Cellular also receives high rankings from CNET readers for its service and fast resolution times. Most say they were able to resolve issues with Consumer Cellular over the phone in fewer than 30 minutes.

T-Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Most popular

T-Mobile is the most popular mobile carrier among CNET readers (29%), followed by Verizon (18%). T-Mobile has several phone plans to choose from, but CNET editors recommend the T-Mobile Essentials Saver 2.0, which starts at $55 per month if you need only one line; the T-Mobile Experience More 2.0 may be ideal if you’re looking to save money from other perks. We like that T-Mobile’s autopay discount qualifies you for a lower price when you use an eligible payment method.

T-Mobile has a few features that make it worth considering if you’re looking for a new mobile carrier. CNET editors say it has a robust 5G network and some money-saving perks, like plan savings with a new line and T-Mobile Tuesdays — the carrier’s weekly appreciation program. And T-Mobile recently unveiled a three-year phone installment plan to make new phones more affordable.

“One advantage T-Mobile has right now is its visibility – customers respond to T-Mobile Tuesdays, its sponsorship of things like a large section of the Formula One Las Vegas Grand Prix and its broad marketing,” said Carlson. “It feels like a place to be, and its mobile plans are well-received. They aren’t the cheapest, but their position here makes me think people are responding to T-Mobile giving them plenty of features for what they’re paying for.”

US Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Data speeds

US Mobile earns a nearly perfect average of 4.65 out of 5 from CNET readers who use it, making it the highest among popular mobile carriers. MVNO competitors Mint Mobile and Consumer Cellular come close to winning this category, with average ratings of 4.63 and 4.48, respectively.

Several factors go into determining data speeds. If you own a phone that’s capable of the highest 5G speeds and you’re in an area that can deliver them, you’ll see the best performance. That could be a device such as an iPhone 17 connected within a pocket of T-Mobile’s 5G Ultra Capacity (its name for 5G millimeter-wave spectrum) signal, which can download files much faster or deliver movies at 4K resolution smoothly.

Like Consumer Cellular, US Mobile isn’t tied to a specific carrier for its infrastructure. It’s able to use the best network available in your area – but US Mobile lets you choose which one to use. For example, if you travel to a location with a stronger network (like an extended vacation or for work), you can switch to that network for a fee. It uses its own names for the networks: Dark Star is AT&T, Light Speed is T-Mobile, and Warp is Verizon.

US Mobile’s ability to leverage the best network in your area likely gives it the edge in this category. US Mobile’s Broadband Facts break down each plan’s data speeds. All three Unlimited plans (Flex, Starter and Premium) have unlimited data, but your download and upload speed will depend on which cellular network you’re connected to. US Mobile’s Dark Star has download speeds up to 389 Mbps, while the Light Speed and Warp networks have download speeds up to 357 Mbps and 702 Mbps, respectively. Upload speeds are much different. Dark Star, Light Speed and Warp have upload speeds up to 33, 32 and 702 Mbps.

Fair pricing

Fair pricing eliminates month-to-month surprises — giving you predictability and peace of mind when paying your bill. That’s why US Mobile also wins for CNET’s Fair Pricing category of People’s Picks, with 98% of US Mobile users saying their bill “remained perfectly consistent” or “actually went down” in the last 12 months. While other mobile carriers reported base monthly prices increasing, US Mobile didn’t report any new fees, perks going away or changes.

US Mobile’s plans start at $25 per month for the Unlimited Starter plan, including taxes and fees, whereas the Unlimited Flex is an annual plan that starts at $17.50 per month, including taxes and fees.

Visible by Verizon

J. Hazelwood/CNET

For unlimited data

Visible by Verizon gets the highest marks from readers who use the mobile service for its no-data-throttling policy. CNET found that 73.3% of Visible by Verizon users say their data is truly unlimited and has never been throttled, whereas 72.9% of readers with Consumer Cellular service say the same. Comparatively, 61% of Verizon postpaid users say the same. You may notice slower internet speeds if you reach your monthly high-speed data limit.

Visible by Verizon offers unlimited data across all three plans, with premium (high-speed) data included on Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro. Customers don’t need to worry about hitting a cap and seeing their speed dropped (though Visible and all carriers reserve the right to slow data if needed). While the Visible plan is listed as the most popular, the Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro plans also offer unlimited data when roaming in Mexico and Canada, but speeds drop after 2GB per day of use.

Google Fi Wireless

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Roaming features

Most (63%) of readers who have Google Fi Wireless are satisfied with its roaming features, the highest among mobile carriers. There are no reports of dissatisfaction or frustration from CNET readers.

CNET’s director of content, Patrick Holland, says Google Fi is one of Google’s best-kept secrets. “Its competitive pricing, international roaming (at no extra charge) and flexible data plans are some of the main reasons that it’s been my carrier of choice for most of the past decade,” said Holland.

Google Fi Wireless has a few standout roaming features among other competitors. International service is available with Google Fi Wireless’ Unlimited Premium and Unlimited Standard plans. The Unlimited Premium plan includes free texts and calls at 20 cents per minute. Some calls to other countries (over 50) are free. Google Fi Wireless also offers 50GB of high-speed data to over 200 destinations, with 256kbps thereafter. Many other providers offer minimal international features.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing laptops survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Methodology

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,198 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken July 1 to July 26, 2026.

Tech.title: Is That Early Holiday Deal or Fake Discount? Our Shopping Expert Chimes In
Tech.content:
It’s hard to believe that the holidays are a couple of months away.

Retailers, like Amazon and Walmart, are just a few of the stores with upcoming early holiday sales to discount popular gifts like tech, kitchen gadgets and toys. But oftentimes, you may wonder whether the sales are really worth it or if retailers are fooling you with fake discounts, inflated original prices and flashy sale badges to make you think you’re getting big savings.

CNET’s latest holiday shopping survey found that US adults are already bracing themselves for frustrations just like that. In fact, 43% are frustrated by fake or misleading discounts, and 35% are worried about inflated baseline costs. So how do you spot a good deal from fake savings and discounts? Here’s how.

More from CNET

Yes, early holiday sales are worth it

James Bricknell, CNET’s managing editor for deals, broke down how some retailers may try to show a deep discount that isn’t quite true — also known as inflating baseline or original prices.

“Often, retailers will not inflate the price per se, but will inflate the recommended retail price to suggest the product sells for more than it does,” said Bricknell. “This makes the discount feel larger, when it may only be 5% or 10% off.”

It’s one of the frustrations that over one-third (35%) of US adults expect when holiday shopping this year, according to CNET’s latest findings. Other shopping pains include deals selling out instantly (39%) and higher prices for outdated tech (33%).

But that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t ignore holiday sales. It could be one way to save on a new device you’re considering, like a laptop or headphones — even if it’s not a deep discount. While some savings may be only 10 or 20%, they could still help shave off some of the cost and avoid paying full price.

But with some retailers adjusting prices to falsify savings, how do you really know you’re getting a deal?

How to spot a good deal during holiday sales

Typically, early holiday sales yield savings on tech but you’ll need to create a plan and do some research before the sales start.

Over the years, CNET has done the work to determine if sales are worth it and shared the best deals on popular tech items. We use several data sources to see when a product is truly on sale, compare the new price with a 90-day average, and share them during big sales, along with expert insight on some of the most popular gadgets to help you shop confidently.

You can take some of the same steps as our deals team by comparing prices across retailers to find the biggest savings.

“Don’t assume the first place you see has the best sale; shop around to make sure the sale price seems legit,” Bricknell said.

If you’re worried about secretly higher prices, Bricknell recommends checking the brand’s official website for the base price. Once you find a good deal, use a price tracker like CamelCamelCamel or Keepa to see historical pricing and determine whether it’s worth buying now or waiting.

Chrome’s Shopping Insights browser extension lets you bookmark a page and track a price. Google says that trackable products are saved to your Shopping list folder by default, too. And now Safari’s Notify Me tool is a built-in tool that can track webpage changes, including price drops. CNET also has a price comparison extension, though it’s probably faster to find what you want through our big roundups of deals during sales.

Bricknell added that if a deal seems too good to be true, it probably is. “A deep discount of 50% or 75% on something that normally costs hundreds is something to be wary of.”

Tech.title: Can Air Purifiers Clear Wildfire Smoke From Your Home? What Our Lab Data Reveals
Tech.content:
On the morning of June 7, 2023, I walked out of my Brooklyn apartment and noticed the skies were hazier than usual, but I chalked it up to a change in weather and headed to work. When I arrived at my Manhattan office that overlooked the Hudson River, though, I knew this was something very different.

On a normal day, I’d have a clear view of New Jersey on the other side of the water, but on this day, it was merely a blur. As I inspected the thick fog, it dawned on me: This wasn’t fog at all. It was smoke from wildfires that were raging in Canada. The air quality monitor on my phone’s weather app confirmed it.

Although there was a thick plume of smoke over the city, I could still see the blue skies peeking through, so I continued to work. But by the end of the day, the sky had turned completely dark with an ominous orange tint. This experience was a first for me, so I was alarmed about having to go back outside to return home, and I wasn’t alone, as people in my office began passing out dust masks. I wasn’t sure if they’d help much, but I took one just in case.

Even in the subway system, the smell of smoke was undeniable. I made it home, took my dog for the shortest walk possible, then immediately went inside, opened my laptop and ordered an air purifier. I’ve had one running ever since.

The view from my office window in the morning, left, and the view from the same window at the end of the workday, right. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

A perfect storm

Although the smoke cleared relatively quickly, and the New York skyline bounced back after two days, not every area is as lucky. Texas and the West Coast are particularly vulnerable to these recurring disasters due to their dry climates and the intensifying effects of climate change. Similarly, the 2023 Canadian wildfires occurred during the country’s driest period since 1980, according to NASA.

Data from the National Interagency Fire Center underscores the increasing threat of wildfires. There were 64,897 wildfires in 2024, a sharp increase compared with 77,850 in 2025. Rising temperatures, reduced rainfall and earlier snowmelt around the world create the ideal setting for wildfires to run rampant.

These types of statistics can feel overwhelming, and while you largely can’t stop a wildfire from happening, you do have control over the air you breathe indoors. To see if air purifiers can make your home’s air safer and cleaner during wildfire season, we tested more than a dozen models to find out.

Key takeaways:

According to our exclusive lab data, air purifiers can help clear smoke from a home, but some do significantly better than others.

After testing 18 air purifiers, the Coway 450 was the best overall in our 2026 tests. It had the best overall average results in our particle-removal test and received an Editors’ Choice award.

The Coway 400S was selected as the best air purifier for wildfire smoke because it cleared T90 fine particles in 39 seconds on high fan, earning it a CNET Lab Test award for that performance.

Best Air Purifiers of 2026 See at CNET

What our testing revealed

To conduct our particle-removal tests at our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, our technicians built a custom smoke chamber to test how quickly an air purifier can remove particulate matter from the air. They created a homemade smoke bomb made from potassium nitrate (KNO3), sucrose (sugar) and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), then placed it in the smoke chamber along with the unit being tested and a particle counter.

This test showcases how well each air purifier works at clearing both coarse and fine particles. When determining which unit is best for wildfire smoke, we paid close attention to the fine-particle result, since, according to AirNow, “approximately 90% of total particle mass emitted from wildfires consists of fine particles.”

Fine particles are also the most detrimental to human health because they are tiny, less than or equal to 2.5 microns, so when they are inhaled, they can embed deep into your lungs and cause numerous health issues.

Our lab data revealed that two Coway air purifiers and one Dreame air purifier especially excelled at clearing fine particles.

The Coway 400S is our top pick for clearing smoke from your home because of its exceptional performance at high fan speed. In our 2026 test, it cleared T90 (the time it took for 90% of particles to be removed) fine particles on high fan in just 39 seconds.

The Coway 450, CNET’s choice for best overall air purifier of 2026, was close to matching the 400S’s performance on high fan, but outperformed it on low fan, taking 1 minute and 53 seconds to remove T90 fine particles.

However, the Dreame Furcatch was the top performer in terms of low fan performance. It cleared T90 fine particles on low fan in 1 minute and 24 seconds, winning a CNET Lab Test award in the process. But it did not perform nearly as well as the Coway options above when set to high fan.

While all three models are great options for different reasons, your choice ultimately depends on how you plan to use the air purifier.

If you need quick bursts at high fan speed in the event of sudden smoke, go with the Coway 400S. If you prefer a unit that does particularly well on low fan and you plan to always keep it on that setting, opt for the Dreame Furcatch. For the most consistent performance at both high and low fan speeds, the Coway 450 is the best option.

In addition to our particle-removal tests, we also tested energy usage and loudness. The Dyson HushJet earned two CNET Lab Test awards for being the quietest and most energy-efficient option on our list.

From left to right, the Dreame Furcatch, the Coway 450 and the Levoit 200S-P, three winners from our 2026 air purifier testing. Zooey Liao/CNET/Coway/Dreame/Levoit

Air purifier use in real life

CNET’s wellness editor, Anna Gragert, has experienced wildfires firsthand. In 2025, California’s Eaton Fire forced her to evacuate her apartment, but luckily, it stopped five miles short of her home.

“Despite taping up our window seams before deciding to evacuate, we returned to an apartment that smelled of smoke, and everything was covered in a thin layer of ash,” Gragert says. “We relied on two air purifiers to filter the air and remove the smoke smell, and wouldn’t have been able to comfortably live in our apartment without them after experiencing a wildfire so close to home.”

While an air purifier won’t protect your home from a wildfire and you should always pay close attention to evacuation orders in your area, it can provide an important line of defense if smoke hits your city so you can breathe easier, both figuratively and literally.

Tech.title: I Visited Lightship’s AE.1 EV Travel Trailer, and Now I Want to Take an Off-the-Grid Road Trip
Tech.content:
I’m approaching the age where I’m supposed to start desiring RV life. I’m not planning to retire anytime soon, but the older I get, the more appealing the idea of abandoning yard work, home repairs and geographic permanence for a life on the open road in a big old house on wheels becomes. My neighbors have an RV they park in the space between our houses, keeping both a permanent location and a home they can travel in; they still have yard work and house repairs, but few complaints.

So it was with some curiosity that I visited a pop-up for Lightship, a Colorado company making EV trailers for RV enthusiasts, outside the flagship Yeti outdoor-recreation store in Austin, Texas. The company’s eye-catching AE.1 trailer was parked and open to the public. (AE.1 refers to Aero-Electric 1.)

The Lightship AE.1 includes lots of modern design touches, like a kitchen area with a two-burner stove, a fridge and freezer, microwave and a hidden compact dishwasher. Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

Lightship staffers handed out brochures, stickers and pins to visitors who climbed into the trailer, some of whom seemed surprised by the sleek, air-conditioned interior. The demo model boasted a cushioned lounge area, appliances including a hideaway dishwasher, microwave, full sink and stovetop, a full bathroom and shower area, and plenty of storage. It can sleep up to six.

More from CNET

The selling point of the highly customizable AE.1, which starts at $157,500, is that it offers a more modern design than most RVs and trailers. It includes thoughtful design touches and an electric-powered motor called TrekDrive that kicks in when in motion to lighten the load on whatever’s pulling the trailer. If it’s an EV truck or SUV, that could significantly extend the range between charges.

Pushing back on decades of RV design

Ben Parker, Lightship’s co-founder and chief commercial officer, worked at Tesla in California as a battery engineer and was inspired while traveling in an RV during the pandemic. Parker started the company with Toby Krauss, another former Tesla employee who worked in finance and product management and serves as Lightship’s CEO.

Parker said there’s a gigantic market of Americans who want to travel in camper RVs, but their options have been limited to a few highly consolidated manufacturers offering unchanging designs. So far, he said, customers interested in Lightship are a mix of EV owners and longtime enthusiasts who want “greater capacity, comfort and independence.”

“Our customers are people who love spending time outdoors and want more freedom in how they travel,” Parker said.

Ben Parker, chief commercial officer and co-founder of Lightship, stands next to the company’s AE.1 EV camper trailer at a pop-up event in Austin, Texas on Sept. 26, 2026. Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

The AE.1’s most notable design feature is that it compresses from a 10-foot-tall Camp Mode with lots of windows and headroom to a Road Mode that lowers the roof to under 7 feet, making the AE.1 more aerodynamic in motion. Most of the trailer’s features, from the lighting to extras like an auto-leveling system and a motorized awning, are controlled by an app. A solar array on the trailer’s roof helps keep power flowing.

If you limit your A/C and power use, the AE.1 can last for about a week off the grid before it needs additional charging, Parker said. The AE.1 has hookups for EV charging as well as the kind of 220-volt hookups found at RV parks. It can hook up to external devices with vehicle-to-load power capabilities.

Some of the more interesting option features include a pull-down bed that attaches to the trailer’s ceiling and a setup for a 4K video projector that can be mounted inside the trailer for viewing on a pull-down screen.

“The demand we’ve seen reflects a broader appetite for innovation in the RV space,” Parker said. “Customers are excited by the idea of an RV that combines modern technology, energy independence and a dramatically improved towing experience in a single product.”

The co-founder said his company wants the buying and using experience of an AE.1 to wow customers enough for Lightship to gain a foothold in a market that’s not very open to newcomers.

“Breaking into any established industry requires earning trust,” he said. “We’ve focused on building a high-quality product that solves real customer pain points and delivering an experience that people can immediately appreciate once they see it and use it for themselves.”

New trailer players

Lightship is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It’s expanding its manufacturing center there to accommodate additional trailer production, as well as production of a carriage-minus-trailer product called PowerSled, which it’s been selling to businesses like movie productions that need a mobile platform with electric power.

Lightship’s mission to disrupt the RV market is not unlike that of another company, Pebble, that has also been making EV trailers in California.

Parker said the main difference between Lightship and Pebble is that Lightship is sourcing more of its materials domestically. Parker estimates that about 75% of the materials used to make an AE.1 are sourced domestically, and all assembly is done in-house.

Pebble, however, is undercutting Lightship on price. Lightship originally planned to offer a lower-priced $125,000 base model without the self-propelled TrekDrive motor. However, the company has since changed its strategy, moving to a single standard base price with a standard 77 kWh battery and various add-on options and upgrades.

Possible retirement plans

For me, a non-RV person, the AE.1 feels design-forward and includes features like a built-in auto-hitch, an auto-leveler, and lots of charging ports and stations, all of which appeal to someone like me who has no idea what they’re doing. The interior feels spacious, but not so much that it makes the exterior look oversized. The ability to shrink down to a smaller size — the AE.1 performs safety checks before compressing to ensure windows aren’t open and nothing will break — brings the wow factor.

It doesn’t take much time in the trailer to imagine traveling in it and using Lightship’s trailer as a mobile workstation (satellite internet service is not included, but it can be hooked up).

The AE.1 isn’t cheap, but it might be worth putting on the retirement wish list. You will still have to wait: the company’s waitlist for delivery is currently about a year long.

Lightship began shipping AE.1 trailers last year and said it expects to produce about 30 over the rest of this year. By sometime in 2027, with its expanded factory floor, it plans to ramp that up to 40 per month.

If you want to check out the AE.1 for yourself, the company maintains showrooms north of Denver and in San Francisco and will host a pop-up event in Las Vegas in late November.
